posts.title: A mark says a machine made it. Who records whose work it learned from?
posts.subtitle: A CLICKNL session in the Dutch Design Week program asks who benefits from generative AI. EU Article 50(2) covers the mark on the output, and a different article covers part of the record of what a model learned from.
posts.seoTitle: AI marks and the missing credit question
posts.description: EU Article 50(2) asks for a mark on AI outputs; Article 53 covers training summaries. A CLICKNL session at Dutch Design Week asks who benefits.

r: A machine-readable mark can tell software that an image came from an AI system. It does not say whose work that system learned from.

That gap is the question I want to follow into a session in the Dutch Design Week program. Design Innovation Sessions | Digital Futures, organized by CLICKNL, takes place on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, from 11:15 to 12:30 at Natlab, Kastanjelaan 500, on Strijp-S in Eindhoven, with a networking lunch afterward. It is held in English, admission is free with registration required, and the listing says it is currently fully booked, with places reopening automatically if someone cancels.

The session sits inside DDW's Digital Futures Mission Day, whose guiding question asks how we can shape digital developments, from artificial intelligence and virtual worlds to platforms and personal experiences.
The DDW listing, the Mission Day page and CLICKNL's own page agree on the date.
The session's theme is "The AI We Choose." Its text asks whether generative AI, which can write, design and create in seconds, is therefore creative, "and who actually benefits."

This essay draws on published pages only: those listings, the text of three EU AI Act articles, two European Commission pages, a US government report on watermarking and provenance, a university news item and a CLICKNL project page. It reports no attendance, no interview and no result of the session. It is educational information, not legal advice.

blocks.x: The law asks for a mark on the output

r: Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act, as the European Commission's AI Act Service Desk publishes it, says that providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content shall ensure that the outputs "are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated."

The same paragraph adds that technical solutions should be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking account of the type of content, the costs and the state of the art. It lists situations where the obligation does not apply, such as systems that perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data.
The paragraph says nothing about training data.

For anyone who retouches rather than generates, the exemption wording matters: the duty does not apply to the extent a system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data. The text I read does not say where the line between retouching and generating falls. The Commission page on the code says it is complemented by guidelines on the scope of the Article 50 obligations, which would be the place to look, and I did not open them.
Timing is now settled in the text I read. The Regulation as a whole applies from August 2, 2026.
Article 111 adds a transition: providers of generative systems placed on the market before August 2, 2026 have until December 2, 2026 to comply with Article 50(2).

That means that on October 21, 2026, the marking duty applies in full to systems placed on the market after August 2, and existing systems have about six more weeks. The Service Desk marks Article 111(4) as an addition made by the Digital Omnibus on AI.
I read these as consolidated texts as at July 27, 2026, and a reader should check for later changes.

The Commission has also published a Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content. Its page says independent experts drew it up in a multi-stakeholder process, that the final code was published after a closing plenary on June 10, 2026, and that about 190 companies and organizations had signed it by the end of July 2026. Adherence is voluntary, and the Commission and the AI Board have confirmed the code is an adequate voluntary tool to demonstrate compliance. The code covers marking and detection for providers and labeling of deepfakes and certain text for deployers.
I did not read the code itself, only the Commission's description.

blocks.x: A mark is a technical object with limits

r: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology published a report in November 2024 on technical approaches to this problem. It separates two families. Watermarks are signals embedded in the content, and metadata is information recorded alongside it.

On the limits, the report is direct. It says metadata is often stripped when content is shared, and that platforms commonly remove some metadata from uploaded files to protect privacy. It says most current watermarking schemes have been found vulnerable to removal. For images, researchers have trained AI systems to strip watermarks without knowing the scheme, and have proven that any scheme that keeps close to the original pixels can be defeated by adding noise and then denoising. For text, watermarks are hard to embed and detect when there are few plausible continuations, and paraphrasing can substantially reduce detection for short texts, though only slightly for texts beyond about 400 words.

The report also describes C2PA, an industry specification for signed metadata that can record an image's origins, edit history and a "chain of provenance," meaning what assets a piece of content was derived from.

That is a record of the content's own history. I found no passage in the report suggesting it records whose work a generative model learned from, and the report's treatment of training data is mostly about filtering harmful material out.
None of this says marking is pointless. It says a mark is a probabilistic aid that can be lost, and the law's own wording (effective "as far as technically feasible") acknowledges that.

blocks.x: A mark records the output, and a credit records the input

r: Think of a museum. A wall label tells you what an object is. A provenance file tells you where it has been and whose hands it passed through. Those are separate records, kept for separate reasons, and nobody mistakes one for the other. That comparison is mine, an analogy and not a legal claim.

Article 50(2) is the wall label. It helps a platform or a viewer recognize synthetic content. A creator who wants to know whether their work was part of what a model learned from needs a different kind of record.

The AI Act does contain one, in a different article. Article 53(1) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, in particular to identify and respect a reservation of rights expressed under Article 4(3) of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive, and to draw up and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, according to a template from the AI Office.

The Commission's explanation of the template shows what that record contains. The public summary has three sections: general information about the model and the types of training content; a list of data sources, covering public and private datasets, scraped data, user data and synthetic data; and information on data processing relevant to copyright, such as the removal of illegal content. For scraped data, the Commission says providers must give the names of crawlers, the period of collection, a description of the content and a list of the top 10 percent of domains scraped (for small and medium-sized companies, the top 5 percent or 1,000, whichever is lower). The Commission says the point is to help rightsholders assess whether the conditions for lawful text and data mining were respected.

The obligation applied from August 2, 2025, models placed on the market before then have until August 2, 2027, and the AI Office can take enforcement action from August 2, 2026, with fines of up to 3 percent of worldwide annual turnover or 15 million euros, whichever is higher.

Put the two records side by side and the gap in my opening sentence changes shape. The second record exists, but at the level of datasets, crawlers and domains. Nothing in the texts I read says that a creator will be able to look up a particular image or a particular piece of work and see whether it was used. Whether a given creator's site falls in a provider's top 10 percent of scraped domains is a matter for the summary itself, and I read no provider's summary. This is my reading of the Commission's description and the Act's text.
I also read nothing in these articles that gives a creator a right to be named or paid. Those questions belong to copyright and contract law, and I did not open them.

blocks.x: The session asks who benefits

r: CLICKNL's text for the session frames a tension. It asks what happens if AI development stays profit-driven, and what it would take for the creative industry to shape its own future instead. It says the session covers topics "from measuring machine creativity to safeguarding human work."

The speakers, as the DDW listing describes them, are Kars Alfrink, a postdoctoral researcher at TU Delft; Monika Kackovic and Ana Oprescu, contributors to the SafeGenAI research project; Daniëlle Arets, a Crown Member of the Council for Culture and Professor of Designing Journalism at Fontys University of Applied Sciences; and Jop Quirindongo, founder of Lowres Creative Studio, Head of Curators at Dutch Digital Design and a member of BNO's Design x AI taskforce. The moderator is Dymphie Braun, a program maker, facilitator and strategist.

I list the roles because they show a session that mixes research, cultural policy, journalism education and design practice. TU Delft's agenda records that Alfrink defended a doctoral thesis on May 23, 2024 titled "Contestable Artificial Intelligence," subtitled constructive design research for public AI systems that are open and responsive to dispute.
That is background on one speaker. I do not know what any of them will say.

blocks.x: SafeGenAI aims at the second record

r: The University of Amsterdam announced on January 28, 2026 that Monika Kackovic, an associate professor at Amsterdam Business School, had received a two-year grant of EUR 727,929, awarded on scientific quality, from the Top Consortium for Knowledge and Innovation for the Creative Industries (CLICKNL). The project, a joint effort with Ana Oprescu, is called "SafeGenAI: Safe Generative AI tools for Creative Industries: current and future practices."

According to the university's announcement, SafeGenAI develops new empirical methods to measure how creative generative AI actually is. By integrating these creativity measures as traceable identifiers into privacy-enhancing technologies, the researchers aim to develop a flexible, "attribution-aware" framework, meaning one aimed at recognizing, tracking and recording who made what, which helps creators protect their work from unauthorized use. With two postdoctoral researchers, the team plans tools that let creators set clear terms of use, follow how content moves through AI-driven processes, and generate evidence such as attribution records and audit trails to support enforcement and responsible reuse. The announcement names five more UvA researchers and five industry partners: the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, the Privacy First Foundation, Cyber Dune, Calango and Storm Post-Productions.

CLICKNL's project page describes the aim more broadly: letting designers, audiovisual creators and cultural institutions work with generative AI without compromising ownership, reputation or income. It lists privacy-enhancing technologies, attribution-aware AI models, a benchmark for measuring creativity and a clickable prototype that lets creators set their rights and see the impact. It also says the tools are co-created based on interviews with creative professionals, and that the project explores new business models and responsible use of generative AI in design education, studios and cultural institutions.
Both pages describe plans. Neither reports results, and neither says the framework will exist, work or be adopted.

blocks.x: What creators say they want

r: A Council of the EU summary of member states' answers to a questionnaire on generative AI and copyright, from December 2024, quotes surveys that member states cited without specifying them. One reported that 93 percent of responding authors held that authors must be able to agree or disagree with the use of their works for AI training, and 97 percent that authors must be remunerated for the input and output. A study by music collecting societies reported that 95 percent of creators and music publishers surveyed were demanding greater transparency from companies developing AI tools. Another study of visual and literary authors reported that 65 percent were opposed to the use of their works for training generative AI, even in exchange for payment.
These figures come from unspecified national surveys, relayed second-hand in a summary, and I give them as an indication of the sentiment that SafeGenAI and the session address, not as a measurement.

The same document notes that several member states saw unclarity over whether the text and data mining exception applies to AI training, and it reports a regional court decision that treated opt-out in natural language as potentially sufficient to meet the requirement for a machine-readable reservation.
I do not know how that ruling sits with later decisions.

blocks.x: Questions a reader can carry to any attribution tool

r: If a tool promises to record who made what, I would ask who holds the record and for how long, who can read it, and what a creator receives if the record shows their work was used. Those are my questions, offered as reasoning. They apply to any attribution scheme, including ones that have not been built.

A record that exists but sits where creators cannot reach it records very little for them. A record that creators can read but cannot act on may still leave them where they started. The NIST report adds a third question: whether the record survives the trip. A mark that disappears when a platform strips the file helps no one.

blocks.x: What we know and what we don't

r: What we know: Article 50(2) requires providers to mark outputs, in the words quoted above, and applies from August 2, 2026, with a transition to December 2, 2026 for systems already on the market. Article 53 requires a copyright policy and a public summary of training content for general-purpose models. The session is listed for October 21, 2026. SafeGenAI is funded, led from the University of Amsterdam and aims at an attribution-aware framework.

What we do not know: what the session will conclude; what SafeGenAI's tools will produce; whether any mark or summary will let a creator trace a specific work; and how companies will comply in practice. I did not read the Code of Practice, any provider's training summary, or any court decision on training data.
The session was fully booked when I last read the listing. CLICKNL's page says the registration form reopens automatically if places are canceled, so it is worth checking again nearer the date.

blocks.x: Before you use an AI image

r: Ask whether it is marked, what the tool learned from, and who gets paid. Then ask the harder one: if the answer to the second question is unknown, who is the person responsible for finding out?

posts.title: Does AI make design more alike? What the studies show before the 5th Design & AI Symposium
posts.subtitle: A fifth Design & AI Symposium takes stock of what AI has done for and to design. The best-known experiment, read in full, says something narrower than its headline, and the design-specific studies point the same direction.
posts.seoTitle: Does AI make design more alike?
posts.description: The 5th Design & AI Symposium takes stock. What Doshi and Hauser, design studies and a 2026 meta-analysis show about AI and sameness.

r: A tool can raise the average quality of a group's work and still shrink the range of that work.

That possibility sits behind the 5th Design & AI Symposium, which is in the Dutch Design Week program on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at Gebouw SFF (Bosch), Torenallee 49, on Strijp-S in Eindhoven. The DDW listing classes it as a seminar with paid registration, gives it the tagline Return on Investment, and says it is organized by design researchers from TU/e, TU Delft and the University of Twente, with Stephan Wensveen, Cristina Zaga, Dave Murray-Rust and Mathias Funk as chairs. It names 4TU.Design United and the Department of Industrial Design at TU/e as sponsors.
Registration goes through Eventbrite, which lists the event as organized by TU Eindhoven Industrial Design and offers refunds up to seven days before.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, the organizers' website, Eventbrite, the earlier editions' pages, and published research. It reports no attendance and no conversation with the organizers, and it cannot say what any speaker will conclude.

I want to use the symposium's own framing, taking stock, to ask what the evidence on AI and sameness actually shows. The headline version is simple, and the full papers are more careful than the headline.

blocks.x: The times differ between two official pages

r: The DDW listing gives the symposium's hours as 09:00 to 12:30 and calls it a one-day seminar.

The organizers' own site describes a full-day event from 9:00 to 18:30 with a breakdown that runs from arrival at 9:00 through lunch at 12:45, a workshop and break-out sessions at 13:45, lightning talks, a panel and network drinks until 18:30.
Eventbrite lists Tuesday, October 20, from 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and a duration of 9 hours 30 minutes.

Two of the three pages agree, and one of them is the organizers' own, so I take the full day as the schedule and read the listing's 12:30 as a mistake or a leftover. I could not confirm which the festival will correct.

blocks.x: What the 2026 program puts on the table

r: The organizers' program is less about measuring a return than the tagline suggests. Maria Luce Lupetti of the Politecnico di Torino speaks on AI counterpublics and everyday acts of gentle resistance. Robert Keus, founder of the AI platform GreenPT, which the program says runs on renewable energy and shows the energy cost of each conversation, is the second speaker. Simone Robutti of the Tech Workers Coalition speaks on the limits of an individual designer's power.
A deep-dive on AI in practice includes a talk by Floris Ketel and Dirk van Alfen asking what becomes the value of design when anyone can create anything.
The afternoon brings a workshop on AI and education, a break-out session on the Dutch AI plan, lightning talks and a panel.
The organizers say they chose speakers and projects that value respect, creative freedom, inclusion and societal purpose beyond hype, efficiency and economic power.

That is a program with a point of view. It is a stock-taking of values and practice as much as of results, and I read the word return in the title as a pointed question about what the sector has gained for what it put in. The listing's own text goes further and speaks of pension money converted into GPUs and data centers. That is the organizers' rhetoric, and I do not rely on it.

blocks.x: The investment behind the word return

r: The break-out session on the AI Delta Plan points at a Dutch policy argument. On November 24, 2025, NL Times reported that more than fifty Dutch experts, writing at the request of the caretaker Minister of Economic Affairs, proposed a national AI Delta Plan modeled on the ambition of the post-1953 Delta Works. Its proposals included a State Secretary for AI, flagship research institutes, expanded AI education and more AI infrastructure. The report puts the country's fastest computer, Snellius, at 640 GPUs, notes a planned 200 million euro AI factory in Groningen with about 2,500 GPUs, and says the experts urged reducing the financial risk for venture capital and pension funds that want to invest in AI.

That gives the listing's line about pension money and GPUs a public context. I read the listing's claim that pension money has already been converted into GPUs and data centers as the organizers' rhetoric, and I did not find a source that quantifies it.
The plan's authors argue from competitiveness and independence from American and Chinese technology.

The symposium's return on investment asks a different question, which is what design has gained or lost. Those two questions can both be right, and the second is the one designers can answer from their own work.

blocks.x: Five years of the same question, asked differently

r: The series has run since 2022, according to the organizers' list of previous events.

The third edition, on October 22 and 23, 2024, was hosted by TU Eindhoven and TU Delft with Design United, took place across two days on the TU/e campus and was reported as sold out, under the theme of embedding the magic and the real. Its registration page listed a regular ticket at 79 euros plus fee.

The fourth, on October 21, 2025, was a full day from 9:00 to 21:30 at Fifth/NRE, with a keynote on measuring how language models respond when users reach out emotionally and another on treating AI as another material.

The organizers describe their stance in 2026 as a productive space for contestation, re-imagination and communal collaboration, between people who find AI inevitable and people who resist reliance on it.

A separate exhibition from the same organizers, Design & AI: Many (Re)Turns, is in the program at the same building and presents three projects about the prompts, artifacts, glitches and messy outputs of designing with AI. Its curatorial text speaks of a turning of outcomes into flat, generic formats and also of turnings toward materiality, craft and taste.
Both ideas, flattening and re-turning toward craft, belong to the stock-taking.

blocks.x: The experiment everyone cites, read in full

r: The best-known piece of evidence on sameness comes from outside design. Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser published an online experiment in Science Advances on July 12, 2024. They recruited writers in the United Kingdom through Prolific and, after exclusions, analyzed 293 stories. Each writer wrote a story of exactly eight sentences on one of three adventure topics. Writers were randomized to write alone, to be allowed one three-sentence story idea generated by GPT-4, or to be allowed up to five.

On the headline, the paper reports that access to AI ideas caused stories to be rated as more novel and more useful by outside evaluators. With one AI idea, novelty rose 5.4 percent and usefulness 3.7 percent. With up to five ideas, novelty rose 8.1 percent and usefulness 9.0 percent.

The next finding is easy to miss: the gain was concentrated in the writers who scored lowest on a creativity test the authors gave them first. For those writers the gains reached about 11 percent in novelty and usefulness, and up to about 27 percent in how well written a story was. Among the most creative writers, the authors report little effect from the AI ideas, and they say they found no evidence that the AI ideas pushed stories past what particularly creative humans could do alone.

So the common shorthand that AI made each writer better overstates the result. In this experiment AI lifted the weaker writers toward the level of the stronger ones and left the strongest about where they were. The authors say this effectively equalizes the creativity scores across writers.
That can look like a win for access, and it is also part of why the stories converged.

On similarity, the authors used text embeddings to measure how close each story sat to the average of the other stories in its group. Stories written with AI ideas sat closer to the group average than stories written alone. In the paper's own scale, the human-only stories spanned a range of about 8 points, and the shift from AI access amounted to 10.7 percent of that range with one idea and 8.9 percent with five. Stories written with AI were also about 5 percent more similar to the AI's idea than human-only stories were to a randomly assigned AI idea, which the authors read as anchoring.

That is a measurable but modest shift, not a collapse of variety. The authors call the pattern a social dilemma, in which writers are individually better off and collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced.
Three more details matter. Writers' own ratings of their stories showed no significant difference between conditions, so the gain was visible to outside readers and not to the writers.
Evaluators who were later told which stories used AI ideas applied an ownership penalty of at least 25 percent, though most still thought the use ethical.
And the authors state the limits plainly: eight sentences, one medium, one prompt, no back-and-forth with the model, and ideas in other media such as images might work differently.

blocks.x: Studies closer to design

r: Three studies come nearer to what designers do, and they are small. In a CHI 2024 study, Samangi Wadinambiarachchi and colleagues asked 60 participants, mostly university students from several fields, to sketch as many chatbot avatar designs as they could in 20 minutes. Participants were randomly placed in a baseline group, an image-search group or a group using the AI image generator Midjourney. The AI group fixated more on an initial example and produced fewer ideas, with less variety and lower originality than the baseline.
The authors say their results describe somewhat naive use of new tools and may change as people learn them.

Barrett Anderson, Jash Shah and Max Kreminski, in a 36-participant study at Creativity and Cognition 2024, compared ChatGPT with another creativity support tool. Different users produced less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT, generated more detailed ideas, and felt less responsible for them.

And Lennart Meincke, Ethan Mollick and Christian Terwiesch, using GPT-4 on a product-ideation task, found that pools of AI-generated ideas were less diverse than those from groups of human subjects, that prompt engineering could improve the diversity, and that chain-of-thought prompting came close to the diversity of human groups.
That last result is a counterweight. It suggests sameness is partly a property of how the tool is used and not only of the tool.

A 2026 meta-analysis puts these together. Alwin de Rooij and Michael Biskjaer, creativity researchers at Tilburg University, Avans University of Applied Sciences and Aarhus University, pooled 19 experiments with 61 effect sizes comparing people working with generative AI to people working alone, and found a statistically significant homogenization effect, strongest in idea-generation tasks. In studies of real-world outputs before and after tools spread, the effect was smaller but still significant, and a small set of studies suggested it could carry over into later tasks. The authors stress that their findings do not show AI reduces creativity. I know this work only through a May 14, 2026 report in PsyPost on their preprint, and I have not read the preprint, so I treat the numbers as reported and not as verified.

A broader review by Zhivar Sourati and colleagues argues that large language models reflect and reinforce dominant styles and risk standardizing language and reasoning when everyone relies on the same models.

Read together, the evidence supports a modest, consistent claim: in short, controlled tasks, AI assistance tends to make outputs across people a little more alike, and the effect is larger when the task is to generate ideas for a defined problem.
It does not show that professional design practice is converging, because no study here observed professional practice over time.

blocks.x: Sameness is not always a flaw

r: My own field, anatomy, depends on standardization. The International Federation of Associations of Anatomists maintains a single international terminology, Terminologia Anatomica, whose second edition was approved and published online, so that one person's description can be read by another.

Sameness there is a feature. That is why I do not treat similarity as a flaw by default. The question for design is which kinds of sameness help the people who use the work, and which kinds quietly remove choices they would have wanted.

The studies cannot tell the two apart, because they measure distance between outputs and not value to a user. A hypothetical makes the point: five designers each use the same assistant to produce first concepts for a public bench, and the concepts converge on a shape that suits most bodies. The set is more alike, and it may also be better. Or the five concepts converge on a shape that suits a typical body and nobody else. The embeddings and the ratings in the studies would score both sets as similar.

blocks.x: Who can see the loss

r: The structure of the finding matters more than its size. An individual designer judges their own work against their own earlier work. By that measure an assistant that improves the draft looks like a pure gain, and in Doshi and Hauser the writers did not even perceive a difference.

The loss of variety is a property of the group, and no single member sees it from inside their own project. That is a reason for gatherings like this one, where researchers from three universities can compare many outputs side by side.

blocks.x: Questions to bring

r: Because I have not read the program's talks beyond their abstracts, I would treat the following as questions for any account of what AI has done to design, including the ones given on October 20.
What counted as a gain, and who rated it? In the writing experiment, outside readers saw the gain and the writers themselves did not.
What was the comparison? A group using AI against a group not using it is stronger evidence than a before-and-after story, and the studies above all used such comparisons.
How was variety measured? Embedding distance, expert ratings and counts of distinct ideas all appear in the studies, and they can disagree.
Who was affected most? The strongest gains went to the weakest starting writers, which is a result about access and not only about sameness.

What was lost, and could it be recovered? Some losses, such as a practice that stopped being taught, are harder to restore than a draft. The program's workshop on AI and education is one place the question could be taken up.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I could not find what the 2026 talks will conclude, or what the ticket costs, since the Eventbrite page I read gave no price and the 2024 price is the only one published.
I do not know which schedule the festival will print for the day.
I have read the Doshi and Hauser paper in full, but the meta-analysis only through a news report, and the other studies through their abstracts and, for the CHI paper, parts of its text.
None of the studies observed professional designers working over months or years. Most used students or online participants and short tasks, and the strongest evidence is about text.
The studies also measure the tools of 2023 and 2024, and tools and habits have moved since. The CHI authors warned of exactly this.
A fifth edition that takes stock after five years of change is well placed to ask whether the pattern still holds, and the evidence I found cannot answer that.

blocks.x: The question to take with you

r: Has AI made your work better, or more like everyone else's, and how would you know?

posts.title: What does making look like when the material is alive?
posts.subtitle: Dutch Design Week lists .Unusual, a Secrid Talent Podium show by Maartje Dros and Eric Klarenbeek built on algae and mycelium. Their record and the museums that hold their work suggest that "alive" describes the making more than the finished object.
posts.seoTitle: When the material is alive: .Unusual at DDW
posts.description: What .Unusual by Klarenbeek and Dros at Dutch Design Week 2026 means by living materials, checked against museums, prizes and research.

r: A chair that once sprouted mushrooms is now, according to the museum that owns it, completely inert. The curator at the Centre Pompidou who says so adds that even the mushroom-like growths on it have stopped, and that the chair was made from living material, the mycelium of a reishi mushroom, which is no longer active.

.Unusual is in the Dutch Design Week program at B4 Klokgebouw, Klokgebouw 50, on Strijp-S in Eindhoven. It is open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, and a DDW ticket is required. The listing's subtitle reads "Living organisms as building blocks for a new production landscape." Maartje Dros and Eric Klarenbeek present it as part of the Secrid Talent Podium 2026. Those are the organizers' details and words.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing in both languages, the studio's own pages, two museum pages, a Paris museum's published collection and teaching material, a prize record, an online museum exhibition, Secrid's announcement and a few outside references. It reports no visit to the show and no conversation with the designers.

I want to take the subtitle seriously, because "living" can mean at least three different things in a workshop, and the answer changes what a visitor should look for. A fungus can be alive while it grows a structure and then be stopped on purpose. A seaweed can be alive in a cultivation system and then be processed into pellets. And a finished object can stay alive, which is the case the sources describe least.

blocks.x: The listing argues that industry is built on sameness

r: The English listing makes its case in four steps. Current manufacturing, it says, relies largely on monocultures: one material, one traditional production process and one way of processing the waste. That pattern comes with high CO2 emissions, unusable residual streams and a loss of biodiversity. The construction sector, the text says, stays especially dependent on extractive materials such as concrete and plastic. Then it turns to the designers, who see nature as something to collaborate with and not as an inexhaustible source of materials. They work with fast-growing microorganisms such as algae and mycelium and test industrial uses for these living raw materials in their workshop and laboratory.

The listing also gives short credentials. Dros and Klarenbeek both graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven and founded .unusual. Dros focuses on sustainable systems and social impact, and Klarenbeek on material innovation and living technologies. The page names Maartje Janse as lead of the Secrid Impact Fund and lists two studio email addresses, which this essay does not reproduce.

The framing matters because it sets the test. The listing does not claim that algae and mycelium are better in every respect. It claims that one-material, one-process manufacturing is a problem and that a different way of making exists. That is a claim a visitor can check against what is on the floor: does the work show more than one material, more than one process and more than one fate for the leftovers?

blocks.x: The two language versions of the listing do not promise quite the same thing

r: The Dutch version of the page carries the same headline claim but not identical words. In English, the short introduction says the designers use biobased materials and 3D printing to develop production methods that help restore, rather than deplete, the Earth and climate. The Dutch text says they develop alternatives to production chains that do not deplete but contribute to a resilient future. The Dutch version also describes Dros as specializing in social-ecological design and sustainable chains, where the English says sustainable systems and social impact.
Secrid's own announcement uses a third phrasing, describing the pair as working with living organisms as new clean raw materials for industry.

None of these is wrong. They are three descriptions of one program entry written for slightly different readers, and a reader who quotes one of them should say which. In this essay the English listing is the reference, and where the Dutch or Secrid wording differs the difference is named.

blocks.x: Concrete and steel are a fair target, but the listing gives no numbers

r: The listing's statement about construction can be checked against a public source. The Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2024/2025, published by the UN Environment Programme with the Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction on March 17, 2025, says the sector consumes 32 percent of global energy and contributes 34 percent of global CO2 emissions. It says the sector depends on materials like cement and steel that are responsible for 18 percent of global emissions and are a major source of construction waste.

That gives the listing's sentence a scale. It also sets a limit on what any single exhibit can show. A show in a former factory hall can present a sample, a panel or a prototype. It cannot show that a grown material replaces cement at the volumes in the UNEP figures, and nothing in the listing says it will try.

blocks.x: "Living" covers three different things

r: The first is the fungus. Mycelium is the thread-like network of a fungus, and the studio says it has used it as a living glue. On its own site it describes a process in which a printer lays down a mixture of local land waste and mycelium, prints the infill and the outer shell together so the fresh mixture holds together, and then places the structure in an incubator to grow and gain strength. Once full-grown and dried, the studio says, the structure becomes stable and renewable and comparable to cork or wood.

The Centre Pompidou's account of the Mycelium Chair, which the museum dates 2018 to 2019, fits that description and adds the stopping point. The museum's teaching page says the chair was built from a 3D-printed structure in which reishi mycelium grew in a mix of water, hemp and sawdust, and that when the fungus had spread enough the structure was dried, leaving a form held together by what the page calls living glue. The collection record lists the materials as Ganoderma mycelium, wood filament, hemp and bioplastic.

A mycologist interviewed in the museum's podcast explains why a dead fungus can still hold a chair together. The cell wall of fungi contains chitin, a sugar polymer that is chemically the same compound as the shell of a crustacean, and once the structure is dried it can last for hundreds or even thousands of years. To stop the growth in general, he says, you heat the filled mold and kill the fungus; the rigid wall remains. The curator adds that the chair today is completely inert, including the mushroom-like growths on it, although it was made from living mycelium.

I find this useful as someone trained in anatomy. In my own field, a specimen is only useful for teaching because someone deliberately stopped its biology, and part of the craft is deciding when. The chair appears to follow the same logic: the living stage is the manufacturing stage. That is an analogy from my field and not a finding from the sources.

The second meaning is the alga. The studio's pages describe a "Seaweed Circle," a local production chain that starts with propagating seaweed embryos and ends with biopolymer pellets, and a material the studio calls Weedware.

The company site for Weedware B.V. describes the end of that chain: a compound of PHA and algae called PHALGAE, grown from North Sea seaweed and compounded in the Netherlands. The same page says about 2 kilograms of cultivated seaweed go into 1 kilogram of the finished compound. Here the organism is alive in the sea farm and the lab, and not in the pellet.

The third meaning is the workshop. The listing's phrase "workshop and laboratory" describes a place where living material is handled, not an object visitors can touch. The Pinakothek der Moderne's page for the studio's Munich show says that exhibition includes an installation section on the field trials and laboratory work, and that visitors find algae pigments in the wall paints, dried Saccharina seaweed hung up in the traditional way and a cream made of salt and algae.
The listing for .Unusual does not say what its own floor will hold.

One more word on the listing's own term. It says "fast-growing microorganisms such as algae and mycelium." The studio's seaweed work is with macroalgae, which are multicellular seaweeds, and its diatom glass work, as the studio describes it, uses single-celled algae. Mycelium is a network of fungal threads. "Microorganisms" is a loose fit for all of them, and the listing does not say which organisms the 2026 work uses.

blocks.x: The studio's record is two decades long, and most of it sits outside the listing

r: The Centre Pompidou's timeline puts the creation of the Klarenbeek & Dros studio in 2004, with research and development projects in urban design for the Dutch ministry responsible for infrastructure and the environment. It records the first 3D printing with mycelium filaments in 2011, the Algae Lab at the Luma foundation in Arles in 2017 and the studio's part in the Pompidou show La Fabrique du vivant in 2019.
The Pinakothek page agrees on the starting point, saying the pair has focused since 2004 on materials that spare the environment and promote biodiversity.
Three public records give outside confirmation of specific steps.

In October 2018, Het Nieuwe Instituut announced that Studio Klarenbeek & Dros and Atelier Luma had won the New Material Award, a prize of 15,000 euros, for Algae Lab LUMA. The announcement was made on October 20, 2018, at the opening of the nominees' exhibition during Dutch Design Week, and it lists fifteen nominees.

In 2020, the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, which was closed for renovation, staged an online exhibition called The Breakdown Economy, and the studio's site dates its contribution to 2020. The museum's text puts the studio's research into a world without plastic at the center of the show and names a material called weed-ware as a natural, degradable alternative to plastic. The colophon lists partners including a seaweed farming group, Wageningen University and Research and the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research.

And in Paris, the Centre Pompidou's public collection database returns 23 works by the studio. Twenty-two are gifts and one is a purchase, 14 were acquired in 2019 and 9 in 2023, and the works include one chair and a group of glasses, carafes, cups, bowls and vials, many credited to the studio with Atelier Luma.

The studio's own pages add projects that I could not confirm elsewhere, and I give them as the studio's account: a remake of Peter Ghyczy's Garden Egg Chair in seaweed-based material for the Vitra Design Museum, a dress printed in cacao-shell filament for a House of Iris van Herpen show, a set of urns made with a stone company that the studio says won the Dutch Funeral Awards, and a mycelium pavilion shown at Dutch Design Week in 2019.

At Dutch Design Week itself the pair has appeared before. In 2025 a project called Growing Facade was listed at Strijp T+R in the Roots exhibition, open October 18 to 26, 2025, with Heijmans, the Hogeschool van Amsterdam and the Municipality of Amsterdam named as supporters.
The week's evening program on October 24, 2025 at the Next Nature Museum included a talk by the pair, and its page described them as pioneers in working with living materials.

blocks.x: Museums hold the stopped version of the work

r: The pattern across these records is that the objects museums collect are finished, dried or processed. The Pompidou chair is inert. The Pompidou's glasses and vessels are made objects. The Boijmans exhibition was an online show of interviews, video and text about a material.

The Munich exhibition makes the pattern easy to see, and it matters for the timing of this essay. Die Neue Sammlung, the design museum, shows Klarenbeek & Dros: Design of the Unusual in the Paternoster Hall of the Pinakothek der Moderne from July 17, 2026 to October 10, 2027. It calls the exhibition the pair's first monographic show and the tenth anniversary of the hall's exhibition series, and its curators are Xenia Riemann-Tyroller and Angelika Nollert. The page describes furniture made from mycelium, glass made from diatoms and vessels made of bioplastics, and it warns visitors that the mycelium, algae and moss can produce their own odors while stating that the materials pose no health risks.
That health statement is the museum's, and this essay does not go beyond it.
So when .Unusual opens in Eindhoven, the same two designers have a major solo show running in Munich. The Eindhoven listing does not mention it, and the Munich pages do not mention Eindhoven.

blocks.x: The venue is a concrete factory from the 1920s

r: The venue adds a detail the listing does not mention. The national monument register entry for the Philips complex at Strijp-S, in the component that lists Klokgebouw 50 among its addresses, describes a multi-story factory building with a built-in water tower, designed by A. de Broekert of the Philips engineering office and built in two phases in 1928 and 1929. The structure is reinforced concrete throughout, and the register's statement of significance calls the large-scale use of reinforced concrete innovative. The component was registered on February 16, 2004.
The register's address list does not say which part of the building B4 occupies, and the listing does not say which hall the show uses.
A show about alternatives to concrete in a protected concrete building is a coincidence, and a visitor may find it worth noticing.

blocks.x: The building-material question is where the claims get thinner

r: The listing's argument is about construction, so the construction record deserves a closer look. The most direct example is the Growing Facade. The studio's page describes 60 by 60 centimeter panels, each a unique relief of printed and cultivated elements made from mycelium combined with wood or seaweed fibers and sawdust. It says a first wall was acquired by the construction company Heijmans and is on view at its innovation lab, that a second set is at the Innovation Pavilion at the Marineterrein in Amsterdam, and that the Hogeschool van Amsterdam and Sensorlab are monitoring the panels.

A trade article published by MaterialDistrict on August 11, 2025, credited to Duurzaam Gebouwd, covers the same project at the Heijmans Hive in Rosmalen. It says the panels are designed with the help of AI models trained on seaweed and marine themes, printed locally without molds or plastic, modular, and good at absorbing sound. It also says the material is fire-resistant, compostable and odor-free, and then states the open problem: current biobased coatings are not yet ideal for outdoor use, so the designers are working with partners on durability outdoors.

Independent research explains why that is the hard part. A peer-reviewed 2019 study in Materials & Design by Appels and eight co-authors found that the density, strength and water uptake of mycelium composites can be tuned by changing the substrate, the fungal species and the processing, and that heat pressing moves performance from foam-like toward cork-like and wood-like.

A 2021 review in Frontiers in Materials describes mycelium composites as suited to insulation, paneling, flooring and furniture, calls them semi-structural, and reports that water absorption can sharply reduce compressive strength.

Put together, the record supports a modest reading. Grown mycelium panels exist, a construction company has taken a wall of them, and their weak point outdoors is acknowledged by the trade press. The sources I opened do not show a grown material carrying a building's load or replacing concrete. The listing does not claim that either, and neither should a visitor assume it.

blocks.x: Some figures on the studio's pages do not match other sources

r: The studio's pages are a primary source for what the studio says, and a few of their numbers differ from outside records.

The first difference is about oxygen. One studio page says algae provide 60 percent of the oxygen production on Earth, and the Weedware page says more than 60 percent comes from algae, more than from all trees. NOAA's National Ocean Service says scientists estimate that roughly half of Earth's oxygen production comes from the ocean, mostly from plankton, and that about the same amount is consumed by marine life. Neither studio page says where its figure comes from, so I treat NOAA's wording as the safer one.

The second is about the first mycelium print. The Weedware page says the founders became the first to 3D-print with living organic matter in 2010. The studio's site says it has developed the technology since 2011, and the Pompidou's timeline and podcast both say 2011. I take 2011 because those three agree. The "first in the world" part remains the studio's claim. The Royal Academy of Art in The Hague carries the sentence in a page credited to the studio, and the Pompidou podcast says it was the first time a chair was 3D-printed from mycelium.

The third is about when the chair first appeared at the Pompidou. The museum's teaching page says it was first presented in 2018 at La Fabrique du vivant, but the same page's timeline says the show was in 2019, and the podcast transcript gives the dates as February 20 to April 15, 2019. The transcript is the more specific record, so 2019 is the exhibition year. The object's own date line, 2018 to 2019, probably covers making and showing.

The fourth is about certification. The Weedware page describes PHALGAE as designed to be home compostable, but notes that EN 13432 and OK Compost HOME certification is in progress and has not been issued. The studio's site describes its mycelium products as fully compostable after use, without that qualifier. The company page is the more careful one, and it is the one I rely on.

The fifth is a number from the Weedware page that I can only restate. It says 10,000 kilograms of seaweed have been cultivated and 16,667 kilograms of CO2 bound in the company's products. That is about 1.7 kilograms of CO2 per kilogram of seaweed on the page's own figures, and the page does not say what the CO2 number includes or how it was measured.

blocks.x: Secrid hosts the stage, and says why

r: Secrid's announcement, dated October 7, 2026 and distributed through a news site's Industry Wire (which labels such items as submitted press releases outside its editorial responsibility), says the Talent Podium was founded in 2022 and each year supports seven designers with a stage at Dutch Design Week, coaching, publicity and 7,777 euros in prize money, a nod to Secrid's seven design principles. It names the 2026 designers selected with the Dutch Design Foundation, among them Dros and Klarenbeek, alongside six others working on topics from dementia wayfinding to discarded clothing.

The Secrid page in the DDW program frames the show as five years and fifty designers, built on an idea called Industrial Evolution: every new product should be better than its predecessors. It also describes a second Secrid presentation, The Original, Made in Europe, which uses the Original Cardprotector to show how material, production, use and repair connect.
The announcement says the community of fifty was formed partly through Secrid's collaboration with What Design Can Do, whose winners Secrid supported each year and also placed on the Talent Podium.

For a reader, the point is plain. This is a company-funded showcase with a stated purpose, and the designers' own record is longer than what the sponsor's page says about them. Reading both together is more informative than reading either alone.

blocks.x: What to ask when you stand in front of it

r: If you go, four questions follow from the sources. Which organism is this, and is it a fungus, a micro-alga or a seaweed? Which stage am I looking at: growing, dried, processed into pellets or finished? What happens to this at the end of its use, and has anyone tested that claim or certified it? And how large is the thing, and could it carry weight, keep out rain or sit outside? These questions are mine, drawn from the gaps between the sources and the listing, and the designers may well answer them better than any document does.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition, and the listing does not say what works it contains. I do not know which organisms, which processes or which objects will be on the floor at B4 Klokgebouw, or whether living material will be on display. The press kit the listing offers was not opened.

I could not open the Atelier Luma site, so my account of the Algae Lab rests on the Pompidou's pages, the Het Nieuwe Instituut prize record and the studio's own text. Swarovski's press page and Dezeen's early coverage of the chair were not available to me. The 2013 date that the Weedware page gives for the first Mycelium Chair is therefore not confirmed by anything I read, and the Pompidou page's caption that places a presentation at Dutch Design Week in March 2014 sits oddly with a festival that runs in October; I did not settle which event it means.

Several studio claims have no outside record in what I opened: the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam acquisition of diatom glass, the museum collections the Weedware page lists beyond the Pompidou, the Vitra remake, the Iris van Herpen dress, the funeral awards, the figure of 10,000 algae cards and the Seaweed Circle's output. The Pompidou's database lists glasses by the studio dated 2018 and 2021, but I could not tell from the list which of them is the diatom glass. The Weedware page pairs an Amsterdam seat with a visiting address in Krommenie, and I did not check the company register.

No source I read gives measured data on the carbon balance of any of the studio's products, and the carbon-negative statements on its pages are its own. The Appels study and the Frontiers review describe mycelium composites in general, not the studio's recipes. I do not know whether the mycelium in the 2026 work is dried, heated or still growing during the week.

If you plan to be in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, take the four questions from the previous section and ask the one you most want answered. Then ask a last one: if the material was alive while it was made, at what moment did someone decide to stop it, and why then?

posts.title: How do you decide what a material is worth?
posts.subtitle: The Textile & Material Innovation HUB asks how we make, use and value materials. In the Netherlands the third verb now has a price tag, a legal target and a deficit, and one listed project asks what a textile is for.
posts.seoTitle: How do you decide what a material is worth?
posts.description: The DDW Textile & Material Innovation HUB asks how we make, use and value materials. Dutch law, 2026 cost figures and one listed project.

r: A kilogram of discarded clothing costs the Dutch collection chain money to take in and money to sort, according to figures that a Dutch producer organization, Stichting UPV Textiel, published in June 2026 from a cost study of the sector.
That sentence sits oddly beside the question a Dutch Design Week exhibition asks: "What if we rethink how we make, use and value materials?"

The Textile & Material Innovation HUB is in the Dutch Design Week program at B4 Klokgebouw, Klokgebouw 50, on Strijp-S in Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00. A Dutch Design Week ticket is required, and the listing marks the exhibition as tactile and fully wheelchair accessible.

This essay draws on public documents only: the festival's pages, Dutch and European legal texts, the Dutch government's letter to parliament, reports from the textile sector, and one review of research. I have not seen the exhibition, and the listing does not say what any object in it looks like.

I want to use the HUB's question as a way of thinking, because I suspect most of us answer the first two verbs by habit and the third by price. The Dutch textile system is a rare place where the third verb has been written down in numbers. Those numbers say more than I expected.

blocks.x: The listing asks three questions and names one participant

r: The HUB listing says designers, scientists, makers and thinkers come together to explore the future of materials and textiles, "from biomaterials and circular production processes to speculative designs that open up new perspectives."
It adds that textiles and materials "are not passive resources" and are connected to history, culture, nature, location and processes of making.

Then come the three questions. What if material becomes relational, affecting our sensorial systems and helping shape how we experience the world? What happens to the role of the designer when materials are no longer fully controlled but collaborated with? What new narratives emerge when waste becomes a material of value and a resource, rather than a problem?
Each question lines up with one of the verbs in the headline question: using, making and valuing.
The listing names one participant, Soft Companions.
A visitor reading the HUB page alone learns nothing about what that project is, but it has its own Dutch Design Week listing, which I come to below.
One detail needs a correction that matters for how the exhibition is described. The 2026 listing says the HUB is hosted by Dutch Design Week.
The 2025 edition's listing said something more specific: the project "was initiated by Dutch Design Foundation but is carried by the participants that showcase their work."
Dutch Design Foundation is the organization behind the festival, and the 2026 listing's About paragraph (in Dutch) says it offers designers opportunities, support, publicity and a platform.
So the foundation's role is real, but the 2026 listing itself names Dutch Design Week as host, and I follow the listing.

blocks.x: The festival asked for this kind of work before it opened the exhibition

r: The HUB is not an accident of one year's program. When Dutch Design Week opened its call for entries for the 2025 edition, the organizers wrote that the festival "especially encourages applications in textile innovation and regenerative building," fields they described as critical building blocks for meaningful change. They added that the rapid progress in material innovation calls for collaboration.

The 2025 Textile and Material Innovation exhibition described itself as a selection of projects that excel in textile or material innovation, either by developing new materials, new uses or interesting collaborations, or by recycling in an unusual way.
It ran in the Klokgebouw from October 18 to 26, 2025, and its listing named one participant, Veenweide Atelier, credited to Tryntsje Nauta, Veenweide Atelier and Faber Futures.

The 2026 call for entries, which closed on June 16, is worded more broadly. It invites "the full spectrum of the field," from the speculative to the industrial and from the research-driven to the hands-on.
The 2026 HUB page keeps the 2025 spirit while changing the framing: the earlier text talked about projects that excel, and the new one asks three questions.

I find the shift from a showcase to a set of questions useful, since a showcase invites admiration and a question invites an answer. It also means the HUB's own position on what a material is worth stays open, and that is the part I want to test against the documents.

blocks.x: The building has changed its worth before

r: The Klokgebouw is a national monument, listed in the Dutch register under number 518769 and entered on February 16, 2004. The register describes a multi-storey factory building with a built-in factory water tower, designed by architect A. de Broekert of the Philips engineering bureau and built in two phases, in 1928 and 1929, in a functionalist style.
It is a concrete structure, six storeys under a flat roof, and the register values it as an example of large-scale industrial high-rise construction and of the application of reinforced concrete.
The register's list of addresses includes Klokgebouw 50, the address the HUB listing gives.

It also includes Klokgebouw 111, which the Dutch Design Awards' organization page gives as the visitor address of Dutch Design Foundation, so the foundation that organizes the festival has its offices in the same registered building.

Dutch Design Week itself has treated the building as a place for technology and innovation. Its 2019 guide called the Klokgebouw one of three main locations curated by the festival, alongside the VEEM building and the Ketelhuisplein, and described it as a former Philips building where "everything revolves around technology and innovation."

A factory that once made things for a company now shows how designers think about materials. Whatever one thinks of that, it is a small, concrete example of a structure being given a new use and, with it, a new kind of worth.

blocks.x: Making: what the numbers say about how much we make and buy

r: Start with the verb that is easiest to count. The European Environment Agency reported in March 2025 that the average person in the EU bought 19 kilograms of clothing, footwear and household textiles in 2022, up from 17 kilograms in 2019. Of the 19 kilograms, 8 were clothing, 7 were household textiles and 4 were footwear.

The agency ranked textiles by environmental pressure. Out of 12 categories of European household consumption, it said, textile consumption ranked on average the fifth largest in terms of environmental and climate pressure, measured by raw material use, greenhouse gas emissions and water and land use.

The European Commission's textiles strategy page gives a different rank: it says EU textile consumption has on average the fourth highest impact on the environment and climate change, after food, housing and mobility.

The two bodies disagree by one place. I cannot tell from the pages which data years or method each used, and the agency's ranking is the more recent and spells out its three measures, so I rely on it for the rank and note the Commission's figure as an earlier official statement.

The same two pages give different numbers for discarded textiles, and here the difference can be explained. The Commission's page says about 5 million tonnes of clothing is discarded each year in the EU, around 12 kilograms per person.
The agency says that in 2022 EU member states generated about 6.94 million tonnes of textile waste, 16 kilograms per person.

One figure is clothing and the other is textile waste in general, so they describe different things. Both say the pile is large, and the agency adds that the total has stayed roughly stable since 2016.
Making has a second half, which is what happens to the material afterward. The Commission's page says that only about 1 percent of the material in clothing is recycled into new clothing.

The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's 2017 report, A New Textiles Economy, described the same problem from the other side and argued that a circular system could capture a USD 500 billion economic opportunity.
That figure is the foundation's own estimate from 2017, and I treat it as a claim, not a measurement.

blocks.x: Valuing: what one country decided a kilogram of textile is worth

r: The Netherlands made its choice in a decree dated April 14, 2023, the Besluit uitgebreide producentenverantwoordelijkheid textiel, in force from July 1, 2023.
Under it, whoever first places new clothing or household textiles on the Dutch market is a producer, and a producer is responsible for what happens to those products when they are discarded.

The decree sets targets by weight, measured against what the producer put on the market the year before. In 2025, 50 percent had to be prepared for reuse or recycled. The target then rises by five points a year to 75 percent from 2030.

Two further targets sit inside the main one. At least 20 percent of products placed on the market had to be prepared for reuse in 2025, rising to 25 percent from 2030, and at least 10 percent had to be prepared for reuse in the Netherlands, rising to 15 percent. Of the material that is recycled, at least 25 percent had to be recycled fibre-to-fibre in 2025, rising to 33 percent from 2030.
The decree also tells producers to take steps to use as many recycled textile fibers from discarded products as possible in what they sell.
The government's own FAQ states the aim as a circular textile industry by 2050.

The explanatory note shows what the government was looking at when it chose these numbers. Households discarded about 305 kilotonnes of textiles and footwear in 2018, or 17.7 kilograms per resident. Of that, 44.6 percent was collected separately and 55.4 percent, about 169 kilotonnes, ended up in household residual waste.

Of the separately collected textile and footwear, 53 percent was wearable again, 33 percent was recycled and 14 percent was a residual mix, and 84 percent of the textile collected in the Netherlands was sold abroad after sorting.

Citing a 2021 study by Rebel Group, the note put the total cost of the producer system at between 82 and 196 million euros, called that estimate uncertain, and noted that 343 million kilograms of new textile reach the Dutch market each year.
The first full year under the targets is now in. Stichting UPV Textiel, which the government's FAQ lists as one of three producer organizations, published its 2025 annual report on September 8, 2026.

It says 51 percent of the textile its participants put on the market was prepared for reuse and recycling, against the 50 percent target, and 37 percent of the sorted textile was reused, against 20 percent required.
The two harder targets were missed: reuse in the Netherlands reached 5 percent against 10, and fibre-to-fibre recycling reached 14 percent against 25.
These are results for one organization's participants, not for the country.

The same organization described what a kilogram is worth on the other side of the ledger. In December 2025 it reported that an update of a cost study by KPMG found falling average selling prices for reuse and recycling in 2025, a slight fall for reuse and a considerable one for recycling, while volumes stayed stable and operating costs for collection and sorting were expected to rise.

In June 2026 it published the updated net cost figures for 2026: intake and cleaning run at a net shortfall of 0.07 to 0.12 euros per kilogram, and sorting at a net shortfall of 0.07 to 0.14 euros per kilogram. In its words, revenues do not cover the costs.

Adding the two ranges is my own arithmetic and the two steps are separate, but together they suggest a shortfall of roughly 14 to 26 cents per kilogram before the textile has been recycled. These figures are about post-consumer textile in the Dutch collection chain. They do not say what a designer pays for a remnant from a studio.

The sector took the problem to the government. A round table called the Textieltafel, chaired by the government's special representative for the circular economy, presented its advice on June 17, 2026. It proposed twenty measures, a bridging scheme and a guarantee fund so that sorting and recycling capacity does not disappear before new rules take effect, and an independent envoy. The press release says that about half of textile in the Netherlands is collected separately and that the quality of collected textile is falling, which it links to ultra-fast fashion and overconsumption.

The cabinet answered on June 26, 2026. It agreed to study the earning capacity of the sorting and recycling industry and to look at extending an existing bridging scheme for plastics to textiles, and it said that hardly any fibre-to-fibre recycled material is yet used in new textiles.

Europe is moving the same way on a longer clock. Directive (EU) 2025/1892, according to the European Parliament's legislative tracker, requires member states to give producers extended responsibility for textile, textile-related and footwear products, with schemes set up by April 17, 2028, and it asks member states to take fast-fashion practices into account when setting producers' fees.
The Dutch cabinet's letter says the Dutch decree will be changed on January 1, 2028 to follow the revised European directive.
The Commission's page also lists a ban on destroying unsold textiles and footwear that began on July 19, 2026 for large enterprises.

Put together, these documents say that the Dutch answer to "how do you value a material?" is a target in percentage points, a producer bill, and a market price for used textile that, right now, does not cover the work of handling it. The word "value" in the HUB's third question does two jobs, as it does in the documents. It can mean what something sells for, and it can mean what a society decides to care about. The law is an attempt to make the second kind of value pay for the gap in the first.

blocks.x: Another listing answers the value question with craft

r: The HUB's list of similar projects points to other work in the Dutch Design Week program, and one of them takes up the third question directly. Piece by Piece: Textile Waste to Designed Space, hosted by Studio Coming Soon, is a separate exhibition at Schellens Fabriek on Bleekweg, with free access.

Its listing says the studio turns discarded textile remnants into handcrafted interior objects using natural dyes and artisanal techniques, and that the project explores how discarded materials "can be given a new life" and "acquire new value."

The listing also says that a sustainable future is about looking differently at the materials we already have, and it presents the value of the material and the making process as the center of the project.

That is a claim by the studio about its own work, and the listing is the only source I have. It is not part of the HUB, and I mention it because it shows a different answer to the same question. The decree counts a kilogram. A craft studio counts what a person can make of a remnant. Neither answer is complete, and a reader can hold both.

blocks.x: Using: one listed participant asks what a textile is for

r: Now the middle verb. The listing for Soft Companions, which names Katrijn Westland as host, describes an ecology of creature-like textile artifacts that explores how lifelike textile companions can evoke reciprocal care through sensory interaction.

It says the companions are made of naturally dyed knitted textiles combined with e-textiles, sensors, pneumatic systems and soft mechanics, and that they "breathe, move, emit warmth and light, purr when content, encourage calm breathing, and wander towards sunlight."

The listing says the work is motivated by "the growing epidemic of loneliness" and by the underexplored role of sensory engagement in caring habits, and that it positions textiles as active companions rather than passive matter.
The creator's biography calls her a textile and interaction designer working with knitted structures, e-textiles, inflatables and natural dye processes.
Technical support is credited to Bram de Groot and Berend te Linde.
Those are the creator's descriptions of her own project. I have no photograph I can vouch for, no description from a visitor and no published evaluation of the work.

The word "epidemic" is the listing's, and it is worth checking against what a health body says. The World Health Organization's Commission on Social Connection reported in June 2025 that one in six people worldwide is affected by loneliness and that loneliness is linked to an estimated 871,000 deaths a year. It defines loneliness as the painful feeling that arises from a gap between desired and actual social connection.
The commission's co-chair called loneliness and isolation "a defining challenge of our time," and the news release does not use the word epidemic.
So the listing is describing a real public health concern in its own vocabulary.

Does a textile companion help? The listing does not claim to treat anything, and I will not claim it either. What can be said is what the research on a related kind of device shows. A 2025 meta-analysis in The Gerontologist pooled 19 studies with 1,083 older adults and found that AI-enabled social robots significantly reduced loneliness. It also found larger effects in studies with control groups and in institutional settings than among people living independently, and it found that robot type did not significantly change the result.

The authors warn that publication bias was detected, which may overestimate the true effect, that most studies came from high-income countries, and that it remains unclear whether short-term reductions persist once novelty wears off.

That review is about older adults and robots, and it says nothing about a knitted creature shown at a design festival. I include it to mark how thin the ground is under claims that a companion object improves loneliness, and to show that the question is being studied.

An anatomist learns early to separate what a structure is described as doing from what has been shown to do it. A listing that says a creature encourages calm breathing is a description. Whether a person breathes more calmly beside it would take a measurement, and I have found none.

blocks.x: Where the three verbs meet

r: A hypothetical shows how the verbs pull on each other. Picture a studio that collects a pile of discarded knitwear, dyes it with plants, and makes a lamp from it. The studio can price the lamp by the hours of skilled work, as the craft listing suggests. A municipality weighing the same pile sees it as a kilogram that someone has to take in and sort, and the Dutch figures suggest that step runs at a loss. The producer who sold the original sweater is, under the decree, responsible for part of that bill. And a designer building a creature that purrs is asking a third question, about what the material is for once it is on a body or in a hand.

None of the three views is wrong, and they do not add up to one number. That is the real content of the HUB's headline question as I read it. The Dutch system has found a way to price the pile, a studio can find a way to price the lamp, and neither price says whether the sweater was worth making.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition, and the 2026 HUB listing names only Soft Companions. I do not know which other projects will be shown, how the space is arranged, or what evidence any project offers for its claims. The listing's own sentence that a new material culture is already taking shape there is a statement of intent, and I cannot test it.

I do not know why the 2026 listing names Dutch Design Week as host while the 2025 listing credits Dutch Design Foundation with starting the project. Both can be true, but no page I opened explains the change.

On numbers, I have not compared the European Environment Agency and Commission figures for discarded textiles against their underlying data, and I could not open the official European Union text of Directive 2025/1892, only the Parliament's summary of it.
The Dutch results for 2025 are from one producer organization, and I did not find national figures for the other two.
The cost figures come from the sector's own organization and from a study that I did not read in full.
I did not find the cabinet's research on the earning capacity of the sorting industry, which the June letter says it will start.

On Soft Companions, I found no published evaluation, no academic paper on the project, and no account of how the companions are meant to be used or by whom. The research on loneliness and robots concerns a different kind of object and population.

If you want to try the three verbs yourself, take one garment you own. Ask how it was made, and look at the label. Ask how you actually use it, including the ways you do not notice. Then ask what it would cost someone to take it back, sort it and send it on, and who ought to pay that. Which material around you would you want to know the full story of?
