posts.title: Who gets to choose what digital futures look like?
posts.subtitle: A free morning at Natlab puts nine design projects on one table, from an AI whose values you write yourself to a perch that lets two shelter parrots choose their sounds.
posts.seoTitle: Who gets to choose what digital futures look like?
posts.description: Nine design projects, one morning at Natlab, and a debate about who authors AI futures. What the project pages and the record say.

r: Two stories about artificial intelligence keep competing for our attention, and neither of them has a place for you in it.

In the first, AI cures disease. In the second, it builds the next bioweapon. 4TU.Design United puts both in the theme text for its Digital Futures session and says each one arrives as prophecy: "a single future, already decided, nobody's hand on the wheel."

The session is 4TU.Design United Dialogues 3: Digital Futures. It is in the Dutch Design Week program at Natlab, Kastanjelaan 500, on Strijp-S in Eindhoven, on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. The listing gives the time as 10:00 to 12:30, says it is free after registration, and asks visitors to register before October 14.
It is the third of five consecutive Dialogues mornings that Design United runs at Natlab, one theme per day from Monday to Friday.

This essay draws on public documents only: the festival's listing, the Design United pages for the session and its nine projects, and a set of outside sources that I chose to test the framing. I have not seen any of the prototypes, and I report no conversation with any designer.

I want to take the framing seriously, because the phrase doing the work is "nobody's hand on the wheel." It claims that the two stories leave no room for anyone to act. My question is whether that is true of the record, and what the nine projects offer in its place.

blocks.x: The record puts both stories in the same sentence

r: The 2026 International AI Safety Report is a synthesis led by Yoshua Bengio, with an expert advisory panel nominated by more than 30 countries and international organizations, the Netherlands among them.

On the first story, it says AI systems can now provide detailed scientific information and assist with complex laboratory procedures, including generating protocols, troubleshooting technical problems and designing molecules and proteins, and that these capabilities have the potential to accelerate drug discovery, improve disease diagnostics and support medical research. The next sentence says they may also assist threat actors in creating biological and chemical weapons.
The report calls the policy problem one of managing dual-use risks while promoting beneficial applications, since some capabilities that can be misused are also useful for medical research.

So the two prophecies describe one set of capabilities seen from two ends. The report adds two cautions that the prophecies leave out. In 2025 several developers released new systems with additional safeguards because they could not rule out that the systems could assist novices in weapons development, and the report also says substantial uncertainty remains about how these capabilities affect risk in practice, given material barriers to weapons production and the difficulty of testing for uplift.

The first story has a documented, narrower form. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction, citing an AI model, AlphaFold2, that has been used by more than two million people from 190 countries, and saying that researchers can now better understand antibiotic resistance.

The Academy says these discoveries hold enormous potential. It does not describe a cure. As an anatomist I read the word "structure" in that citation with respect and the word "cure" with caution, because a structure is a map and a cure is something a patient receives.

None of this settles the organizers' point. It does suggest the stories are more specific than prophecies usually are. A claim that AI "cures disease" or "builds bioweapons" is a claim about particular systems, particular safeguards and particular institutions, and each of those has people who made choices. That is the opening the session uses.

blocks.x: The morning is built as an argument

r: The session's theme text is blunt: "futures are designed, not forecast."
The longer program text on the 4TU page says that when AI comes up the conversation splits in two, and that "a prophecy leaves you nothing to do but wait."

It then sets out the format. Nine designers each put one provocation on the table: three minutes, one slide. Visitors spend half an hour with the prototypes behind them. Then each visitor picks an argument and has it at a table with the designer present, and at some point is asked to argue the side they do not hold. The organizers say they are not after consensus. They want "positions clear enough to disagree with, and the thing each would oblige us to build."
What the room produces may go into the Design United e-Magazine.

The schedule has five steps. A 9:45 walk-in, a 10:00 welcome whose stated framing is "Two prophecies, neither of them designable," a provocation round with the pitches and a demo carousel from 10:10, a break at 11:05, a design debate from 11:15, a "taking positions" part from 12:00, a closing question at 12:25 ("what would we have to design to move this one step?") and a network lunch at 12:30.
The DDW listing gives the event as starting at 10:00 and the 4TU page says 9:45 to 12:30. Both fit together: 9:45 is the walk-in and 10:00 is the welcome.

The format is a deliberate move away from the panel talk. A panel ranks expertise, with people on a stage who know and people in the audience who ask. A table with the designer present and an instruction to argue the other side asks visitors to commit to something and to find out what it would cost. That is my reading of the format, and I have no account of how it plays out in the room.

Design United has run a version of this before. In 2025 its Digital Futures morning ran from 9:30 to 12:30 at Natlab with eleven projects, under the title "From Alternative Presents Toward Digital Futures," and the 2025 theme text described projects that treat AI as a creative material and as a tool for slowing down.
The 2026 text is more pointed. It names a binary and sets out to break it.
The organizers are Tilman Dingler of TU Delft's Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering and Tuan (Ting) Huang of Eindhoven University of Technology's Industrial Design department.

Design United describes itself as the leading platform for design research in the Netherlands, which is its own claim, and the session sits inside a week-long Dialogues program whose stated purpose is to bridge the gap between what emerging technologies offer and the value they create for people and society.
The "4TU" in the name stands for the four Dutch universities of technology, which DDW's own 2019 guide listed as Delft, Eindhoven, Twente and Wageningen.

blocks.x: Nine projects, read from their own pages

r: The DDW listing sorts the nine projects into two groups. In the first, projects help people make sense of their surroundings and the technology inside them. In the second, the listing says, the projects step into the future and design alternatives where humans and animals alike have agency over their preferred lives.
Each project has a page on the 4TU site, and these pages say a good deal more than the listing's one-line summaries. They are the projects' own accounts, and I treat them that way.

, by Joe Oliver Grimshaw, is a music-discovery system for the home. A listener places a personally meaningful household object on its surface, a camera reads the object's texture, color, wear and form, and an associative AI turns those qualities into a provisional interpretation and proposes a track. The AI is deliberately prevented from identifying or naming the object, which the page says leaves a gap the listener fills.

The page calls Curio a critique of "frictionlessness" and says the project produced four physical prototypes, speculative devices meant to provoke reflection and not to work as commercial products. It also draws its own boundary: tasks with a single, objectively correct outcome should stay frictionless.

, by Mert Akay, Abhigyan Singh and David Keyson of TU Delft, starts from the observation that heat maps built from sensors and satellites do not capture how a place feels. A reading of 34 degrees Celsius, the page says, tells you nothing about the relief of standing under a tree. The interface layers "thick data," short stories and ratings that residents pin to a map, over measurements such as heat maps, tree cover and building shade, and a built-in assistant lets visitors "ask the city" questions.
The page names its own challenge: gathering enough voices takes time and trust, and lived experience is harder to standardize than a sensor reading.

, by Kealan Stewart, built four smart-speaker probes with identical function and different form, and gave them to four users for a week. The page reports that the probe with a familiar, mute form made its user forgetful and was seen as a friend, that a probe built on a virus analogy left its user uncomfortable, that a probe with a button in place of a wake word made its user less forgetful, and that the most expressive probe, which exposed the internal workings, was turned away and covered.

The project's own conclusion is modest. Expressive form can reliably communicate a device's unethical character, but cannot by itself communicate whether its function is ethical. The page calls the resulting honesty only partial.

, by Mariska Geelhoed of Saxion and the University of Twente, is part of a research project on getting people to maintain household appliances. The page says the main barrier is lack of urgency, since an appliance that still works can be left alone, and that Repair Cafés see coffee machines more than any other household electrical appliance, with Senseos common. In the project, owners join a group chat with people they know and their personified machines, which gossip about them and grow more critical when maintenance is neglected.

It was tested with owners in daily life. The page's summary is careful: it did not lead directly to more maintenance, it made maintenance more visible and discussable, and the results do not show that gossiping appliances will improve maintenance.

, by Liam Hayes, embeds repair guidance in three consumer electronic devices. The page argues that intimidation, and not only access to parts and tools, stops people from attempting a repair, and quotes Carsten Frauenheim of iFixit: "Intimidation is a major barrier to even attempting a repair." In A/B tests with participants of varying experience, the guidance made repair tasks easier to interpret and reduced uncertainty. The page notes it was tested on a limited range of devices.

, by Beatriz Monteiro, Mathieu Gielen and Değer Özkaramanlı of TU Delft, is a card game for children aged 7 to 11 in which the players take the role of the person creating fake news, pairing statements with persuasion techniques such as impersonation and judging which is most convincing. The page says the game was co-designed with children in four phases and ties it to inoculation theory. Its own stated limit is that recognizing a technique in play does not guarantee resisting it in real life.
Designing Interactive Sound Enrichment for Captive Parrots

, by Yinglan Deng, builds a computer-vision perch system. A camera detects where a parrot sits, and moving between perch zones triggers different audio clips. The page says the work was done with the ROZE animal shelter and explored with two parrots, and that short-term engagement cannot show long-term improvement in wellbeing.

, by Giulia Talamini, worked with the Kröller-Müller Museum. The page says seven visually impaired participants each trained a personal AI classification model with their own words, such as "lively," "unfortunate" or "educational," to sort 75 artworks, and the surprises in the models' predictions became the research material. It reports that seven people required seven different things, and it frames accessibility as a direction of travel and not a finished state. The page says the work is irreducibly specific, which complicates institutional implementation.
, by Femke Veenvliet, I take up on its own below.

Two things stand out when the pages are read together. Every one of them states its own limit, in the same plain terms. And in none of them is the person at the center of the design reduced to a user who accepts a default: the listener fills the gap, the resident adds the story, the owner is gossiped about, the child makes the fake news, the parrot picks a sound. That pattern is mine, and the organizers do not draw it.

blocks.x: The wider record behind some of the projects

r: Three of the projects touch bodies of evidence that the project pages mention only in passing, and I looked at each.

On repair, the United Nations Global E-waste Monitor 2024 found that the world generated a record 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, and that less than a quarter, 22.3 percent, was documented as properly collected and recycled. It lists limited repair options among the challenges behind the widening gap.

Europe has since changed the rules. The European Commission says that from July 31, 2026, consumers can ask manufacturers to repair products that are technically repairable under EU law, including washing machines, vacuum cleaners, mobile phones and tablets, for free or at a reasonable price, and that manufacturers must provide accessible information about repair services and spare parts.
The law addresses access. The Accessible Repair page addresses the confidence of the person holding the screwdriver, which is a different obstacle, and the two fit together.

On misinformation games, the best-known test of the idea behind Con/Vince is a 2019 study of Bad News, an online game developed with the Dutch media platform DROG in which players take the role of a fake news producer and learn six techniques, among them impersonation. It reported a pre-and-post comparison with 15,000 participants and initial evidence that people's ability to spot misinformation strategies improved after play.
The authors state their limits too: the sample was self-selected and unrepresentative, and they call for modeling how quickly the effect decays.

The Con/Vince page says that most such interventions have been designed and tested with adults, and its contribution is to work with children. That is what the Bad News study would lead one to expect, and Con/Vince's own caution about "understanding" versus resistance is consistent with the 2019 authors' call for follow-up.

On animal choice, a 2023 paper in the proceedings of the ACM CHI conference described a system that let pet parrots start video calls with other parrots and ran a three-month study with 18 birds. Its review of earlier work notes that the definition of "choice" is debatable and that the perception of self-agency can benefit animals.
The Deng page rests on the same premise, that greater choice and control support wellbeing, and it adds that its evidence is short-term.
The honest summary is that giving an animal a say is a plausible design principle with early support, and that neither project shows lasting welfare gains.

blocks.x: The Constitution Builder asks the question the morning turns on

r: The page describes the project in terms that mirror the theme text. Your AI assistant has values, it says, and you did not choose them: somewhere a small team at a large company decided how honest it should be and whose interests come first. Instead of a settings menu, the Constitution Builder tells three illustrated stories, each a dilemma: a visit home, something witnessed, a month away. The user chooses under pressure and then reflects, and the tool reads the pattern beneath the choices, which values hold steady and which shift with context. That pattern becomes a "constitution," a plain-language rulebook that changes how an AI talks to that person.
At a live demo, the page says, visitors blind-drew a stranger's values from a card and watched two screens give different answers to the same question from the same model.

Then comes the finding I find most useful. Participants could point at their AI's behavior and say that it was them. But the page reports that feeling in control and actually being in control were two different things, and that the assistant people trusted most was not always the one built most accurately on their values; sometimes it was just the bluntest one. Authorship as a feeling and authorship as a fact, the page concludes, are not the same.

That result does not settle anything yet. It is a project page, and I have not seen the study behind it, so I cannot say how many people took part or how trust was measured. It does connect to an existing debate. In December 2022 researchers published Constitutional AI, an Anthropic-developed method in which the only human oversight of a model's training is a list of rules or principles.

In October 2023 the company and the Collective Intelligence Project reported a public input process with roughly 1,000 Americans, who contributed 1,127 statements and cast 38,252 votes, to draft a constitution for an AI system. The company's own account says the process showed it plays an outsized role in choosing such values, that the public and in-house documents overlapped in about half of their concepts, and that the experiment was preliminary.

That account comes from the developer, which is an interested party, and I include it as one documented example of an attempt to widen the authorship. No source I opened says that the Constitution Builder draws on it.

The contrast is instructive. The 2023 process asked about 1,000 people to agree on shared rules. The Constitution Builder, as its page describes it, produces one rulebook per person. Those are different answers to the question of who authors an AI's values, and the second raises a problem the first avoids: if each assistant holds its owner's constitution, what happens when one owner's values harm someone else? The page does not address that, and I would want to hear the designer's answer.

blocks.x: Whose hand, in practice

r: A free morning with registration is open to many people, and some more than others. It is on a Wednesday morning, at a fixed address on Strijp-S, with registration closing a week before.
A debate between designers and a self-selected audience can be lively, and it still leaves out people who have a stake and no morning to spare.
The projects show the same issue at a smaller scale. Situated Access worked with seven people, The Virus In Our Home with four, and the parrot study with two birds.
cliMATE names the problem directly: it needs many voices, and getting them takes time and trust.

Small studies are a normal and often valuable way to learn what to ask, and the pages are open about their size. They also mean that "who gets a hand in the design" is answered by a handful of people in each case, and the session's own format of one table per argument will produce positions from whoever sits there.

I raise this because the best version of the organizers' premise treats it as a standing question and not a slogan. If futures are designed, the designers owe the public some account of who else was consulted. A provocation is a good way to start, since it is deliberately incomplete and invites a reply. It is a weaker way to finish.

blocks.x: The place

r: The session is at Natlab. The City of Eindhoven's tourism pages say that in 1923 Philips opened the Natuurkundig Laboratorium, the Physics Lab, at Strijp-S, and that Natlab today is a cinema and theater.

The history of the lab itself starts earlier. A 2014 history in Europhysics News by Dirk van Delft of Museum Boerhaave says the physicist Gilles Holst started work on January 2, 1914 on the fourth floor of the Philips factory building in Eindhoven, and that the NatLab later gained international fame.
A memoir by a former employee, Henk Hagenbeuk, is titled as a recollection of the Philips Nat.Lab. on the Kastanjelaan, which fits the street in the DDW listing's address.

I did not find a document that ties the listing's exact address, Kastanjelaan 500, to the laboratory building, and I do not know whether the session room is in the space the lab once used. If it is, a place that once housed a company's research into the future is hosting a public debate about who designs it, and I would not make more of that than a small coincidence.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen any prototype, and the pages describe designs and results in the projects' own words. I cannot judge how any of the nine works, how large their studies were beyond the numbers on their pages, or whether their findings would hold up elsewhere.
I do not know what happens in the debate. The format is published, and what the room concludes is not. The listing does not state the language of the session.

The DDW colofon names seven design researchers, and the 4TU pages credit nine project teams. The Gossiping Senseos and Situated Access pages name researchers who are not among the seven, and I do not know why the colofon differs.
On the wider record, the safety report is a synthesis, not a measurement, and it says uncertainty remains.
The Anthropic account of public input is the developer's own.

I compare no other developer's published rules, because I read only this one. The Bad News study measured adults who opted in, and no source I read measures the effect of such games on children's later behavior.
If you could write one value into an AI, what would it be, and what would you want to happen when someone else's value collides with yours?

posts.title: What happens to the industries left off the growth list?
posts.subtitle: A Dutch Design Week symposium asks what the creative sector adds to economic growth. The report behind the question is public, and reading it shows how a sector ends up off a list.
posts.seoTitle: What happens to industries left off the growth list?
posts.description: A DDW symposium asks what the creative sector adds to growth. What the Wennink report, the coalition agreement and policy history actually say.

r: A list of priorities is a short document with a long reach, and the things it does not name still have to live with it.

The list in question comes from a report by Peter Wennink, the former president and CEO of ASML. On Monday, October 19, 2026, he is the keynote speaker at "Symposium: De creatieve economie," which is in the Dutch Design Week program at the Next Nature Museum, Noord Brabantlaan 1A, Eindhoven. The DDW listing gives 10:00 to 12:30 and says the session is paid, with registration.

The Dutch Design Foundation's own event page adds that doors open at 10:00, the symposium starts at 10:30, the working language is Dutch, and an optional design tour follows the networking lunch at 13:30 with a separate ticket.
The organizers are Brainport Development, Dutch Design Foundation and Design Development Eindhoven.
The listing asks: "What can the creative industries and cultural sector contribute to economic growth in the Netherlands?"

This essay draws on public documents only. It rests on the report itself, which I read in its English edition and searched for every mention of the sectors the symposium cares about, alongside the coalition agreement, the 2005 and 2011 policy documents, and the sector's own statistics.
I have not seen the symposium, I report no conversation with any speaker, and I have not read the newspaper article the organizers mention. Every translation from Dutch below is mine.

I think the question deserves a serious reading, because the interesting part is the assumption inside it. A sector is being asked to prove its worth in the terms of a document that, on the organizers' account, did not mention it. The first job is to check that account against the document.

blocks.x: What the symposium says about itself

r: The listing's long description makes four claims. It says Wennink's report on the Netherlands' long-term earning capacity forms the basis of the national growth strategy and the coalition agreement. It says the report identifies four areas for investment: digitalization and AI, security and resilience, energy and climate technology, and life sciences and biotechnology. It says "the creative industries are absent." And it says that while the Innovation Platform and the Top Sectors policy still regarded the sector as a driver of innovation, it has disappeared from today's economic debate.
The central question, in the listing's words, is for the sector itself: "do we dare to commit explicitly to the Netherlands' national growth ambitions?"
That is a pointed way to put it. It treats the growth strategy as a given and the sector's willingness as the open variable.

The program is a keynote by Wennink, an opening overview of the state of the design sector by Willem van Zeeland, director of Dutch Design Foundation, and Anna van Nunen, director of Eurosonic Noorderslag, and then responses. The responders are Jeroen Bartelse, director of TivoliVredenburg and chair of Kunsten '92, on culture as an economic driver; Anne Ligtenberg, designer and program director of Design Development Eindhoven, on design and societal transitions; Mark van Iterson, chair of the designers' professional body BNO, on entrepreneurship and revenue models; the economist Barbara Baarsma; Jeroen Dijsselbloem, the mayor of Eindhoven; and the filmmaker Kiriko Mechanicus. Monique van Dusseldorp moderates.
The roles come from the organizers' pages.

The organizers' announcement in Emerce, published on September 15, 2026, is labeled in the trade site's own footer as a submitted item outside the editors' responsibility. It repeats the four areas, says the creative industry was not named, and adds that Van Zeeland and Van Nunen wrote an article in Trouw earlier this year arguing it should not have been missing.
Each of these claims can be tested, and the rest of this essay tests them.

blocks.x: What the report is, and how it chose

r: The report is titled The Route to Future Prosperity (in Dutch, De route naar toekomstige welvaart). It was presented on December 12, 2025, and the Minister of Economic Affairs sent it to parliament that day with a letter saying it contains recommendations for a following cabinet and therefore carries no cabinet appraisal.
It describes itself as an independent advisory report answering a request to translate the Draghi report on Europe's earning capacity to the Dutch context.
Trade articles from that month give the date as December 12 or December 14, and the parliamentary letter and the report's own site settle it as December 12.

Its argument starts from growth. To pay for rising costs in healthcare, pensions, defense and the energy transition, it says, the Netherlands needs annual growth of at least 1.5 to 2.0 percent, against forecasts from the central bank and the planning bureau of 0.5 to 0.9 percent. Growth, it argues, will have to come almost entirely from higher labor productivity, and that requires investment of at least 151 to 187 billion euros in the high-productivity parts of the economy over ten years, largely from the private sector.

Then comes the choice that matters for this essay. The summary says it is essential to focus on domains "where we can build and maintain a strategic position," on high-end niche technologies that are harder to imitate, and it names four: digitalization and AI, security and resilience, energy and climate technology, and life sciences and biotechnology. It gives the reasons: they form the backbone of the great transitions of the century, they are characterized by explosive growth in demand, and they increasingly determine the geopolitical balance of power.
These are criteria. They are the terms in which a sector would have to make its case to be added.

The investment pipeline is built the same way. The report says over a thousand experts from business, universities and (semi-)public institutions developed 51 propositions within the four domains, in more than 30 consortia, together worth about 126 billion euros, of which 70 percent comes from private investors. The figures were supplied by the consortia themselves.

By the report's own chart, digitalization and AI account for 49 billion, life sciences and biotechnology 38 billion, energy and climate technology 26 billion, mainports 9 billion and security and resilience 3 billion.
The project proposals appendix groups the propositions under the four domains plus an infrastructure category for preconditions.

This matters because it shows how a pipeline like this fills. A proposition has to be organized, costed and submitted by a consortium inside one of the chosen domains. A sector that is not among the domains was never asked to submit, so its absence from the 126 billion says nothing about its worth. It says the survey had a boundary. That is my reading of the method, and I flag it as analysis.

blocks.x: What the report does not say

r: I searched the full text of the English edition for the sector's names. The words "creative industries," "creative sector," "arts," "fashion," "gaming," "film," "music" and "Dutch Design Week" do not appear. "Design" appears only in engineering and governance senses, such as the design of equipment or of government. "Creativity" appears once as a national strength, in the preface ("knowledge, creativity, capital and a strong tradition of cooperation"), and twice in passing as a quality that solutions require; "creative destruction" appears as an economic term.

The only place a cultural category appears is a chart of gross value added by sector, built from Eurostat data, that lists "Culture & other services" and "ICT & Media" as categories. As I read the chart, culture and other services show 2 percent of value added in both 1995 and 2024.
That is a statistical category and not a discussion of the creative industries, and I do not know how Eurostat's grouping compares with the Dutch definition of the creative industries.
The organizers' sentence "the creative industries are absent" is therefore accurate for the report's text, and so is Emerce's narrower phrase "not named."

The narrower phrase is the better one. A report can fail to name a sector and still imply a role for it. The Dutch association of pop venues and festivals, writing on December 18, 2025, makes that argument. It says culture is not named as a separate policy domain in the report, and it argues that cultural facilities fit the report's logic as a condition for attracting knowledge workers.

The report itself, in the text I searched, does not make that argument. It does not discuss cultural amenities as a location factor. So the association's reading is its own inference, and a reasonable one, and the report does not say it.

blocks.x: The coalition took the list

r: The symposium listing says the report is the basis of the coalition agreement. The agreement of D66, VVD and CDA, dated January 30, 2026, confirms the link. In its economic section it says that "in line with the Wennink report" the government steers actively toward 1.5 percent structural economic growth, and that it chooses four domains essential to the future economy and social wellbeing: digitalization and AI, security and resilience, energy and climate technology, and life sciences and biotechnology. Within these it aims to build technological niche positions.

The agreement does not use the words creative industry. Culture appears elsewhere, in a section on media and culture, which promises to protect artistic freedom, to revise the financing structure of the cultural sector and give makers and institutions multi-year certainty, and to reduce regulatory burden for the sector.
So the sector is present in the government's plan as culture and absent from it as growth. That split is what the symposium is trying to close.

blocks.x: The sector has had a seat at this kind of table before

r: The listing says earlier policy treated the creative sector as a driver of innovation. The record supports that.

The Innovation Platform, a body chaired by the prime minister, counted the creative industry among its key areas. Its midterm review, dated December 7, 2005, lists the key areas from its October 2004 proposals as Flowers and Food, high-tech systems and materials, Water and Creative Industry, with chemistry added later, and describes a report on the creative industry presented on September 30, 2005, titled "Creativiteit. De gewichtloze brandstof van de economie" (Creativity: the weightless fuel of the economy), which proposed a national program to give the sector an extra boost.
A participant's account from 2013 says the platform was abolished in June 2010 and that the creative industry became one of the top sectors in the new policy of the incoming minister.

The cabinet's response of September 13, 2011 confirms the next step. It sets out actions for each top sector and calls the creative industry "a young and powerful top sector with great growth opportunities." It announced a Fund for the Creative Industry of 11.4 million euros a year, to be set up by the State Secretary for Education, Culture and Science, and an 8 million euro window in an innovation loan fund for private investment funds in the creative industry. The letter came from the Minister of Economic Affairs, Agriculture and Innovation together with the State Secretaries of Finance and of Education, Culture and Science.

So at two points, in 2005 and 2011, the Dutch government named the sector in its growth and innovation policy. The 2013 account adds a caution: the sector had to organize itself to be taken seriously, and a 2009 review had warned it of exactly that.
I did not find a source for the sector's current status within the top sector policy, and I do not know what became of the label after 2011.

The phrase on the listing, that the sector "has disappeared from today's economic debate," is therefore a claim about change over time that the policy documents partly support. The sector was named in 2005 and 2011, and it is not named in the 2025 report or the 2026 coalition agreement.
Whether it has vanished from the wider debate is something I cannot measure.

blocks.x: What the numbers say about the sector

r: The sector's own data are plentiful, with a warning attached. The Cultuurmonitor, a monitoring site for the cultural sector, says each publication defines design slightly differently and that figures from different sources cannot be added into one coherent story.

With that caution, it reports 57,700 jobs in design in 2024, including about 43,500 self-employed workers, and says design is the fastest-growing branch of the creative industry, growing by 37,400 jobs between 2014 and 2024.
It reports that design added 2,150 million euros of value in 2024, which it puts at 7.8 percent of the added value of the whole creative industry.

Dividing the first figure by the second share gives a creative-industry total of roughly 27.6 billion euros, which is my arithmetic and not a published number. An earlier edition of the Monitor Creatieve Industrie, as summarized by an advocacy group, put the sector's added value at nearly 21 billion euros in 2022.
The tenth edition of the monitor says the sector's contribution to jobs and gross domestic product has again grown faster than average over the past decade.

The same sources describe a sector built unlike the pipeline. The average firm in the creative industry has 1.7 jobs, against 4.7 across the economy, and almost 52 percent of workers were self-employed in 2022.

I would not compare any of these figures with the report's 126 billion euros, since one is value added by an existing sector and the other is investment potential submitted by consortia, and they measure different things. The comparison that does matter is structural. A growth strategy that is assembled from consortia of large organizations meets a sector made of very small firms and freelancers. That is my observation. It would explain part of the gap without any ill will on the part of the report's authors.

blocks.x: Where design already touches the four domains

r: The organizers argue that the report's own challenges, from the energy transition to digital sovereignty, need the imagination and systems thinking of designers.

Their evidence is partly their own program. Dutch Design Week 2025 listed ministries, among them the Dutch defense ministry, and companies such as the energy company Vattenfall as participants showing how design can contribute to social challenges.

The Cultuurmonitor describes projects it attributes to the What if Lab, part of Dutch Design Foundation: designers helping ProRail with its aim of circular design for all railway stations by 2050, and a 2024 Vattenfall project, Upcycled Turbines, that asked designers for new uses for end-of-life wind turbines.

It also describes a multi-year program, De Publieke Ontwerppraktijk, begun at the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and run by Dutch Design Foundation from 2024 to 2027, to bring design methods into government work, including a pilot with the grid operator Alliander.

These are the sector's accounts of its own work, and the Cultuurmonitor is summarizing them. They show contact with the energy and security themes. They do not yet show what the Wennink report asks for, which is a strategic position in a high-end niche technology. A designer who helps a railway operator plan circular stations adds to the energy transition in a loose sense. Whether that raises Dutch labor productivity, or builds a position that others cannot copy, is a different claim, and I found no source that tests it.

The sector's strongest argument may therefore lie elsewhere: as a precondition for the four domains, in talent and in the usability of what they build, or as a way to make technologies acceptable to the people who must adopt them. That is my reasoning, offered as a hypothesis the speakers may or may not take up.

blocks.x: Who is asking

r: I want to keep the organizers in view. Dutch Design Foundation organizes Dutch Design Week, its director opens the symposium, and its submitted announcement is the source of the "absent" account that I have now been able to check.
The foundation also runs the public design practice program mentioned above.
Brainport Development, a co-host, describes itself as the economic development agency for Brainport Eindhoven.
The Wennink report names Brainport Eindhoven more than once as an example of a high-tech innovation ecosystem.

So one of the co-hosts represents a region the report singles out as a strength. None of this makes the question unfair. A symposium on whether the creative industry belongs on the growth list is a natural thing for these organizers to host. It does mean that the loudest advocates for the answer are also those with something to gain from it, so the evidence has to come from more than the advocates, which is why I went to the primary documents.

blocks.x: The frame

r: The symposium's question, whether the sector dares to commit explicitly to the national growth ambitions, accepts a particular frame. In that frame growth is measured by productivity, investment is organized in consortia, and a sector earns attention by showing it moves those numbers.

The report itself is more careful about its frame than the debate around it. Its preface says that being a force in chip technology, renewable energy, healthcare innovation and defense is not an aim in itself but a means to maintain freedom, solidarity and prosperity, and that the report is about more than competitiveness: it is about societal resilience.

That language leaves room for a sector to argue its value in terms of resilience and trust, not only in terms of output. Whether the sector can make that case with evidence is one of the questions I would put to the room.

Some of what design does, such as making a public service usable or helping people understand a rule, may be worth having without belonging to a sector that expands every year. I do not know how the speakers will handle that tension, and I think it deserves a place in the room.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not read the Trouw article the organizers cite, and I cannot say what evidence it uses.
I do not know what Wennink will say about the creative industries on October 19, 2026, or whether he considers the omission a choice or an oversight. The report does not discuss the question.
I do not know the current status of the creative industry within Dutch top sector policy. I found the 2005 and 2011 documents and a 2013 insider account, but nothing more recent that states it.
Nor do I know whether the cabinet that took office in 2026 plans to revisit the list: the coalition agreement repeats the four domains and says nothing more on the creative industry.
I did not find any of the 51 propositions that concerns design or the creative sector, and I did not read each proposal in full, only the overview of the appendix.
The sector's size figures come from monitors that define it differently, and one of them reaches me through an advocacy group's summary.
Last, I could not open the Monitor Creatieve Industrie 2025 itself, because its file host refused automated access, so the newest figures come from the Cultuurmonitor's summary of it.

A reader can use the symposium's question without a ticket. Pick an industry you know well. Search the current national plan for its name, and then ask what it would take for the people in it to describe their value in the plan's own terms. Should design count as a growth industry, and what evidence would convince someone who thinks it should not?

posts.title: Can a sound make you feel unsafe before you know why?
posts.subtitle: Fifteen Emerging Talent finalists are up for a Dutch Design Award. One of them has spent years asking what sound does to us, and the research behind her question is more specific than the question sounds.
posts.seoTitle: Can a sound make you feel unsafe before you know why?
posts.description: Dutch Design Awards Emerging Talent finalists, how the shortlist was made, and what research says about sound, fear and hospital noise.

r: Most of us can recall a sound that changed the mood of a room before anyone said a word.

The question comes from the Dutch Design Awards' Emerging Talent shortlist. On July 9, 2026, the awards announced fifteen finalists, called the Dutch Design Awards Class of 2026, and said that three of them will each receive a grant of 10,000 euros, provided by the Keep an Eye Foundation.
The three winners are to be announced at an invite-only ceremony on Saturday, October 17, 2026, during Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven.

This essay draws on public documents only: the awards' pages, the finalists' own sites, the research literature on sound, and reports on the topics their work touches. The ceremony is invite-only, I have no word on who wins, and I have seen none of the work in person.

I want to follow one finalist's question, because it is a good test of how we talk about sound and technology. Colette Aliman, according to the awards, "utilizes sound knowledge as a critical methodology for immersive installations and acoustic art."
The question in the headline is mine, not the awards', and it is my way of putting what her work is about. The first thing to ask about any shortlist is how it was made.

blocks.x: How the shortlist was made

r: The awards say the fifteen were selected by an internationally oriented jury chaired by Borre Akkersdijk, following an open call to the design community to nominate talented individuals.

The jury announced in April 2026 consists of Imruh Asha (fashion director at Dazed), Gabriele Chiave (creative director at Controvento and a former global creative director at Estée Lauder Companies), Karin van Gilst (director of the FOAM museum in Amsterdam), the architect and researcher Afaina de Jong, Christian Luiten (co-founder of Avant Arte), Nalden (founder and investor) and Hussein Suleiman (co-founder of Daily Paper).

The eligibility rules are specific. Candidates must be based, educated or practicing in the Netherlands and active in the field between April 1, 2025 and April 1, 2026, and the stated criteria are a coherent portfolio with depth, vision and evolution, a boundary-pushing approach that challenges the status quo, a broad understanding of design across disciplines, and the potential to influence the field.
Each of the three winners receives 10,000 euros, a masterclass and recognition within the awards' network.
The awards say 30,000 euros in grants are given each year, made possible by the Keep an Eye Foundation.
The foundation describes itself, in Dutch, as a foundation that has supported young makers since 2008 in developing their talent and their route to a sustainable professional practice.

The Dutch Design Awards were established in 2003 by BNO, the professional body for Dutch designers, and DesignLink, have been based in Eindhoven since 2005, and are part of Dutch Design Foundation, which also organizes Dutch Design Week.
The previous class, in 2025, produced three winners: Vera van der Burg, Willem de Haan and Plasticiet.

The jury's own summary of the 2026 class is worth reading as a statement of intent. It says the list "brings together 15 visionaries who choose to raise their voices and critique the world through design," and that emerging talent is defined by persistence in perfecting a craft, building new systems and making the invisible physical.
That is the jury's framing, and it applies to a very broad set of practices.

blocks.x: The fifteen

r: The awards describe all fifteen finalists in one line each. Colette Aliman works with sound. Esmay Wagemans molds wearable objects directly on the body. Estelle Barriol and Fanny Bordes of Studio ACTE use local reused materials in a temporary experimental pavilion. Gijs Schalkx builds operational vehicles by hand. Hsin Min Chan turns experience, identity and gender politics into artifacts. Julia Janssen makes the challenges of a digitalizing society and the relationship with AI tangible through installations. Jun Fujisaku crafts objects such as an office chair that dismantle embedded values of domesticity. Maggie Laylon Saunders, of Striptopia, reimagines strip club culture as consent-driven design. Necim Abiadh works on identity and cultural hybridity. Ori Orisun Merhav explores new manufacturing methods with natural materials such as lac. Rosalie Apituley makes prototypes and visualizations for alternative representations of energy systems. Sondi explores how power and narratives operate in game mechanics. Ülkühan Akgül bridges heritage craftsmanship with digital media. Yorick Westerkamp reworks the clothes in his own wardrobe into a collection. Yuro Moniz is a ceramist.

I have picked five of these because their descriptions place technology or media next to a body, a belief or a habit: Aliman, Janssen, Sondi, Akgül and Wagemans. That grouping is my reading, and a different reader would choose differently, including Rosalie Apituley's work on how energy systems are represented.

blocks.x: A question that grew out of earlier work

r: The sound-and-fear question is not new in Aliman's work. In 2020 she and Lauriane Heim, working as Studiocalh, made Soundscapes of Fear. Aliman's site says it was part of the FORMAT 2020 program at Z33 in Hasselt, supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, and presented in October 2020 at the Temporary Art Center in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week.
The project's guiding question, in the artists' words, is what we can learn when we consider fear from a sonic perspective.

CLOT Magazine covered it in December 2020. It describes an installation of two viewing stations fitted with sound vibration exciters, with video projections that borrow imagery from popular culture, an aluminum structure designed so that sound waves disperse across its surface and turn it into a speaker, and a podcast series, Conversing Our Soundscapes of Fear, as the first outcome of the research.
The designers say they held conversations with specialists in psychoacoustics, biology and sociology while developing it.

A live-streamed panel during Dutch Design Week 2020, Sound Design and the Spectrum of Fear, brought together a sound designer, an audio scientist and a professor of the social and cultural history of technology at Eindhoven University of Technology.
One thread of the research examined the sound of the DP-3 radiation meter in the 2019 television series Chernobyl, which the article says became a soundmark of the disaster.

Studiocalh's own remark, as quoted by CLOT, is that sound is "a vibrational force" that can travel through bodies and even raise adrenaline and the nervous system, and that sound can affect us on subliminal levels.

Those are the artists' framings of their own work. The articles describe the approach and report no measured results from the installation, so I will not say the installation proved anything about the ear or the body.

blocks.x: What research says about a rough sound

r: The question has a research literature, and one paper in it bears directly on the headline. A 2015 study in Current Biology by Luc Arnal and colleagues analyzed human screams and found that they cluster in a narrow range of rapid amplitude modulation, roughly 30 to 150 hertz, which corresponds to a perceptual quality called roughness. Ordinary speech lies outside that range, which the authors say helps avoid false alarms in normal communication.
The same roughness appears in artificial alarm signals such as buzzers and horns, but not in musical instruments, and adding it to sounds made them easier to detect in several tasks.

In a brain-imaging experiment with sixteen participants, unpleasant sounds produced larger responses in the amygdala on both sides and in primary auditory cortex, and the amygdala, but not auditory cortex, was most sensitive to the rough modulation range.
The authors suggest roughness may work by targeting subcortical circuits that speed up reactions to danger.

That is a real finding about a specific acoustic feature, and it supports part of the headline: some sounds are built, by evolution or by engineers, to grab attention and register as alarming. Several limits apply. The participants rated sounds in a laboratory, and the ratings concern unpleasantness and fear, not whether anyone felt unsafe in a room. The imaging shows where activity rose and does not show why a person felt what they felt. As an anatomist, I read a scan result as a location and not an explanation.

The words "before you know why" carry a second claim, that the response precedes awareness. On that, the literature is less settled. A 2010 commentary by Luiz Pessoa on emotion and attention says the question of whether emotional stimuli are processed automatically, independent of attention, "remains unresolved and controversial," and the evidence it discusses comes mostly from faces and not sounds.

So the careful version of the headline is that rough sounds are detected quickly and engage structures involved in appraising danger, while how much of the effect happens outside awareness is still debated. That is my summary of two papers, and a hearing scientist would put it better.

blocks.x: The hospital as a place where this matters

r: Aliman's recent work moves the question into a setting close to my own field, medicine. Her site lists Centering Listening in Designed Places of Care, produced from 2024 to 2026 and shown at ArtEra at Erasmus MC in Rotterdam. The project invites viewers to reflect on the sounds they meet in healthcare settings and to imagine their future soundscape, presenting digital sculptures designed with sound as the primary sculpting material.

Her page says that instead of modifying existing machines to "fix" their sound, she proposes that the design of medical machines consider sound and function together from the start. It says her research office gathered insights through surveys of patients and medical professionals at Erasmus MC and two workshops there.

The site also reports that she received the Better Sound Award 2026 in the Sound Art and Social and Culture categories of the International Sound Directory Awards for it, in a news item dated September 21, 2026.

The documented background is not flattering to hospitals. Johns Hopkins acoustical engineers reported in 2005 that average daytime sound levels in hospitals worldwide had risen from 57 to 72 decibels since 1960, and nighttime levels from 42 to 60, all above the World Health Organization's 1995 guideline of 35 decibels for patient rooms.

A 2013 study in Critical Care measured five adult intensive care units in the Thames Valley in England. Average levels always exceeded 45 dBA, peaks above 85 dBA occurred at every site up to 16 times an hour overnight, and the WHO levels could be reached in a side room only by switching all equipment off.
The authors concluded those levels are too low to be achievable in an ICU as it operates.

Alarm design appears in that study too. The authors recorded alarms from a Philips patient monitor, a ventilator and an infusion pump, and report that staff considered some monitor alerts disproportionate to their urgency, a mismatch between loudness and importance that may lead to desensitization.

Put the two papers side by side and a pattern emerges. If alarm sounds are engineered with rough modulation because it grabs attention, then a room full of them is a room full of signals built to be hard to ignore.
That inference is mine. Neither paper says it, and the ICU study did not measure how patients or staff responded to roughness in particular.
What the record cannot say is whether Aliman's approach works. The page I read reports surveys and workshops, not outcomes, and I have not seen her data.
An award is recognition of the work, and it does not show that redesigning a machine's sound changes how a patient feels.

blocks.x: Four other questions about technology and the body

r: Julia Janssen "makes the challenges of our digitalizing society and relationship with AI tangible through performative and interactive installations," in the awards' words.
Her own site lists an exhibition of Chadding and Ask Anything at the SFF Building on Strijp-S during Dutch Design Week, October 17 to 25, 2026.

Her project page describes Chadding as a conversational installation that debuted in Davos during the World Economic Forum in 2026 and has since been rebuilt as a touring model, made of three large hovering pieces carried by metal frames. It says that she questioned ChatGPT about whether conversations might include ads, and received different answers on repeated asking, from yes to probably not to no. The page concludes that answers are often neither neutral nor objective and that "plausibility" replaces truth.

Those are Janssen's claims about her work and about what the chatbot said. A chatbot's answer to a question about its own business model is not evidence about the business model. The public record is that on January 16, 2026 OpenAI said it would begin testing ads in ChatGPT for logged-in adults in the United States on its free and low-cost Go tiers, placed at the bottom of answers when a relevant sponsored product exists, and that a company executive said ads would not influence the answers.
I could not open OpenAI's own announcement, so I rely on a trade site's report of it.

The installation's point, as I read the page, is about automation bias, which the International AI Safety Report 2026 defines as the tendency of users to rely on automated outputs while discounting contradictory information.
The work asks whether a smooth, plausible answer makes us stop checking. The report treats that tendency as a documented risk, and says it discourages active reasoning and verification.

Sondi, a Cameroonian-German artist and researcher based in Amsterdam, builds immersive 3D worlds in game engines that, she writes, trace encoded biases, algorithmic discrimination and game mechanics, and she holds a BA from the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague (2021) and an MA from the Sandberg Institute (2023) and teaches at the Design Academy Eindhoven.
Ülkühan Akgül is described by the awards as bridging heritage craftsmanship with digital media.

Amsterdam Fashion Week reported in December 2025 that Akgül and Batuhan Demir, working jointly as ÜLKÜHAN&BATUHAN, won the Frans Molenaar Prize 2025, a 10,000 euro prize established in 1995 and awarded again after an eight-year pause.

Esmay Wagemans, an Amsterdam-based artist, studied Transformation Design at the Willem de Kooning Academy and uses lifecasting and molding with silicone, resin and composites to make wearable pieces that her site places between installation and cyborg fashion.
I have not found a published DDW location for Sondi, Akgül or Wagemans, and Aliman's site, in the news items I read, lists a September workshop at the Nieuwe Instituut and no DDW 2026 presentation.
A finalist may well show work I could not locate.

blocks.x: What a shortlist can and cannot tell us

r: A shortlist is a selection by a jury, after a nomination process, against stated criteria. It says the jury found these practices worth attention. It does not say the work answers its questions, and it does not rank the finalists.
The ceremony will name three winners, and the other twelve remain finalists whom the same jury chose.

The criteria are also worth noticing. They reward coherence of portfolio, a boundary-pushing approach, breadth across disciplines and potential influence, and they say nothing about whether a project's claims have been tested.

That is appropriate for a design award. It does mean that a work asking whether sound can make us feel unsafe, or whether a chatbot erodes trust, will be judged as a practice, and the factual questions inside it stay open for researchers. I would like to see the two in conversation.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who wins, where most finalists show work during the week, or what the ceremony will say.

On the science, I have read two papers on sound and fear in the human brain and two on hospital noise, and I have not surveyed the field. The Arnal study used short laboratory sounds and small groups. The hospital studies are from 2005 and 2012 and from the United States and England, and I found no equivalent measurement for Erasmus MC or for Dutch hospitals.
I do not know what Aliman's surveys and workshops found.
On Chadding, I rely on Janssen's page and a trade report about OpenAI's announcement. I have not seen the installation and cannot judge how well it represents what chatbots do.
On the organizers, the awards sit within the same foundation that organizes Dutch Design Week, and the jury is assembled by its chair.
I have no information about how nominations were weighed.
When did a sound last change your mood before you could say why, and was it designed to?
