posts.title: If the prompt is the new brush, who is the artist?
posts.subtitle: A Dutch Design Week seminar at Next Nature Museum calls the prompt a creative instrument. Courts in the United States, China and Europe have already tested that claim, and they do not agree.
posts.seoTitle: If the prompt is the new brush, who is the artist?
posts.description: Next Nature Museum calls the prompt a creative instrument. What courts and regulators say about who authors a prompted image.

r: A brush carries the mark of a hand, and a prompt carries a request that a machine answers.

Next Nature Museum in Eindhoven holds PROMPT: Not the Brush, but the Prompt on Friday, October 23, 2026, and lists it in the Dutch Design Week program. The DDW listing and the museum's own event page open with the same claim. Oil paint, photography, video, the internet and 3D printing each transformed the arts, they say, and a new artistic medium is emerging in artificial intelligence. The prompt, which both pages define as the instruction through which an artist directs an AI, is becoming a new creative instrument. Those are the organizers' words and the organizers' position.

This essay uses public documents only: the organizers' pages, court rulings, agency texts and legal commentary, all listed at the end. It reports no visit to the evening and no conversation with anyone involved. I come to this as an anatomist and medical educator who writes about design and technology, so what follows is a reading of sources for general information, not legal advice.

I want to take the claim seriously. The way to do that is to ask what the word "artist" in that definition would have to mean, and what courts and lawmakers in Europe, the United States, China and the United Kingdom have said so far about the person who types the instruction.

blocks.x: The organizers ask the authorship question themselves

r: The DDW listing names no speakers and no book. The museum's own event page names both, and it asks the authorship question out loud. It wants to know whether the prompt has become the new sketchbook. It asks what originality means when humans and algorithms create together. And it asks what the role of the artist is in a world where anyone can generate images.

The page also describes a book. PROMPT: Art & Design in the Age of Artificial Intelligence is edited by Peter Lunenfeld and Mieke Gerritzen, and the page calls its launch the highlight of the evening. According to the page, the book gathers dozens of artists, designers and researchers who share their ideas about AI and also the prompts behind their works, something the page says usually stays hidden. It presents the prompt as a new artistic language, in the page's phrasing, and compares it to the sketchbook, where artists once revealed their working process.

The publisher's own product page describes a 288-page paperback, due in fall 2026, that treats AI as a new medium for human creativity comparable to photography, cinema and digital media. A listing from Hachette UK gives a release date of November 19, 2026 and a price of 15.99 pounds.
A book that prints prompts next to the works they produced is a useful object for this question, because the legal discussion below turns on exactly what a prompt does and does not control.

blocks.x: What the evening is, and who is on it

r: The museum's page gives a run of show. A welcome at 19:00 from the moderator, Marsha Simon, is followed by presentations from Lev Manovich, Noëlle van Dijk and Silvio Lorusso. A performance by the theater collective URLAND comes next. Then Peter Lunenfeld, Rosa Menkman, Constant Dullaart and Sander Veenhof give short introductions and join a panel, and the evening closes at 20:40 with the book launch, which includes Mieke Gerritzen, Harm van Kessel of BIS Publishers and Lunenfeld.

The page describes Manovich as a Presidential Professor at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and the author of Artificial Aesthetics: Generative AI, Art and Visual Media (2024). It says Lorusso teaches at Design Academy Eindhoven, and that Gerritzen is Creative Director of the Next Nature Museum.
Lunenfeld confirmed the evening and the speaker list on his own site on August 29, 2026, and described himself and Gerritzen as the people who produced the book.

The listing's practical details are these. The DDW page says access is paid with registration, the event type is a seminar, and the venue is the Next Nature Museum at Noord Brabantlaan 1A, 5652 LA Eindhoven, which DDW places in its West area as location C1.
The DDW highlights release of September 29, 2026 names Prompt as an AI art event at the museum.

One detail conflicts between sources. The DDW listing gives the hours as 18:30 to 22:00. The museum's event page and Lunenfeld's post both give 18:30 to 21:00, and the museum's own schedule ends with the book launch that starts at 20:40.
I take the organizer's figure, 21:00, as the better supported end time, because the organizer wrote the schedule and a co-editor repeated it. The DDW figure needs confirming with DDW.

blocks.x: Photography had this argument in 1884

r: The listing's list of earlier media is a good place to start, because the law has already had this argument about one of them. In Burrow-Giles Lithographic Co. v. Sarony, decided on March 17, 1884, the United States Supreme Court heard a defendant argue that a photograph is a mere mechanical reproduction of physical features. On that view the effect of light on a prepared plate may be a discovery, but the rest of the process is mechanical, with no room for originality.

The Court did not accept that for the photograph in the case, a portrait of Oscar Wilde. It relied on the trial findings that the photographer had made the picture from his own original mental conception, which he gave visible form by posing Wilde, selecting and arranging the costume and accessories, arranging the light and shade and evoking the expression. Those findings, the Court said, showed an original work of art of which he was the author.

The opinion also turned on proof. Whether a photograph is a mechanical reproduction or an original work, it said, depends on facts of originality, thought and conception, and those facts have to be established when copyright is disputed.

The Court also quoted an English appeal decision from 1883, Nottage v. Jackson, that had asked who the author of a photograph was when an employee operated the camera. One judge there described the author as the person who superintended the arrangement and was effectively the cause of the picture.
I find that phrase worth carrying forward. It looks at who shaped the result, not at who pressed the button. The modern rulings below ask the same thing about a person who presses "generate."

blocks.x: The United States: prompts alone are not enough, for now

r: In the United States, the Copyright Office has published the most detailed analysis of prompts. Its Part 2 report on copyrightability came out on January 29, 2025. It concludes that, given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not give users enough control over the output to make them its authors. Prompts function as instructions that convey ideas, and even detailed ones do not control how the system processes them.

The report takes up the claim that revising a prompt many times should change the answer. It says no. The time and effort spent are irrelevant, because copyright protects original expression and not hard work. And submitting a revised prompt, in its words, is like re-rolling the dice: it produces more outputs to choose from but does not change the user's degree of control. The report also says that identical prompts can generate different outputs, which it takes as further evidence that control is limited.

The same report says what does count. Human authors keep copyright in their own expression that is perceptible in an AI output, such as a drawing the AI incorporated. They keep it in the creative selection, coordination or arrangement of AI material, and in creative modifications of an output. Tools that let a user select and place individual elements can produce copyrightable results, case by case. The Office says the question can be settled under existing law and sees no need for new legislation. It also says that further advances could give prompts enough control some day, and that a different conclusion might follow.

Two registration decisions show the line in practice. In Zarya of the Dawn, a graphic novel, the Office wrote on February 21, 2023 that the author owned the text and the selection, coordination and arrangement of the words and images, but that the Midjourney-generated images were not the product of human authorship.

In the case of Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, a Midjourney image that won a state fair art prize, the Office's Review Board wrote on September 5, 2023 that the applicant's claim of at least 624 revisions and prompts did not make him the author, because the steps depended on how Midjourney processed them. The Board said the work could not be registered unless the AI-generated material was disclaimed, and it left open a new application that disclaims it and claims the human edits.

That second case is in court. According to a case tracker, the applicant, Jason Allen, sued in the District of Colorado on September 26, 2024, moved for summary judgment on August 25, 2025, and was awaiting a ruling as of March 30, 2026. I could not find a ruling after that date, and I could not open the court's docket directly.

A third case is often cited with these two and it deserves a precise description. In Thaler v. Perlmutter, decided on March 18, 2025, the D.C. Circuit held that the Copyright Act requires an author to be a human being. But Stephen Thaler had named his software as the sole author of the work and himself only as its owner, and he told the Copyright Office the work lacked traditional human authorship. The court did not decide how much a person's prompting counts. It said the rule requires only that the author be a human being, the person who created, operated or used the AI, and it noted that the Copyright Office had already refused some applications where a human was listed, citing Zarya of the Dawn.
The Supreme Court denied review on March 2, 2026.
So Thaler settles that a machine cannot be the author. It leaves the prompter's question where the Copyright Office report put it.

blocks.x: China decided a similar picture the other way

r: The most useful contrast comes from a court that was shown a prompt-driven image and asked the brush question directly. In a judgment dated November 27, 2023, the Beijing Internet Court dealt with a picture a plaintiff had made with the open-source image model Stable Diffusion and then posted on a social media platform. A defendant had used the picture without permission and removed the plaintiff's watermark.

The court found that the picture was protected. It reasoned that the plaintiff had designed the character's presentation, chosen and ordered prompt words and negative prompt words, set parameters, and chosen among outputs. After a first result, the plaintiff added prompt words and changed parameters, and the court treated those adjustments as aesthetic choices. The court also noted that different people entering different prompts and settings would get different pictures, so the result was not a mechanical product.

The judgment reads almost like a reply to the museum's listing. The court compared the situation to cameras. Before cameras, it said, people needed painting skill to reproduce an object, and as long as a photograph reflects the photographer's original intellectual investment it is a protected work. It treated the AI model as a tool with no free will and no legal personality. It found that the model's designer had made a tool and was not the author of the picture, and it noted that the model's license said the designer claimed no rights in the output.

Two details in the judgment are easy to miss. The court awarded the plaintiff 500 yuan in damages. And it said the plaintiff should prominently mark the AI technology used, in line with good faith and the public's right to know, and it accepted the plaintiff's "AI illustration" hashtag as proper practice.

The Copyright Office report describes this case as one where the court relied on more than 150 prompts. I read the English translation of the judgment and found no count of prompts in it, so I will not repeat that number as the court's.

blocks.x: The Netherlands and the EU start from a human maker

r: Dutch law is built around the word "maker." The Auteurswet, in Article 1, defines copyright as the exclusive right of the maker of a work of literature, science or art. Article 10 lists the kinds of works, among them drawings, paintings, photographic works and film, and closes with any product in the literary, scientific or artistic domain, in whatever way or form it is expressed.

The Dutch Supreme Court has said what makes a product a work. In its ruling of May 30, 2008 about transcripts of conversations with police, known as the Endstra tapes, the Hoge Raad set out two elements. The product must have its own original character, which means its form is not borrowed from another work. And it must bear the personal stamp of the maker, which means a form that results from creative human labor and thus from creative choices, a product of the human mind. Anything so banal or trivial that no creative labor can be pointed to falls outside.

The same ruling added a point that matters for prompting. The court said this is a characteristic that can be read from the product itself, so a maker cannot be required to have consciously set out to create a work or to have consciously made creative choices.

That cuts in two directions. A prompter cannot win by saying "I meant it as art," and a prompter's lack of a hand-made mark is not decisive by itself either. What counts is whether the form that resulted came from the person's creative choices. The case was sent back to another court on that question, so the ruling states the test and does not decide the tapes.

At EU level, the standard is the author's own intellectual creation, expressed through free and creative choices. The UK government's March 2026 report on copyright and AI summarizes it that way and notes that the EU provides no specific protection for computer-generated works without a human author.

A December 4, 2025 judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union on applied art, Mio and konektra, restated the standard and added that a free choice is not necessarily a creative one. A Dutch law firm's summary of the ruling says the focus must stay on the object and whether it embodies creative choices.
I could not open the judgment on the Court's own site, so I rely on that summary and on the UK report for the Court's wording.

On AI specifically, the Council of the EU published a summary of member states' answers on December 20, 2024. It found no national legislation, guidance or soft law on copyright in AI-generated content, and a general view that works may be eligible only if the human input in their creative process was significant. It also found a clear understanding that only a natural person can be an author, so purely AI-generated works cannot be protected.

Three states reported court decisions, without naming the courts. One decision held that a logo made with AI is not automatically ineligible and that each case depends on the human input. Another held that an image the plaintiff made with AI was not an original result of a natural person's creative activity. The third concerned a training data set.

A named European example is the Municipal Court of Prague in 2024. It held that a DALL-E image of two parties signing a contract could not be a work, because it was not the result of a natural person's creative activity. A commentator noted that the court did not rule out authorship by the claimant, whose own witness evidence was not enough to prove it.

On March 10, 2026, the European Parliament adopted a resolution on copyright and generative AI, which, according to a summary by the European Audiovisual Observatory, insists that content generated fully by AI which does not meet the criteria for copyright protection should remain ineligible, with the public domain status of such outputs clearly determined. I could not open the resolution itself, so that is a secondary report of it.

The United Kingdom stands apart on paper. Section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 says that for a computer-generated work, the author is the person who undertakes the arrangements necessary for its creation.
The government's March 2026 report says the protection departs from copyright's core rationale and proposes to remove it, while continuing to protect works made with AI assistance.
A provision that once looked like a ready answer for prompters is, on the government's own proposal, on its way out.

I did not find a Dutch court ruling on whether a prompted image is a work. The Council's summary leaves three court decisions unnamed, so I cannot rule one out. What I can say is that no source I read names a Dutch ruling on the question.

blocks.x: Three imagined prompts

r: Authorship questions are easier to think about with cases. These are hypothetical and describe no real person or work, and I use them only to sort the sources above.

Imagine a one-line prompt, typed once, with the first image accepted as it comes. Imagine a second person who writes four hundred words of instructions, supplies reference material, rejects dozens of results, rewrites the request each time and then edits the final image by hand. Imagine a third person who asks an AI to suggest prompts and picks one.

The sources do not give a single answer, and the cases fit the three people differently. For the first, the Prague court's facts are the closest: a basic prompt and a claimant whose own witness evidence was not enough. The Copyright Office's report points the same way, since prompts alone are unlikely to give enough control.

For the second, the answers divide. The Copyright Office treats repeated prompting as re-rolling, which would not help, but it protects what a person adds by hand, which is where the editing would count. The Beijing court looked at the same kind of iteration and counted it as choice.
The Dutch standard asks whether the resulting form came from creative human labor and creative choices, judged from the product, so the hand edits are where that would show.

For the third, no source I read speaks to prompts suggested by the machine. The Copyright Office report quotes a view that selecting one output from several offered is not itself a creative act, and that is the nearest point of reference.

I would add one thought from my own field. In anatomy teaching, a diagram earns its place by what its maker chose to show and what the maker left out, not by how long it took to draw. The Copyright Office makes the same point about effort in different words, and I find it a useful way to hold the question.

blocks.x: Authorship, ownership and the terms of use are three questions

r: Being called the artist, holding the copyright and holding a contractual right to use an image are different things. Thaler shows the first two pulling apart: he claimed to be the owner of a work whose author, on his own account, was a machine, and the court answered that the author has to be human.
The Beijing court looked at a third layer. It read the model's license and noted that the designer claimed no rights in the output.

A tool's terms of use matter for the same reason. Where a work is not protected by copyright, a contract binds only its parties, and a stranger who copies the image is not one of them. A commentator on the Prague decision draws that same practical conclusion, that anyone relying on AI images in Europe may need contractual protections because copyright may not be available.

I tried to read the current terms of two widely used image tools and could not, because both sites refused automated access. So I cannot tell you what they say today, and I recommend reading the page yourself.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know whether the speakers will address any of this. The museum's page asks about originality and the artist's role, and it does not mention copyright or ownership.

I do not know whether the book's printed prompts are presented as protectable. The Copyright Office report says that prompts themselves, if sufficiently creative, may be copyrightable as text, and that this gives their author no copyright in the output. The Review Board said in 2023 that it could not consider the creativity of one applicant's prompts because he had not disclosed them.
The end time is 21:00 on the organizer's pages and 22:00 on the DDW listing, and I have not been able to confirm which is current.
The Allen case may have been decided since March 30, 2026. I found no ruling and could not open the docket.
I could not read the Court of Justice's own text of Mio and konektra, the European Parliament's resolution, or any Dutch ruling on a prompted image.

The Court of Justice has a first generative-AI case before it, Like Company v. Google, referred by a Hungarian court on April 3, 2025. Its questions concern reproduction and press publishers' rights, not who the author of an output is.
A ruling there would not settle the question of this essay. I read only a law firm's description of the referral.

blocks.x: A question to carry into the room

r: If you make images with an AI tool and plan to sell one, three questions are open to you now, whatever the evening concludes. What did I write? What did the tool add? What do its terms say I own? The first is about your own record: prompts and the choices around them are easy to lose. The Prague court found a claimant's own witness evidence too thin, and the Copyright Office asks what the person actually controlled. A saved history of what you asked, what you rejected and what you changed by hand is the kind of record that helps answer both.

The next step is a small one. Open the terms for one tool you use and find the sentence about who holds what comes out of it. Then ask whether that sentence matches how you describe yourself when you share the image. If the prompt is the new brush, whose name belongs on the canvas, and what would you show to prove it?

posts.title: What would you pack if you moved out of a platform?
posts.subtitle: Trisha Koevoets frames leaving Big Tech as a house move. The law gives you two ways to take your data with you, and the Commission itself says the harder part is finding the door.
posts.seoTitle: What would you pack if you left a platform?
posts.description: A DDW project calls itself a Big Tech moving service. What GDPR Article 20 and DMA Article 6(9) let you take, and what they leave behind.

r: Trisha Koevoets opens her Dutch Design Week project with a question: when was the last time you felt at home on the internet?

Her project, The Internet Used To Be a Home, is listed as an exhibition at station F4, Young Graduates HUB | DDW x Design Perron, Kennedyplein 300 in Eindhoven. It is open daily from October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00, and a DDW ticket is required. The listing contrasts an older internet of pages, hyperlinks and websites with an endless stream of algorithmized content that keeps people on Big Tech platforms, and it calls the project "The Big Tech moving out service." The listing describes her as a Dutch designer from Breda who focuses on digital human rights. All of this is her stated position.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, the maker's own published research pages, official texts from the European Commission and the European data protection authorities, and a few sources on internet history. It reports no visit to the exhibit and no conversation with the maker. I am an anatomist and medical educator who writes about design and technology, so this is a reading of sources for general information, not legal advice.
I like the metaphor because it makes a technical question easy to say out loud. If a platform is a home, what do you take when you leave, and what does the law say you are owed?

blocks.x: The maker's own research says more than the listing does

r: The listing is short. The maker has also published a long working record of the project on a personal site on the hotglue platform, which says it was last modified on June 18, 2026. It describes itself as an appendix to her graduation exploration.

That site names the project The internet used to be a home. It also settles a question the earlier version of this essay left open. Her portfolio lists a project called The Internet Used To Be A Place, and the portfolio's entry links straight to the same research site, so the two titles belong to one body of work. "Place" is also the title of one chapter of her desk research.

The research site states a research question about how the state of the internet has changed in recent years and how far that affects daily life, and a design question about how an interactive critical design installation could start a conversation about the internet's current state and our longing for a better one.

It reports 13 surveys with participants aged 17 to 29, and a dot survey on posters in public space in which the tallies shown were 20 for the internet of the past, 3 for the internet of now and 3 for the middle. The site itself says the survey group was selective, which is why it added the dot survey.
Those are small, self-selected samples, and she presents them as steps in a design process, not as a measurement of anyone's opinion.

The final concept, in her words, grew out of 26 different concepts. It is a fictional moving company where internet users can move everything they love on the internet to a better new internet, imagined as a digital city focused on a social internet. The installation takes the form of two linked moving boxes, which can be experienced separately, and a website that presents itself as a service.

Her design criteria add that the installation should be made for public space and work autonomously, should use a layer of irony over a heavier message, and should start a conversation as a work of critical and speculative design.
I have not seen the installation. This is what the maker's published process says it is.

blocks.x: The old web she remembers, checked against the record

r: Her research page tells a story about the old internet that is worth checking, because the exit metaphor depends on it. Some of its claims, and the context around them, can be tested against other sources.

The first concerns the web's openness. CERN's own history says that on April 30, 1993 it put the three components of the World Wide Web software in the public domain, and that in 1994 it moved to an open source license under which anyone could use and modify the software. That release is one reason anyone could build on the web without asking permission.

The second concerns GeoCities, which her page uses as the model of a homely old web, with neighborhoods and residents. Archive Team's record agrees on the structure: GeoCities was founded in 1994 and bought by Yahoo in 1999, and it gave users personal publishing space organized in neighborhoods. It also records how the story ended. Yahoo announced in April 2009 that it would close GeoCities, set October 26, 2009 as the date in July 2009, and offered paid hosting plans to move data elsewhere. Volunteers then copied as much as they could.
Her page says 38 million sites went dark. The sources I opened say millions of files and accounts and give no total, so I cannot confirm that number.

I read that history as an argument against one half of the nostalgia. The old web had a door, in her image, but the door was a feature of how pages linked to each other. It was not a right, and when a landlord closed the building the only exit offered for sale was a hosting plan. The exit she wants is a more modern idea, which is why the law is worth looking at. This is my reading, not a finding of either source.

The third claim concerns infinite scroll. Her page says that in 2006 Aza Raskin proposed removing the next button. The BBC reported on July 3, 2018 that Raskin designed infinite scroll in 2006 and had said he did not recognize how addictive it could be.
That matches her account in outline, though the BBC does not mention a next button.

The fourth concerns the word she builds her argument on. Her page says Cory Doctorow coined enshittification in 2022 and published a book of that name in 2022. The first part is consistent with his site, which uses the term in a post of November 28, 2022 about Amazon, and in a post of January 21, 2023 that states the cycle: platforms are first good to their users, then abuse users to benefit business customers, then abuse those customers to take the value for themselves.
The book part does not hold. Doctorow's own site lists the book as published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux on October 7, 2025.
Her page also describes the cycle in three steps of its own wording, a simplified version of his.

Doctorow draws a conclusion that matches the exit theme. In the 2023 post he writes that policymakers should focus on freedom of exit, the right to leave a sinking platform while staying connected to the communities left behind and keeping the data created there.
That is the right this essay is about.

blocks.x: What the law says you can take

r: Two European laws give a user rights to take data away. They overlap and they differ, and the listing does not say which one the project has in mind.

The older is Article 20 of the General Data Protection Regulation. According to the guidelines of the Article 29 Working Party of European data protection authorities, last revised on April 5, 2017, it gives a person the right to receive the personal data they provided to a controller in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, and to transmit it to another controller without hindrance. Where technically feasible, the data can be sent directly from one controller to the other. The right applies to data processed by automated means on the basis of consent or a contract.

The guidelines read "provided by" broadly, to include observed data such as search history, traffic data and location data, but they exclude inferred and derived data created by the service, such as the results of an algorithm. They also say the GDPR does not oblige a controller to adopt systems compatible with a competitor's, though it forbids creating barriers to the transmission.

That exclusion matters for the theme of the project. The profile a feed builds about you to decide what to show next is the kind of derived data the guidelines place outside the right. You can ask for your posts, your likes and your search history. The model of you that the platform made from them is not part of the package.

The newer rule is Article 6(9) of the Digital Markets Act, which applies to a short list of very large platforms. The Commission's portal lists seven designated gatekeepers, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Booking, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft, with 23 core platform services in total, among them YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn.

The text of Article 6(9), as quoted in the Commission's and the European Data Protection Board's draft joint guidelines, requires gatekeepers to give end users and third parties they authorize, at their request and free of charge, effective portability of data provided by the end user or generated through the end user's activity, including free tools and continuous, real-time access.
The Commission's portal summarizes it as three things: portability, free tools, and continuous and real-time access, with the user's permission extending to third-party businesses.

The draft joint guidelines explain how Article 6(9) differs from Article 20. It applies whatever legal basis the platform relied on for the data, it requires continuous and real-time access, and it must be free. It covers data actively provided and data generated through use, including data the gatekeeper observes such as engagement, and it reaches data processed on the device. Like the GDPR right, it does not cover data the gatekeeper derives or infers. Unlike the GDPR right, it can include personal data about other people, where those people appear in the dataset the user provided or generated.
These are draft guidelines that went to public consultation in late 2025. The Commission said on March 12, 2026 that it expects the final text in the last quarter of 2026.

I could not open the regulation's text on the EU's legal database, which returned only a site shell to my requests, so the wording above is quoted from the Commission and the Board's draft and the Commission's portal.

blocks.x: The tools that exist now

r: The portal lists the tools by company. Alphabet offers a Data Portability API, and the portal's example is a user sharing Google Search history with an authorized third-party app, with the user choosing the duration, up to 180 days per authorization, at no cost. Amazon, Apple, Booking and ByteDance have their own pages, Meta lists a page for downloading information and a developer guide, and Microsoft lists LinkedIn tools for downloading account data and for member data portability.

The Commission's review of the DMA, published on April 28, 2026, says the tools are in use. Its staff working document states that gatekeepers rolled out new application programming interfaces and enhanced existing ones, many of which started as solutions for GDPR Article 20, that let end users download or transfer posts and likes on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, purchase history on Amazon and search history on Google. It says thousands of end users are taking advantage of them and around 40 third parties have integrated with the interfaces. It also reports that Meta merged two tools, Download Your Information and Transfer Your Information, into one interface called Export Your Information, with recurring transfers up to three years, and that Apple and Alphabet are building a device portability solution whose beta started in December 2025.

I would not read "thousands" as success or failure. The Commission gives no total and no share of users, so I cannot say what fraction of users that is. What the document does show is that the Commission itself treats finding the tools as a problem: it says it will step up efforts to raise awareness of the portability obligations and has set up a page that gathers links in one place. Respondents to its consultation asked for clearer guidance and more effective mechanisms.
A footnote adds that Amazon's portability solution is offered outside the EU at a fee.
All of that is about finding the door, which is a different matter from having the right.

blocks.x: Where would the boxes go?

r: A move needs a destination. The Mastodon documentation shows what a working exit looks like on the receiving side. You create an account on another server, export your list of people you follow, set an alias, and then move your followers, whose accounts are switched over automatically if their software supports it. The same page says your posts are not moved, because of technical limitations, and that follows, blocks, mutes and bookmarks have to be imported from exported files separately.
That is a real moving service with a real gap in it. The people come along. The history stays behind.

The people question is the one the maker's own research flags first. Her desk research lists the lack of large alternatives as the first reason people do not leave: if you want to go and keep your friends, everyone has to go, and they have to bring their own friends.
Doctorow describes the same hostage dynamic on Facebook in the 2023 post.

The law treats this partly as a data question. The data protection authorities say a contact directory relates to the person who built it, so a controller should transmit it to that person, as long as the receiving service uses it only for personal purposes and does not use the contacts for its own, such as marketing.
The draft joint guidelines add that Article 6(9) can reach personal data of other people in the dataset, and that those people should be informed about recipients of ported data.
The data can move. Whether your friends move with it is a decision for them.

Her fieldwork offers one human version of the same finding. In a prototype where test users built their own internet by deciding who should be in charge of its places, she reports that people put "human" in the places they most like to visit and machine and surveillance in the places they like less, using terms she deliberately left unexplained.
That is a small test and not a general finding. It does fit the project's suggestion that people want a different destination as well as a way out.

blocks.x: A right and a door are different things

r: Suppose, hypothetically, that a person decides to move their photo library from one service to another. The right to the data exists on paper. The practical questions are whether they can find the tool, understand what it will give them, and get a file the next service can use. A right can exist and still be hard to use.

The Commission's phrase "free tools to make portability easy" is a design requirement as much as a legal one. Easy is a property of an interface, and no regulation can supply it by itself. Neither the maker's pages, the listing nor the Commission's documents measure how easy any given tool is. I have not tested one. The one thing the Commission does state is that it intends to raise awareness, which implies that the existing awareness is limited.

The project's title suggests a way to hold both ideas. A house has a door, and it also has an address you can find. The maker's installation, as described, is a joke with a serious edge: a moving company for the internet that does not yet exist. The sources suggest that parts of it do exist, in tools provided by the gatekeepers and in federated services that accept a move, and that the missing part is the one she is designing for, which is the experience of finding it.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the exhibit contains beyond the maker's own description of two moving boxes and a service-style website. The listing does not describe its objects and the press kit was not opened.
I do not know whether the project refers to the law at all. The maker's pages I read do not mention the GDPR or the Digital Markets Act.
The school is not named on the pages I read; her site and research pages say Communication & Multimedia Design, abbreviated CMD.
I could not confirm the 38 million figure for GeoCities, and the one fact about uptake I have is the Commission's statement of thousands of users and about 40 third parties.

I did not read the regulations' texts on the EU database, only quotations of them in official documents, and the joint guidelines are drafts. I did not test any portability tool, and I did not cover services outside the gatekeeper list, such as X, Bluesky or Mastodon, apart from Mastodon's own documentation. The GDPR applies to them as controllers, but I read no source about their tools.

blocks.x: One account, three questions

r: If you want to try this yourself, pick one account you would hate to lose. Ask what you can take, where the tool is and where you would go. If the account is on one of the seven listed gatekeepers, start with the company's portability page linked from the Commission's portal. If it is not, ask the service for your data under the GDPR and see what comes back. Write the answers down before you need them.
The last question is the hardest, because it asks whether anywhere else would feel like home. Where would you go?

posts.title: What does an AI guess about soil, and what does the soil say back?
posts.subtitle: Merel Mierop's NAITURE sets image predictions of decay beside buried fabric. What would make that comparison fair, and what does EU law now say about labeling the AI side?
posts.seoTitle: What does an AI guess about soil?
posts.description: NAITURE buried fabric letters and compared them with AI predictions. What a fair test needs, and the EU AI Act labeling rule as it stands.

r: A prediction means more once something real can answer it.

NAITURE, by Merel Mierop, is listed as an exhibition at station F4, Young Graduates HUB | DDW x Design Perron, Kennedyplein 300 in Eindhoven. It is open daily from October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00, and a Dutch Design Week ticket is required. The same project appears on the website of ArtEZ University of the Arts as a 2026 Graphic Design bachelor's project from Zwolle, on a page last updated on June 23, 2026. Both pages are the maker's account. This essay draws on public documents only. It reports no visit to the exhibit and no conversation with the maker.
I like the design of the test. The listing sets up a question with an answer that does not depend on anyone's opinion, because fabric buried in soil does something, and then it can be looked at.

blocks.x: What the project says it did

r: The first part, according to the listing, buries a series of fabric letters in the earth as material input for nature. An AI receives a text prompt and a photograph of the original letter. The listing says the prompt does not direct the outcome and only gives information about the material, the environment and the conditions, so the AI must determine for itself how those factors act. After periods the listing puts at one month to one year, the letters are dug up and compared with the AI's predictions.

The ArtEZ page gives nearly the same account and adds two things the listing does not. It says the letters stayed in the ground for periods ranging from several months to a year, and it says some disappeared entirely and were absorbed by nature.

Those two descriptions of the burial time differ, one month to one year on the DDW page and several months to a year on the ArtEZ page. Both are the maker's words, and the ArtEZ page is the more recent and the more specific, so I treat "several months to a year" as the better figure and the DDW range as a wider statement of the same experiment. I cannot settle it from the pages alone.

The second part, in both accounts, uses AI as a design tool. The listing says the specifically chosen uppercase letter R combines a bowl, a diagonal leg, a horizontal arm and a vertical stem, and that from those forms AI can generate a complete Latin alphabet.

ArtEZ states the question behind the project as where the boundaries of AI lie when it comes to predicting natural processes through image generation. It also says AI can reproduce but cannot live as nature does, within the impermanence of emergence, transformation and decay, and that the project has no definitive ending because AI keeps evolving.
One more detail comes from the listing's hero image, whose caption reads "Close-up unbleached cotton and synthetic felt" and is credited to the maker.

It does not say which letters were made of which material or whether the image shows buried fabric. It does tell me the project works with a natural fiber and a synthetic one, and that matters for what follows.

blocks.x: Why soil is a hard thing to predict from a picture

r: Whether a prediction counts as good depends on what the real process depends on. Three sources give me a sense of that.

The first comes from the Netherlands. In 2013 a team at Utrecht University introduced the Tea Bag Index, which uses commercial tea bags as standardized test kits for decomposition. By burying two tea types of contrasting decomposability, they construct a decomposition curve from a single measurement in time. Their paper reports that within one ecosystem the index responds to differences in conditions such as soil temperature and moisture content.
That is the reason the maker's prompt is limited to conditions. In a real burial, the conditions decide the outcome, and a sentence cannot carry a soil's temperature and wetness through a winter.

The second concerns the fabric itself. A 2023 paper in the journal Materials, in a literature survey, describes a soil burial study of fabrics made from cotton, viscose, modal, Tencel, polylactic acid, polyethylene terephthalate and polyacrylonitrile. After four months the weight loss for modal, cotton and viscose fabrics was about 90 percent, Tencel about 60 percent, and among the synthetic fabrics only the polylactic acid sample lost weight.
The same survey cites a field study that ranked the degradation rates of rayon, cotton and Tencel as rayon above cotton above Tencel.

I cannot map those results onto the maker's letters, because I do not know her fabrics, her soil or her sites. They do show that a cotton letter and a synthetic felt letter should not be expected to meet the same fate, and that this is a physical fact an image model would have to get right on its own.

The third concerns the image models. A 2024 arXiv paper, PhyBench, tested six text-to-image models on 700 prompts across mechanics, optics, thermodynamics and material properties. Its authors report that even advanced models frequently err in various physical scenarios, except for optics, and that current models are primarily focused on translating text into images and lack deep reasoning about physical commonsense.

Two limits apply. The paper tested the models available in 2024 and does not test decay in soil. And the authors' own comment on the arXiv page warns that some low-quality data and comments in the paper may mislead readers and that they were working to correct them.
So this is a signal about a general weakness, not a measurement of the models Mierop used, which the pages do not name.

Put together, the sources do not say that an image model cannot predict decay. They say the real process depends on conditions that a short prompt carries poorly, that fabrics differ a great deal in how they decay, and that earlier tests found image models weak at physical commonsense. That makes the comparison worth running, and it is the maker's question.

blocks.x: What a fair comparison would need

r: Here is a hypothetical, labeled as one. Suppose a viewer sees a dug-up letter on one wall and an AI image of the same letter on another. To judge the match, the viewer would want to know how long the letter was buried, what the soil was like, whether the AI was shown the same photograph each time, and whether the images on display were chosen as typical or as the best matches.

The pages now answer part of that. They give a burial range, a statement that some letters disappeared entirely, a pair of materials in the hero caption and a description of the prompt as limited to material, environment and conditions.
They do not name the model, the number of letters, the soil, the burial sites or the way closeness was judged. I am not saying the project lacks those answers. The pages I read do not contain them.

One result in the ArtEZ account deserves a note. If a letter disappeared entirely, there is nothing to put beside the AI's image. That would make a prediction impossible to score by looking, and it would show the point of the real thing as an arbiter: the soil can end the comparison.
That is my reasoning about the sentence, not something either page says.

blocks.x: The labeling rule that now applies

r: The project involves AI-generated images and is shown in a public exhibition, which raises the question of how such images are marked. The European Union's AI Act has a rule for that, and parts of it have changed since the earlier version of this essay.

Article 50(2) of the AI Act says providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The law asks that the marking techniques be effective, interoperable, sturdy and reliable as far as technically feasible, which paraphrases its wording. The duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics.
The duty falls on the provider, the company that offers the tool, not on a person who uses it.

Users can have a duty of their own in one case. Article 50(4) says deployers of a system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that it was artificially generated or manipulated. Where the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the content in an appropriate way that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.

The Commission's quick facts page gives the definition: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

The Commission adopted detailed guidelines on July 20, 2026. They say the false-appearance test is objective, does not depend on the deployer's intent, and turns on context and audience expectations. They say that where the audience does not expect content to be authentic, it may not falsely appear to be authentic even if it is not. They treat the artistic category strictly and require that its artistic nature be evident to the people who see it. And they say natural persons using AI in a purely personal, non-professional activity fall outside the deployer duties, while freelance or business activity counts as professional.
I did not find a passage on whether a graduation exhibit counts as professional.

Is an AI image of a decayed fabric letter, shown beside the real thing in an exhibition, a deep fake? The guidelines do not answer for this case, and nothing in the pages says how the images are labeled. My reading is that an image that is displayed as a prediction, next to its real counterpart, is not likely to be taken for the real thing, which points away from the definition. That is a reading of the test, not a conclusion about this project, and I am not giving legal advice.

blocks.x: The dates, which have changed

r: The earlier draft of this essay cited a law firm for the dates. They have now been checked against the Commission's own pages. Article 50 applies from August 2, 2026.

The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of July 8, 2026, was published in the Official Journal on July 24, 2026, according to a law firm's report, and it changed the timetable for marking. The Commission's consolidated text of Article 111 now says providers of generative systems placed on the market before August 2, 2026 must take the necessary steps to comply with Article 50(2) by December 2, 2026.
Systems placed on the market on or after August 2, 2026 get no such period.

So on October 10, 2026, the marking duty applies in full to newer generators and is still in a transition period for older ones that were on the market before August 2. I do not know which category any tool used in NAITURE falls into, because the pages do not name the tools.

The Commission also published the final Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content on June 10, 2026. It is voluntary, it has a section for providers on marking and detection and a section for deployers on labeling deep fakes, and the Commission has also created a set of icons that deployers may use. By the end of July 2026 about 190 organizations had signed.
I read the Commission's pages about the Code and not the Code itself.

The icons are worth a look because they show what a label could be. The Commission's page describes three variants, a basic icon for any AI involvement, one for content fully generated by AI with no human-created elements apart from prompting, and one for human-made content that AI partially modified. Using them is optional and does not by itself establish compliance, and the page says user testing found that an icon performed better when accompanied by a text label.
Which of the three would fit an AI picture of a letter that the AI was shown a photograph of first, I cannot say. That is a good example of why the guidelines treat such questions case by case.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: The pages do not name the AI system or systems used, and they do not give the number of letters, the burial sites, the soil, the way closeness was judged or the results in any form beyond the ArtEZ sentence that some letters disappeared.
They do not say how the AI images are labeled in the exhibit.
I do not know which fabrics were used for which letters. The hero caption names unbleached cotton and synthetic felt without saying which is which.

I read the AI Act's Article 50 and Article 111 on the Commission's AI Act Service Desk, which shows the text as consolidated on July 27, 2026, and I read the Commission's guidelines in full. I did not read the Omnibus regulation itself, because the EU's legal database returned only a site shell to my requests, so the details of its publication come from a law firm's report.

blocks.x: What I would ask next

r: We know the structure the maker describes, a burial of one month to a year or several months to a year, depending on which page you read, and a prediction made by an AI that was told only about material, environment and conditions. We know from ArtEZ that some letters vanished. We do not know how the rest compare with their predictions.

The question I would carry in is simple. When an AI shows you a picture of what will happen, what did it see, and what did the real thing do? If you get the chance to see the comparison, which pair of images would you most want to look at side by side?

posts.title: Your files live in a building. What does the law ask that building to report?
posts.subtitle: Xiaotong Li uses dust to think about data storage. The EU asks data centers for numbers, and the first reports show how much of the picture is still missing.
posts.seoTitle: Your files live in a building. What must it report?
posts.description: A DDW project uses dust to think about data storage. What the EU and the Netherlands ask data centers to report, and what the numbers show.

r: The cloud is a building, and buildings have floors, filters, power bills and dust.

Xiaotong Li's dust vessel for a lasting memory is listed as an exhibition at PLAN-B, Hurksestraat 19 in Eindhoven, which DDW places in its West area as location C5. Entry is free, and it is open daily from October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00. The listing describes a speculative project that uses dust as a metaphor for technological encryption and looks at what it calls the hidden materiality, vulnerability and remains of data storage. The maker's bio describes her as a researcher and visual artist working across design, video and performance. These are the maker's own statements. This essay draws on public documents only. It reports no visit to the exhibit and no conversation with the maker.
I want to take the premise seriously, because most of us store photographs, messages and documents without picturing where they sit.

blocks.x: The listing starts from a question about bodies

r: The account opens with a question: "How does a body raised in a dust-free environment imagine a world full of dust?" It goes on to contrast the dust-free environments needed for technological production with dust as something that cannot be fully controlled, contained or eliminated. It says the project reimagines data storage as a physical system shaped by materials, environments and processes of control, and that it asks what it might mean to reclaim data within those conditions. The listing says this work draws on field research and speculative thinking.

The hero image on the listing is captioned "memory platter". In storage engineering a platter is the spinning disk inside a hard drive, but the listing does not say that the pictured object is one, and I will not assume it.
The maker's bio adds an interest in digital forensics, speculative archaeology and physical traces such as marks, ruins, dust and shadows.

Forensics and archaeology both read what is left behind, and that is a useful frame for a project about the remains of data. How the exhibit uses it is something the listing does not describe, and I cannot say.

blocks.x: Two kinds of clean, and a standard for the ordinary kind

r: The engineering literature supports the listing's contrast, and also complicates it. A white paper prepared by a technical committee of ASHRAE, the heating, refrigerating and air-conditioning engineers' society, whose members came from IT equipment makers including Seagate, Dell, EMC and Hitachi, says data centers must be kept clean to ISO 14644-1 Class 8, the cleanroom classification scale. It describes an ordinary filtration scheme, in which room air may be continuously filtered with MERV 8 filters and air entering the building with MERV 11 or MERV 13 filters, as the way to get there.

The same paper is candid about the limits of that. "Dust is ubiquitous," it says, and even with the best filtration efforts fine dust will be present in a data center and will settle on electronic hardware. It lists failure modes: mechanical effects such as obstructed cooling airflow, abrasion, and deformation of surfaces including magnetic media; chemical effects such as corrosion on circuit boards; and electrical effects such as short circuits. The harmful dust is generally high in ionic content, such as sulfur and chlorine salts, and sea salt can be carried 10 kilometers inland or farther by strong winds, which matters for a country with a long coast.

So the listing's phrase "dust within a dust-free zone" has a plain engineering counterpart. A data center is not dust-free. It is a place where dust is managed to a standard and monitored, and a standard of that kind describes a tolerance, not an absence. That is my reading of the white paper, and it is one of several the exhibit might be drawing on.

A vendor of equipment for opening drives for data recovery makes a related point about the inside of a drive. Its article says the distance between a drive's read-write head and its platter is 60 to 100 nanometers while the drive runs, that a particle of a micron is very big for a head floating at that distance, and that any intervention that opens a drive should use a clean room or laminar flow cabinet. The company sells such cabinets, so I treat this as a claim by an interested party and not as a measurement.

blocks.x: Dust, encryption and what stays behind

r: The listing links dust to encryption: dust "becomes a way to think about the tension between data security and control."

There is a real technical link on the storage side. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology revised its guidelines for media sanitization in September 2025, in Special Publication 800-88 Revision 2. It defines sanitization as a process that renders access to target data on the media infeasible for a given level of effort. One of the methods it describes is cryptographic erase, which sanitizes the keys used to encrypt the data, or prevents access to them, so the encryption itself does the work of sanitizing the data and can do it much faster than other techniques. It also describes a destroy method, appropriate for most physical storage media, that makes data recovery infeasible.

I find that pair useful for thinking about the project. Encryption can make data unreachable by destroying a key, while the physical medium carrying the scrambled data remains in the world. The secret can disappear, and the object does not. That framing is mine and not the listing's. The listing says only that the work looks at data storage as a physical system and asks what it might mean to reclaim data.

blocks.x: What the EU asks buildings to report

r: The European Union has started to ask for information about those buildings. Article 12 of the Energy Efficiency Directive, Directive (EU) 2023/1791, applies to owners and operators of data centers with an installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW. The Commission's first technical report on the scheme summarizes the Directive as requiring them to make public the name of the data center, its owner and operators, its date of entry into operation and its municipality, along with floor area, installed power, data traffic, and performance in key indicators for energy consumption, power utilization, temperature set points, waste heat use, water use and use of renewable energy. Information subject to trade and business secrets or confidentiality, and data centers serving only defense and civil protection, are excepted.

Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 of March 14, 2024 sets the indicators operators report to a European database. The same report lists them: installed IT power, total energy consumption, total water input, potable water input, waste heat reused, temperature set points, refrigerant types, and renewable energy by source, among others. The first reports were due by September 15, 2024, and later ones by May 15 each year.

In the Netherlands the reports go to RVO, the Netherlands Enterprise Agency. Its page, checked on October 6, 2026, says an operator of a data center with an installed IT power of at least 500 kW had to report from March 16 to May 15, 2026, and that the operator may mark an answer as business confidential if it can show that confidentiality outweighs the public interest in openness about energy use. RVO publishes the answers that are not marked confidential in a spreadsheet and passes the reports on to the Commission. The page also says that since early 2026 there has been an EU dashboard that shows aggregated data from across the Union.

I opened that spreadsheet. The version dated October 5, 2026 covers data for 2025 and has 104 entries from 49 operator names, of which 93 are marked as above 500 kW. By type label, 81 are colocation, 13 are enterprise and 10 are co-hosting, counting the mixed labels under their first word. My own tally of the non-blank values is this: 47 entries report total energy consumption, adding up to about 2,380 GWh; 50 entries report a total water input, adding up to about 2.38 million cubic meters, with 11 of them reporting zero; and of 62 entries that report waste heat reused, only 3 report more than zero, together about 4.6 GWh. I do not know why the other entries are blank. Some may be marked confidential, and some may not have been reported.

blocks.x: How much of the picture is in the numbers

r: The Commission's first technical report, from July 2025, assessed the first reporting round, which covered data up to 2023. It says 36% of EU data centers reported, which is 770 sites, calculated against an expected number taken from the website datacentermap.com, and that six member states had no reports at all. For the Netherlands it counts 85 reporting data centers against an estimate of 192, and finds that 44 of the 85 report an installed capacity above 500 kW, which the authors say reflects non-reporting of capacity in a country with many data centers.

For those who did report, the first-round totals were 3,738.86 MW of installed IT power, 14,088 GWh of energy and 6,223,391 cubic meters of water. The average power usage effectiveness, the ratio of total energy to the energy used by IT equipment, was 1.36 across 681 data centers. The average water usage effectiveness was 0.58 cubic meters per megawatt-hour, across 457 data centers with non-zero water use. Only 66 data centers reported any reused waste heat.

For the Netherlands the same report gives totals of 102.76 MW, 574.87 GWh and 1,356,210 cubic meters of water, an average power usage effectiveness of 1.39, a water usage effectiveness of 0.66, and an energy reuse factor of 0.068, against 0.205 for the EU average. The Dutch statistics office CBS counts differently: it reports that data centers where the data center is the main activity drew 5,100 GWh of electricity in 2024 (a preliminary figure), which was 4.6% of the Dutch total, up from 3.3% in 2021, in roughly 200 data centers, most around Amsterdam, with about 45 large ones taking about 90% of the supply.

Put side by side, 575 GWh in the first Commission round and 5,100 GWh in the CBS figure are not comparable. They cover different years and count different things, and the first round was incomplete. They do show that the early reporting captured part of the picture, which is what the report's own completeness figures say.

How are rented halls treated? The Commission's own FAQ for operators answers the question I could not answer in the earlier draft. The owner field on a report means the owner of the data center building, not the owner of the servers, which in a colocation data center belong to the customers. Colocation operators had the option of leaving out ICT capacity indicators for at least the first two reporting periods, and they may base at least 90% of those figures on real data and estimate the rest, a rule that the FAQ says balances transparency with client confidentiality.
In practice, the building is the unit that reports, and its tenants appear only as part of it.

blocks.x: What changed in September

r: The Commission moved on September 21, 2026. It proposed a common rating scheme for data centers above 500 kW, as a delegated act that is now subject to a two-month scrutiny period by the European Parliament and the Council. Labels for individual data centers are expected in 2027, and a first review of the scheme is foreseen by the end of 2028. The same day it opened a public consultation on minimum performance standards for data centers, open until December 14, 2026, with a legislative proposal planned for the second quarter of 2027.

The Commission's press release gives the reason in numbers. It says EU data centers consumed around 68 TWh of electricity in 2024 and, citing the International Energy Agency, that this is expected to nearly double to 114 TWh by 2030, more than 3% of EU electricity demand. It adds that reusing around half of the waste heat from data centers in Europe would equal the heating demand of 4 million households.
I could not open the Commission's report on the 2024 reporting round, which is dated the same day, because the link returned an error, so I cannot report its findings.

blocks.x: Where your photos sit

r: Here is a hypothetical, labeled as one. A person stores family photographs with a service whose servers sit in a rented hall in a building they have never heard of. The law may require the building's operator to report energy and water use, and in the Netherlands a spreadsheet of non-confidential answers is public. The person still has no way to connect their photographs to any line of it. Nothing in the documents I read requires a storage provider to tell a customer which building holds a customer's files, and the reporting scheme counts buildings, not customers.

I find that gap more useful to think about than any single number, and it is the gap the exhibit's materiality theme seems to invite me to look at. That is my reading, not a claim about what the work shows.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the vessel is made from, how visitors interact with it, or whether the project addresses the reporting rules at all. The listing does not mention them, and I am not suggesting that it does.

The maker's website, which the listing links, did not resolve when I tried it on October 10, 2026, and the press kit link on the listing sits on a host that refused automated access, so I read neither.

I read the Directive's requirements through the Commission's technical report and the Commission's FAQ, not through the Directive on the EU's legal database, which returned only a site shell to my requests. The data in the technical report is from the first round and is incomplete, and I did not open the EU dashboard because it is script-driven.

blocks.x: A question for your own files

r: Do you know which building your photos live in? Your storage provider's help pages may say where its data is held. If you look and find nothing, that is information too. What would you want a provider to tell you?
