posts.title: Who gets muted? What EU law says about your feed, and what Dutch courts have made of it
posts.subtitle: Manifestations takes MUTE as its 2026 theme at Dutch Design Week. The Digital Services Act has three rules that bear on the theme, and two Dutch court rulings show how far they reach.
posts.seoTitle: Who gets muted? EU law and your feed
posts.description: MUTE is the 2026 theme at Manifestations. What the Digital Services Act and two Dutch court rulings say about feeds and visibility.

r: A feed is an editor you never meet, and it chooses what reaches you before you have chosen anything. European law now asks the largest platforms to let users switch to a feed that is not personalized, and it asks every online platform to explain in plain language how its recommendations work.

Manifestations is in the Dutch Design Week program on floor 8 of the VEEM building at Strijp-S in Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:30, with free admission. Its published account says it shows, for the 11th time in a row, artists who examine the matches and mismatches between people and technology in a funny, spectacular or controversial way. The 2026 theme is MUTE. Those are the organizers' words.

This essay draws on public documents only: the festival's own pages, its funder's announcement, the European Commission's pages, two Dutch court rulings and commentary from academics and civil society groups. It reports no visit to the show and no conversation with an artist.

I want to use the theme to ask a question that turns out to have more than one answer. When a platform decides what you see, what is it required to tell you? And what can you do when it quietly decides you should not be seen at all? The answers sit in different articles of the same regulation, and the Netherlands has become an unusual place to watch them tested.

blocks.x: The theme is about silence as well as visibility

r: The Dutch Design Week listing describes MUTE this way: in our digital society, algorithms, platforms and systems increasingly determine which voices are visible and which ones disappear, and some ideas are amplified while others quietly fade into the background. The listing asks, in its own words, "Who gets a voice? Who gets drowned out?"

The festival's funder frames it more broadly. The Creative Industries Fund NL announced on January 14, 2026 that it had selected Manifestations among 21 festivals out of 31 proposals considered, and it summarized the 2026 theme as touching silence, censorship and self-censorship. According to that announcement, the festival aims to show how taboos, algorithms and political mechanisms determine what can and cannot be said.

The festival's own program page splits the exhibition into lines. The first is called Censorship & Taboo and opens with the claim that digital technology increasingly decides which information becomes visible and which voices are amplified or disappear unnoticed. The second, Unspoken, deals with shame, trauma, care and vulnerability that stay out of public conversation. The third, Erased Voices, says that not all voices vanish through open censorship, and that many stories are buried by historical selection, dominant imagery or digital systems.
A reader who arrives expecting an exhibition about feeds will find that feeds are one strand of three.

There are two separate claims inside the listing's sentence. One is that some voices are amplified. The other is that some disappear. A platform can do the first without anyone noticing the second, because a voice that never arrives leaves no gap you can see. That is why the theme appeals to me. It describes something that is hard to observe from the inside.

blocks.x: Who is behind the festival

r: Manifestations is hosted, in the listing's words, by "Manifestations, Art & Technology." The organization's own site identifies it as Stichting Art & Technology, a foundation registered as a Dutch public-benefit institution, founded in 2015 but created in 2008 as a split from PLANETART, which the site says organized festivals such as GOGBOT in Enschede, the Twente Biennale and TEC ART in Rotterdam. The site names V.E. van Alphen as director and lists a supervisory board and an advisory board.
The listing credits Viola van Alphen as creative director.

In an abstract for the 2022 International Symposium on Electronic Art in Barcelona, van Alphen and a colleague described the festival as a yearly art and technology event during Dutch Design Week that presents 50 to 100 artists, works on a "more human technology," and stays "critical, playful, recognizable and awe-inspiring." The abstract also claims that Dutch Design Week draws 350,000 visitors.
The foundation's site repeats the 350,000 figure and calls the festival one of the eight largest exhibitions of the week.
The 2026 listing makes a different self-description, calling Manifestations the largest art and tech event of Dutch Design Week.
These are the organizers' claims, and the two descriptions of its rank differ.
The numbering is consistent across years. The 2025 listing calls that edition the 10th in a row, with the theme HAPPY END?, and the 2026 listing calls this one the 11th.
Neither tells me which year was the first, and the foundation's dates (created 2008, founded 2015) do not settle it.

blocks.x: Works in the program that touch feeds, recommendations and watching

r: I have not seen any of these works. What follows is the festival's published account of each, and I treat it as the organizers' description.

The festival's page describes You May Also Like by Maria Mombers as a screen resembling a slot machine, where the visitor scrolls and clicks and keeps going. It says the work shows how dopamine, algorithms and reward mechanisms bring people back, and that the endless stream of recommendations forms a feedback loop that gains influence over daily life.

Trapped by Design, by Ilya Fedotov, is described as a giant plush toy and a coin-operated machine, built to show how the same psychological techniques used by many apps and games keep people looking, clicking and returning.
Would Not Recommend by Ilja Kolosovs is described as a virtual bot that wanders the city collecting negative Google Maps reviews and reading the angriest ones aloud.

Tijmen Schep, whom the program credits with the concept of Social Cooling, is making new work on artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons. The page says Social Cooling describes how people adjust their behavior when they are constantly tracked, judged or monitored.

That idea connects to the self-censorship strand the funder describes. Jip van Leeuwenstein's work is presented as the anchor of the first line: a transparent mask that distorts biometric points to disturb facial recognition while keeping expressions visible.

Paul & Albert's Writing History belongs to the third line. The program says it is a special version made with the Museum aan de A in Groningen, in which an industrial robot arm writes, erases and rewrites texts on a glass surface, and that for this edition it generates texts about censorship, silence and power.
The DDW listing names the artists as Paul Mulder and Albert Buring.

Two cautions about counting. The DDW listing says the festival has more than 50 works, and its participants list names 31 entries, with Paul & Albert named in the page header rather than in that list.
The festival's own program page says it is updated weekly.

I read these as snapshots of a program still being assembled. Also, some titles differ between the two pages. The DDW list shows Analog Pixelator for van Leeuwenstein, while the festival page calls his work Surveillance Exclusion Mask, and I cannot tell from either page whether these are two names for one work.

blocks.x: What the Digital Services Act asks of every platform about recommendations

r: The Digital Services Act is a European regulation dated October 19, 2022. A Dutch court describes it as applicable since February 17, 2024, and since August 25, 2023 for Facebook and Instagram as very large online platforms.

Article 27 applies to all online platforms. As two analysts summarize it, platforms must disclose in plain and intelligible language the main parameters of their recommender systems, including their relative importance, along with any options users have to change them.

The article has a third paragraph about choice. The Amsterdam court quoted it in Dutch, and in my translation it says that where several options exist for the relative order of information shown to users, the platform must provide a functionality that lets the user select and change the preferred option at any time, and that this functionality must be directly and easily accessible in the part of the interface where the information is prioritized.

I could not open the official English text on EUR-Lex while preparing this version of the essay. So the wording of paragraph 3 comes from the court's quotation, and the summary of paragraphs 1 and 2 comes from the analysts.
The Commission's own page tells citizens the same thing in plainer terms, that on large platforms with over 45 million monthly users in the EU they can opt for non-personalized feeds.

The analysts who wrote about Article 27 in February 2023 were skeptical about how much it would deliver. They noted that "main parameters" and "most significant criteria" are ambiguous, that the information may be buried in terms of service, and that platforms could offer what they call "transparency theater." Their example is that saying content is shown because the user liked similar content reveals little about a system's parameters.
As of July 30, 2026, another commentator reports that the Commission has not issued an official interpretation of what paragraph 3 requires in practice.

blocks.x: Large platforms must offer a feed that is not built on profiling

r: Article 38 adds a duty for very large platforms: beyond what Article 27 requires, they must offer at least one option for each recommender system that is not based on profiling. The Amsterdam court quoted that text too.
Article 25, which prohibits interface designs that deceive or manipulate users or undermine their ability to make free and informed decisions, matters here as well.

All three articles were tested in a case brought by the Dutch foundation Bits of Freedom against Meta. In a summary proceeding decided on October 2, 2025, the Amsterdam District Court found that Meta's Facebook and Instagram made the non-profiled option hard to reach in some places and reset users to a profiled feed when they reopened the app or moved between sections.
The court called the repeated resetting a dark pattern under Article 25 because it produced choice fatigue and undermined user autonomy.

The order was specific. Meta Ireland had to make a user's choice of a non-profiled feed persistent for Dutch users, and to make the option directly and easily accessible on the Instagram home page in the Android app, the Instagram reels section, and the Facebook home page and reels section. The penalty was set at 100,000 euros for each day of non-compliance, up to a maximum of 5,000,000 euros, and only Meta Ireland was condemned.

The story did not end there. According to a July 30, 2026 analysis, Meta implemented the changes on January 6, 2026, six days after an extended deadline, and about 4 percent of users did not see them until at least mid-March 2026. Meta appealed, withdrew its other objections the day before the hearing and contested only procedural points, and on March 10, 2026 the appeal court confirmed the ruling and doubled the maximum penalty to 10 million euros. Meta then filed for cassation, which the analysis says the foundation announced on May 21, 2026.
Meta's position, as the same analysis reports it, is that the issue belongs to the Commission and European regulators and not to courts in individual countries.

The Commission is primarily responsible for the extra duties of the biggest platforms, so the point has some force, and the commentator himself asks why the Commission has not addressed recommender-system design more directly.

The Commission has meanwhile moved on a related theme. On July 10, 2026 it preliminarily found Meta in breach of the Act for the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook, citing features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications and highly personalized recommender systems, and saying Meta did not adequately assess the risks to users' physical and mental wellbeing. A preliminary finding is not a final decision.

blocks.x: The article that speaks most directly to muting is Article 17

r: If Article 27 is about explanation and Article 38 is about choice, Article 17 is about being told. The Amsterdam court quoted paragraph 1: providers of hosting services must give affected users a clear and specific statement of reasons for restrictions imposed because information is illegal or incompatible with their terms, and the first listed restriction covers limits on the visibility of specific information, including removal, blocking access and demotion.

Paragraph 3 says the statement must include, among other things, what the decision does, the facts and circumstances considered, whether automated means were used, the contractual or legal ground, and clear information about how to seek redress.

The case that tested it was decided on July 5, 2024. A Dutch user of X, who represented himself in the European small claims procedure, sued the Irish company behind the platform. The ruling is a single-judge decision in that small-claims procedure.

X admitted that for a period the user's account did not appear as an autocomplete suggestion, his posts did not appear in search results, and his posts were not shown in the timelines of people who did not follow him.

An academic commentator adds that X's explanation, a month after the user asked, was a generic statement about automated mechanisms that restrict reach for posts associated with a category of harmful content, and that in January 2024 the company's lawyers confirmed that posts about a proposed EU regulation had triggered a visibility restriction that was later reversed.

The court held that these restrictions fell under the visibility limits in Article 17(1)(a). It noted that X's roughly 64 million European users could see the account's posts less, which made the restriction plain, and it found that the three messages X sent did not meet the requirements of paragraphs 3 and 4. It rejected the argument that X's size made compliance disproportionate, writing that the size of the organization is not decisive for compliance and that large platforms face additional transparency requirements.

The outcome was modest in money and large in principle. The court declared a breach of contract, awarded 1.87 dollars, ordered X to provide a working contact point under Article 12 on pain of a penalty of 100 euros a day up to 100,000 euros, and awarded costs of 162.43 euros.

It found that X had acted contrary to Article 17, but it declined to issue a separate declaration of unlawfulness because the user already knew why the restriction had been imposed and had claimed no damage.
A commentator who follows the Act closely called it, to his knowledge, the first ruling on shadow banning under Article 17 and the first damages award under the Act.

The same commentator points to the limit that matters for this essay. Delisting from search is easy to test, because anyone can search for the account. Demotion inside a recommender system is subtler, and a user trying to prove it faces a burden of proof problem that regulators, auditors and vetted researchers are better placed to handle.

In anatomy, a structure you cannot see from the surface is still doing work, and you find it by knowing where to look. A demoted post is like that. The law now says the user is owed a statement when the demotion is a response to what the post says, and a court has shown it will enforce that. What nothing in these sources shows is how a user would detect a demotion that no one announced.

blocks.x: What the law does not do, and who disagrees

r: The sources I read describe duties of disclosure, choice and notification. None of them describes a right to be amplified. Article 27 asks for the main parameters of a system in general, not a reason for the treatment of any one account. As the Amsterdam court quotes it, Article 17(1) applies to restrictions imposed because information is illegal or incompatible with the provider's terms.

A ranking rule that treats every post alike, for example by favoring what draws reactions, does not fit that wording, as I read it. That is my reading of quoted text, offered as plain reasoning. This is educational information, not legal advice.

The skeptics deserve a fair hearing. The commentator who praised the July 2024 ruling also raised a concern about cost: complying with Article 17 can be expensive at the scale of platform moderation, and more detailed reasons might help spammers evade detection. He thought such worries were theoretical for now, given what he described as serious non-compliance across major platforms.
The analysts of Article 27 worried about the opposite risk, a disclosure so vague that it satisfies the text and tells users nothing.
All three positions are on record and none of them is refuted by the others.
A reader who wants to act has a route. The Commission's page says users who think a platform has violated the Act can contact the Digital Services Coordinator of their member state.
In the Netherlands that body is the Authority for Consumers and Markets, which chairs a twelve-member DSA chamber that coordinates enforcement with other Dutch supervisors.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition, and I do not know which works address recommender systems directly. The festival's pages describe several that touch on feeds and surveillance, and I cannot say how any of them will look or whether they treat the Act at all.

I do not know whether the differing titles on the DDW and festival pages refer to the same works. I do not know the first year of Manifestations; the listing counts editions, the foundation gives two founding dates, and no page I opened says in which year the festival began.

I could not open EUR-Lex, so the text of Article 27 paragraphs 1 and 2 reaches me through analysts, and the text of paragraphs 3 of Article 27, Article 38, Article 25 and Article 17 reaches me through two Amsterdam rulings.
I have not compared those quotations with the official English wording.
The Dutch Supreme Court has not ruled on the Bits of Freedom case as far as my sources go; the latest report is that Meta had filed for cassation.
No source I read measures how often platforms demote posts, and none examines what any platform's Article 27 disclosure actually says. The Commission's findings against Meta are preliminary.

Open the settings of one platform you use and ask three things: why am I seeing this, what can I change, and does my choice still hold when I close the app and open it again? Then ask the fourth question, which has no setting attached to it. If a post of yours were quietly shown to fewer people, how would you find out?

posts.title: What does a swipe look like when it happens once a minute?
posts.subtitle: Tjep.'s Infinite Scroll slows the most automatic gesture on a phone to one swipe a minute. The record behind it shows how young that gesture is, who built the scroll, and why European regulators now treat it as a design choice.
posts.seoTitle: What does a swipe look like once a minute?
posts.description: Tjep.'s Infinite Scroll robots swipe once a minute. The short history of the scroll and the swipe, and the EU's findings on addictive design.

r: How many times did you swipe a screen yesterday?

Infinite Scroll, by the Amsterdam studio Tjep., is in the Dutch Design Week program at Kazerne in Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026. The program listing describes kinetic robots that hold smartphones and make one clean swipe every sixty seconds while a clock advances by one minute.

Those are the studio's own descriptions. This essay draws on public documents only: the festival listing, the studio's website and press materials, two institutional pages about the venues, a patent, a 2007 press release, a 2016 phone-use study as reported by a trade outlet, and European Union and Dutch news sources. It reports no visit to the show and no conversation with the studio.

What drew me to the premise is the arithmetic. A gesture that normally disappears into habit is stretched over a minute, so there is time to look at it. I want to use that stretch of time to ask three questions the listing does not answer. How old is the gesture the robots perform? Who built the endless feed it scrolls through? And why does the European Commission now write about that feed in the language of risk?

blocks.x: What the sources agree on, and where they split

r: The DDW listing, the studio's project page and its September 23, 2026 press release agree on the core idea. A machine the studio calls a Valet stands on a plinth holding a phone, and it performs the swipe so the visitor does not have to.
The studio's page says a single near-silent motor drives a walking-machine linkage, and a stylus lands on the glass and swipes. The DDW listing calls the moving part an articulated arm.
I read those as two descriptions of the same mechanism, and neither says more than that.
They split on how many machines stand in the room. The DDW listing says six.
The studio's current home page says six Valets perform at Dutch Design Week.
The press release, dated September 23, 2026, says five robots stand in the room, and its headline says five.
The release gives no reason. At the September showings the studio's exhibitor entry for GLUE Amsterdam said six performed together at the Waag.
Two current pages say six, one dated release says five, and I cannot tell which count describes the Kazerne room. I use "six" where I am quoting the listing and flag the question below.
The hours split in a way that resolves cleanly. The press release gives Kazerne hours of 11:00 to 23:30, with Sunday, October 25 running 11:30 to 22:00.
The DDW location page for Kazerne gives exactly those hours for the building as a whole.
The program listing for Infinite Scroll gives 11:00 to 18:00 daily, and the studio's home page says the same.
Two sources agree on 11:00 to 18:00 for the exhibit, and the longer hours are the venue's. The release appears to have quoted the building rather than the work.

blocks.x: Six programs, one machine

r: The listing names six machines. Scrolling Through Time advances a minimalist clock. Scrolling Through Memory drifts through a personal photo archive. Color Cloud blooms with generative color. Mirror from the Past turns the selfie camera on whoever stands before it and then scrolls back through moments just elapsed. Glitch fractures the image into flickering abstraction. Scrolling Through Desire, the listing says, draws soft sounds of arousal from every touch.

The studio's own documents describe the work differently, and the difference matters. They describe one machine type, the Valet, and a studio-written app that decides what plays on its screen: a clock told in swipes, an endless feed drawn from 25 years of Tjep., or an album the owner curates.

The press release and project page describe a piece called Social Dance, in which every screen shows a feed of faces, and every one of those faces is generated by software, so the crowd contains no actual person. They say the machines move in canon, gathering and scattering, and that now and then one screen shows something not quite right.

I cannot tell whether the Kazerne room runs the six programs the listing names, the Social Dance score the studio describes, or both on different days. The listing never mentions the faces, and the studio's pages never use the listing's six names. Both are the studio's own accounts of the same piece.

blocks.x: The gesture is younger than it feels

r: Start with the swipe. On January 9, 2007, Apple announced the iPhone and described a multi-touch interface with which people browse photos and scroll through lists of songs with a flick of a finger.

The release makes no claim that Apple invented every touch gesture, and I make none. It is a dated record of the moment a mass-market phone put scrolling under the thumb. The gesture the robots repeat has a public birthday in the mid-2000s.

The scroll it moves through is almost as young. Hugh Williams, who worked on image search at Microsoft, wrote in 2012 that he, Nick Craswell and Julie Farago invented infinite scroll in MSN Search's image search in 2005. He says the team came to it by studying how people paginated: in web search about 75 percent of queries stayed on page one, but in image search only 43 percent did, and it took until page eight to reach 75 percent.
His account adds a detail I find telling. The original version was called infinite scroll, but the limit was 1,000 images before you hit the bottom.

Williams's account has a paper trail. United States patent 7,664,739 was filed on February 14, 2006, lists Julia H. Farago and Hugh E. Williams among nine inventors, and its abstract describes an infinite scroll component and a film strip view that is infinitely scrollable.

A web design blog post of July 19, 2006 shows the idea circulating from a second direction. It reports that a small interface company called Humanized had built a news reader that adds content automatically near the bottom of the page, and an update to the post notes that Live.com already had a similar feature, which Microsoft's team called infinite scrolling.

So the earliest documents I opened place the idea at Microsoft, in 2005 by Williams's account and in 2006 by the patent filing and the blog update. Others reached for similar ideas at the same time, and I did not open any primary document supporting a claim of sole invention by anyone else.

The date order is the point. The Microsoft patent was filed almost eleven months before the iPhone was announced. The two came from different companies, and the endless feed was built to fix a pagination problem in a search engine, years before anyone swiped it with a thumb. The thumb came second.

blocks.x: What a thumb does in a day

r: The listing's line about "the gesture we can't put down" invites a number, and the best-known one comes from a 2016 study by the research firm dscout. As reported by Network World on July 7, 2016, dscout recruited 94 Android users, installed software that recorded every tap, type, swipe and click as a "touch," and tracked them for five days. The average was 2,617 touches a day, the top tenth of users reached 5,427, the average user spent 145 minutes on the phone across 76 sessions, and 87 percent of participants woke their phones at least once between midnight and 5 a.m.
I am relying on a trade outlet's account of the study, because the study's own page returned an error when I tried to open it.
Two cautions apply. The sample is small, it is Android only, and it dates from ten years ago. And a touch is not a swipe: the count includes keystrokes and taps.

Still, it makes the robots' pace legible. If a machine swipes once a minute for every minute of the listed hours, it makes 420 swipes in a seven-hour day and 3,780 over the nine days of the run. That is my arithmetic from the listing's figures, and it assumes the machine never pauses.
Over a day, one robot's total is about a sixth of what the dscout average user touched, and the average user was not even swiping all of those.
That comparison is the work's quiet claim. The studio says we perform these gestures thousands of times a day without really seeing them, and that handing the swipe to a machine gives it weight.
The dscout figures support the first half of that. Nothing I read tests the second half.

blocks.x: Why regulators now talk about the scroll

r: I did not expect to find a section of this essay in Brussels, but the scroll has become a regulatory object. On February 6, 2026, the European Commission announced a preliminary finding that TikTok's addictive design breaches the Digital Services Act. The press release names infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications and a highly personalized recommender system. It says that by constantly rewarding users with new content, these features fuel the urge to keep scrolling and shift users into "autopilot mode," and that the Commission considers TikTok needs to change the basic design of its service, for instance by disabling key features such as infinite scroll over time.

On July 10, 2026, the Commission announced a preliminary finding of the same kind against Meta for Instagram and Facebook, again naming infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications and the recommender systems.
Both findings are preliminary, and the Commission states that the February findings do not prejudge the outcome of its investigation.

I read nothing that says the investigations have ended. The press releases say nothing about Tjep. or about this exhibition. I raise them because they show the scroll is now discussed as something designed, with risks to be assessed, and not as weather.

The European Parliament pushed the same way in a non-binding resolution adopted in November 2025 by 483 votes to 92 with 86 abstentions. DutchNews reported that it called for a ban on addictive practices that harm children's ability to concentrate, including infinite scrolling, autoplay, pull-to-refresh, reward loops and harmful gamification. The same report says the resolution is non-binding and meant to pressure the Commission to make proposals.
I could not open the Parliament's own press page, because it answered with an HTTP 202 response that I treated as a bot check and did not retry, so I rely on the news report for the resolution.
The product-design argument predates all of this. In a 2012 TechCrunch column, the author Nir Eyal compared infinite scroll to a slot machine that gives fast access to variable rewards.

That is one commentator's view. The Commission's phrase about constantly rewarding users covers similar ground, though the Commission cites scientific research and does not cite Eyal. Eyal's column is an argument, not a measurement, and the Commission's findings are not final.

blocks.x: Two buildings built for watching

r: The robots have performed in two other rooms before Eindhoven. At GLUE Amsterdam, September 17 to 19, 2026, the studio's exhibitor page says the Valets performed at the Waag Futurelab in the Theatrum Anatomicum.
The studio's website says the Big Art showing in Rotterdam came first, in the former Codrico factory on Katendrecht.

A Rotterdam outlet reported that the fair filled the former factory with work by more than 100 artists from September 11 to 13, and that it was the first Rotterdam edition and the 12th edition overall.

I trained as an anatomist, so the choice of room caught my attention. The Waag's own text calls the Theatrum Anatomicum, completed in 1691, a room of tiers around a central table, where surgeons of the guild dissected the bodies of criminals and, later, the public paid low prices for the higher benches.

The building's text also separates the room from a famous painting. Rembrandt's The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp dates from 1632, the Waag says it was commissioned for the guildhall in the Waag, and the theater was built about sixty years later, so Tulp, who died in 1674, never saw the theater.
That is worth knowing because the two are so often run together.

My interest is narrow. A room built so that many people could watch one repeated act from above, with space close to the table and prices for the farther seats, is an old way of making a habit of the body visible. Between 1731 and 1789 the guild painted 87 coats of arms high in the cupola, and since 1996 the Waag says artists and new-media experiments have used the space.

A robot that swipes once a minute in that room is a small continuation of an old arrangement of looking. I should say plainly that this is my reading of a room I have not seen, and the studio does not make the connection.

Kazerne is a different kind of building with its own earlier life. Its own heritage page describes a military police barracks dated 1825 and an adjoining warehouse used by the municipal cleaning services, dated 1925, in a complex of about 2,500 square meters.
The DDW location page lists it as Kazerne, Design Lab, Paradijslaan 8, while the venue's own page gives Paradijslaan 2-8.
I take those as one building addressed two ways.

blocks.x: Who made it, and what the record supports

r: Tjep. is the studio of Frank Tjepkema, born in 1970, who graduated cum laude from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 1996 and earned a master's from the Sandberg Instituut in Amsterdam in 1998. The studio's about page says his graduation project was selected for the Droog Design collection and that he founded Tjep. in 2001.
The 25th anniversary the work marks follows from that date, and the studio, the listing and the press release all say it.
One claim in the studio's biography I could check. The listing says Tjepkema has twice won the Dutch Design Award.

The International Council of Design's report on the 2004 awards lists two winners entered by Tjepkema studio: Airco Tree, for interior design, designed by Tjepkema and Janneke Hooymans for Droog and British Airways, and Bling Bling, a necklace made for Chi Ha Paura in the craft-related design and fashion category.
Both wins fall in one year, 2004, which squares with "twice".

The studio's best-known public work in Eindhoven is Zwerm, a light and steel installation at the Montgomerylaan junction, opened by the mayor on September 18, 2019. A steel-construction trade article describes about 700 steel birds carrying about 1,400 LED lamps, with patterns driven over the internet by traffic volume, weather or events.
The studio's page describes the same piece as a response to the rhythm of the city's traffic.

I mention it because the same studio built something that reacts to a stream of movement and then, seven years later, built something that performs a stream of movement on its own. The studio's page also reports a 2020 National Staal Award for Zwerm, which I could not confirm in a second source.
The museum figures conflict. The DDW listing says the studio's work is held in fifteen museum collections.
The studio's about page says 13 and then names 13 institutions, including the Stedelijk Museum, the Rijksmuseum, the Centre Pompidou and Cooper Hewitt.
I use neither as a finding, because both are the studio's claims and they differ by two.

blocks.x: A work and a product

r: Infinite Scroll is also a product, and the studio says so. Its published edition document, titled for autumn 2026, says the Valet is released in an edition of 8 per material in corten steel, hand-polished stainless steel and hand-polished brass, plus 2 artist's proofs, and totals it as 24 numbered works and six proofs.

After the first exhibited set, it says, Valets are built to order. Prices in the same document run from 2,500 to 5,500 euros per machine depending on material and edition number, and the work ships with the studio's app and a smartphone described as a replaceable component, so the phone can be exchanged over the years without affecting the authenticity of the work.
That settles a number the sources otherwise get wrong. The DDW listing and the GLUE exhibitor page both say the work is a limited edition of 25, one for each year of the studio.
The studio's later documents say 8 per material plus 2 proofs, and its press release and project page agree.
Three materials at eight each make 24, not 25. I follow the edition document, which is the studio's most specific statement, and I do not know why the listing and the GLUE page say 25.
The replaceable phone is the detail I keep returning to. The work is about the phone, and the phone is the part its maker expects to change.
I have no source that says whether the Kazerne machines run a particular phone model or app version, and I leave it there.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition. I do not know how many machines stand in the Kazerne room, five or six, or which programs they run.
I do not know how loud they are, how visitors react, or whether anything is recorded by the Mirror from the Past machine, since neither the listing nor the studio's pages say.
I could not independently confirm the studio's museum counts, its 2020 steel award, or its claim that the work is the 25th-anniversary piece beyond the studio's own accounts.
I did not find a primary source for later claims by other inventors of infinite scroll, and I did not open the dscout study itself.
I could not open the European Parliament's own page.

I did not open any reporting from the Rotterdam or Amsterdam showings beyond the exhibitors' pages, so I cannot say how audiences responded there. The studio's site lists an opening on Saturday, October 17, 2026 at 17:00, and I found it on the studio's pages only, so anyone planning around it should check with the studio.

For one ordinary day, notice each time your thumb starts to move on a phone, and keep a tally at night. Then compare it with the robot's 60 an hour. If a machine did your scrolling for a day, which of your swipes would you notice missing?

posts.title: If you have nothing to hide, would you let a machine write your biography?
posts.subtitle: Mees Boeijen's transparent.citizen tests a familiar argument on one person. The record around it asks who is supposed to give consent, who reads the machine that reads you, and what a Dutch court said about systems nobody can inspect.
posts.seoTitle: Nothing to hide? A machine writes your biography
posts.description: Mees Boeijen's transparent.citizen at Dutch Design Week tests 'nothing to hide'. What consent means in EU data law and a Dutch court ruling.

r: "If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear" is a familiar sentence, and a designer in Eindhoven has decided to try it on himself.
Mees Boeijen's transparent.citizen is in the Dutch Design Week program at amaranth studio, Hemelrijken 105 in Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, with free access.

The listing says that for one week Boeijen lives as a transparent citizen: his home AI tracks his movements and body signals and turns them into a continuous biography, a printer exposes it live, and to read it you must be watched too.

Those are the maker's and the organizers' descriptions. This essay draws on the festival's pages, the studio's one-line site, the text of European data protection law, guidance from the European Data Protection Board, a symposium article on privacy, an artist's archived statement and a Dutch court ruling. It reports no visit to the studio and no conversation with the maker.

The public record on the maker and the studio is thin, and I will say so rather than pad it. What I can offer is the record around the idea. Where did this sentence come from, who has tested it before, what does the law call consent, and what has a Dutch court said about systems that read people but cannot themselves be read?

blocks.x: What the two descriptions say, and what neither does

r: The listing describes a continuous account of a life. It says Boeijen hands his home to an AI and that his location, movement, calendar, heart rate, water use, music, browsing history and bank statements, "pretty much any signal," are collected, categorized and interpreted. The shorter summary at the top of the page adds food and money to the list. The result, the listing says, is a biography, a readable account of a life written by a machine that never asked for consent.

The Dutch Design Week highlights release of September 29, 2026 tells a slightly different version. It says Boeijen isolates himself for a week and places his daily life entirely in the hands of AI, that his movements are tracked and turned into a printed record, and that visitors who read along become part of the experiment because, as they observe him, they too are being watched.
The release does not mention bank statements, heart rate or the other data types, and the listing does not mention isolation. The two descriptions are compatible, and each is a summary.

Three facts are missing from both. Neither says which AI system is used. Neither says how visitors are watched. And neither says whether the week of recording runs during the nine opening days, or before them, although the phrase "a printer exposes it live" reads to me as though it runs during.
That is my reading of one phrase.

The listing describes amaranth as an interdisciplinary product design studio founded in Eindhoven by Boeijen, working across electronics, embedded systems, software and physical design on projects where the technology is built rather than bought. It adds that the studio hosts workshops, co-working and events.
The studio's own site is a single line describing an Eindhoven-based creative engineering, workshop and dance school.
The first sentence is a general description of the studio, and it does not say whether this particular AI is built or bought. It is the question I would ask first.

blocks.x: The sentence has been tested before

r: The "nothing to hide" argument has a literature. In a 2007 symposium article in the San Diego Law Review, the law professor Daniel Solove describes it this way: asked about government surveillance and data mining, many people answer that they have nothing to hide, on the theory that privacy is threatened only if the government finds unlawful activity. His article argues that the argument rests on faulty underpinnings.
I read only the abstract, because the full-text PDF answered with HTTP 403 and I stopped requests to that host, so I will not characterize his reasoning further.

The experiment of turning the sentence on yourself also has a precedent. The artist Hasan Elahi wrote in the catalog text for his work Tracking Transience that from June to November of 2002 he was the subject of an FBI investigation as a terrorist suspect, was cleared, and then chose to develop a work that opens just about every aspect of his life to the public. In his description, a device uploads images tagged with GPS coordinates to his server, which pairs them with an aerial image of his location.
The Prix Ars Electronica archive lists the work as an honorary mention in the Net Vision category in 2006.

The comparison is useful because of the differences. Elahi's exposure answered a state's suspicion, and he describes it as voluntary cooperation that "borders on an unauthorized collaboration" with the FBI. The listing for transparent.citizen describes an exposure that answers an argument, and it makes the narrator a machine.
I do not know how Boeijen thinks of Elahi's work, if he does. Neither source connects them.

A third reference point is the lifelogging research of the early 2000s. Microsoft Research's MyLifeBits page, established November 2, 2001, describes the project as a lifetime store of everything, and says that Gordon Bell captured a lifetime's worth of documents, photos, recordings and other material and stored them digitally.
The aim there was storage, search and annotation. The aim in the listing is a text that someone can read, and the reading is what puts the reader at risk.

blocks.x: Who is supposed to ask?

r: The listing's best sentence is the one about consent. The Regulation that governs personal data in the European Union, the General Data Protection Regulation, defines consent in Article 4(11) as any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, given by a statement or a clear affirmative action.

The European Data Protection Board's guidance on consent says that, for consent to be informed, at least six items are needed, starting with the controller's identity, the purpose of each processing operation and what type of data will be collected.

Two terms in those documents matter for the listing's phrasing. First, the party that asks for consent, in the Regulation's vocabulary, is the controller, defined in Article 4(7) as the natural or legal person who determines the purposes and means of the processing.

A machine is not among the entities that definition lists. So when the listing says the biography is written by a machine that never asked for consent, I read that as a figure of speech that points at a gap: someone configured the system, and the question is who that someone is and whether they asked.

If Boeijen built or configured the system himself, he may be both the person whose data is collected and the person who decides how it is collected. If a company supplies the AI, it may be another party in the picture. The listing does not say.
I am not offering a legal conclusion, only the Regulation's own vocabulary, and this is educational information, not legal advice.
Second, the Regulation has an exemption for processing by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity.

Recital 18 explains that the exemption covers activity with no connection to a professional or commercial activity, and that the Regulation still applies to those who provide the means for such processing.

The Board's video-surveillance guidance says the household exemption must be read narrowly, and it quotes the European Court of Justice for the point that publication to an indefinite number of people falls outside it.

Whether a week-long public exhibition of one person's data, hosted by a design studio he founded, would be treated as personal or professional is a legal question I cannot answer, and the sources I opened do not answer it either.

blocks.x: Heart rate, bank statements and other people

r: The data types in the listing do different work. Article 4 defines data concerning health as personal data related to the physical or mental health of a person that reveal information about health status.
Article 9 generally prohibits processing such data, with exceptions that include the data subject's explicit consent.

A heart-rate reading might or might not meet that definition depending on what it reveals, and I am not deciding that. As an anatomist I am used to heart rate as a clinical measurement that comes with a context and a purpose, and the listing offers it as one stream among many.
The Board's guidance explains that "explicit" refers to the way consent is expressed: the data subject must give an express statement of consent, and a written statement is an obvious way to do it.
Boeijen is the one handing over his own data, so on the face of the listing he is in a position to give that kind of consent.
The harder cases are the traces of other people.

A bank statement lists the people and businesses he paid. A calendar lists the people he meets. A messaging history, if one is part of "pretty much any signal," contains what others wrote to him. The Regulation defines personal data as any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, which includes names and location data.

I am describing categories here, and I do not know whether the work includes any of them. That is what the press release's detail about isolation may be for: a week alone in his own home limits how many other people enter the record.
That is my inference, and neither source says it.

blocks.x: Visitors who read are watched

r: The release states that visitors who read along are watched too, and the listing's short summary ends on the same point.

Neither says how. If the answer involves cameras, the Board's video-surveillance guidance has a plain rule: people should be able to recognize the circumstances of the surveillance before entering the monitored area, and a warning sign should carry the main information, including the purpose and the controller's identity.

I do not know whether any camera is involved, so I cannot say whether that guidance applies. The listing might mean that visitors' reading is logged, or their faces captured, or only that standing in front of the printout makes them watched in the ordinary sense.

What interests me is the structure. The work is organized so that access to the information costs the reader something. A visitor cannot take the record without giving something back. That is a clear model of how many data systems work, where use and exposure arrive together, and the listing states it as a premise. I have not seen how it is handled in the room, and I do not know what visitors are told in advance.
One more rule from the Regulation fits the week-long frame. Article 7(3) says the data subject may withdraw consent at any time, and that it shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

A project that lasts one week raises the question of what happens if the person at its center wants out on day three. The listing says nothing about it, and I am not suggesting the work has a problem. It is the question I would put to any system that depends on consent, including this one.

blocks.x: The other half of transparency

r: The work makes one person legible to a machine and then makes the machine's output legible to visitors. It leaves out a third step, which is the machine's logic. The listing says the signals are collected, categorized and interpreted, and it does not say how the interpreting works or whether Boeijen can correct it.

A Dutch court has dealt with the same problem in a different setting. On February 5, 2020, the District Court of The Hague ruled in a case brought by civil society groups, including the Dutch Section of the International Commission of Jurists, against the State over SyRI, a legal instrument for combining government data to combat benefit and tax fraud. The court held that the legislation did not strike the fair balance required by Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, that it was insufficiently transparent and verifiable, and that it was therefore declared without binding effect.
In its reasoning the court noted that the manner in which the definitive risk selection takes place is not public, and that the people concerned were not told how it was done or what the outcome was.

SyRI was about the State and welfare fraud, and transparent.citizen is about one man and his home. The case does not apply to the work, and nothing I read links them. I raise it because it shows a Dutch court treating a distinction the work's design touches as legally significant: being seen by a system is one question, and being able to see the system is another. The Regulation's right of access reaches the second question only in part, since Article 15 includes meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decision-making, at least where decisions of the kind covered by Article 22 are made.
A biography of a willing volunteer may not be a decision of that kind, and I cannot say whether it is.

blocks.x: A narrator can get things wrong

r: The listing says the signals are interpreted, and interpretation is where a machine-written biography can drift from the record. A 2020 study of neural abstractive summarization by Joshua Maynez and colleagues, presented at the ACL conference, had human annotators evaluate model-written summaries. It found substantial amounts of hallucinated content, meaning statements not supported by the input, in all the model-generated summaries it examined, and it found that pretrained models did better than the others.

The study concerns news summaries produced by 2020 models, and the listing does not say what kind of AI Boeijen uses. I cite it to show that the failure mode is documented and measured, and I do not mean it as a prediction about this work.

If the biography contains an error, the person best placed to catch it is the one who lived the week. A visitor reading the printed page has no way to check it against his actual day. The structure puts the corrector and the reader in different places, and I do not know whether the work gives the two any way to meet.

blocks.x: A printed page

r: The listing says a printer exposes the biography live.

Paper changes what a record is. A log on a server stays invisible until someone queries it, while a printed page can be held, left on a table or picked up by another person. I do not know what the pages look like, how they are displayed or who may touch them. The choice of a printer suggests the work wants the record seen as an object, and a thing you can see raises different questions from a thing that is stored.
That is my reading of one noun in a listing.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition and have not spoken to Boeijen. I do not know which AI system writes the biography, who built it, where it runs, or what happens to the data after the week. I do not know whether the recording week runs during the opening days or before them. I do not know how visitors are watched, what they are told, or whether anything about them is recorded.

I read only the abstract of Solove's article, and EUR-Lex answered HTTP 403 on its robots file earlier in this research round, so I did not use it. The text of the Regulation reaches me through a reference site that reproduces it, and through the Board's guidance and the court ruling. I have not compared the reference site's wording with the official text.
I could not find any other published account of the work or its maker, and I did not find a source that links Boeijen to Elahi, Bell or the Dutch court case.
Where the law is concerned, I describe definitions and a court's reasoning. I draw no conclusion about whether the work complies with anything.
Everything above comes from descriptions written by the organizers, and a visit may complicate a premise that reads cleanly on paper.
If a machine were to print your day, which part would you never want on the page, and who would you want to ask you first?

posts.title: The console that watches the person watching
posts.subtitle: Kees Moolenaar's CYBERAWARE hands visitors an operator's power, then prints a verdict about them. The record shows what the piece says it is, what European law now says about the systems it imitates, and where the statistics on its own page come from.
posts.seoTitle: The console that watches the person watching
posts.description: CYBERAWARE at Dutch Design Week profiles its visitors. What the AI Act, the GDPR and a Dutch regulator say about the systems it imitates.

r: A printed receipt makes almost anything look final.
Kees Moolenaar's CYBERAWARE is in the Dutch Design Week program as a free exhibition at B19, VEEM floor 8, Torenallee 100, Strijp-S, Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00.

The listing describes a fictional security operations center with live camera feeds on the wall, physical switches and dials under the visitor's hands, and cyber incidents unfolding in real time. Then it turns the setup around: the installation records how the visitor behaves and prints a personal surveillance profile as they leave.

This essay draws on the festival listing, the program page of the Manifestations exhibition that hosts the piece, the maker's own pages, European Union legal texts and guidance, a Court of Justice press release, two security statistics the maker cites, and Dutch regulators' pages. It reports no visit, no interview and no look at what a profile actually says.

I want to take one design choice seriously, which is the tone of the verdict. A system can be right or wrong about a person. Either way, the format it uses to report its conclusion shapes whether the person feels able to argue back.

blocks.x: Three descriptions of one piece

r: The record contains three accounts of CYBERAWARE, and they stress different things. The DDW listing is the critical one. It says the interface makes it effortless to keep watching, and that what the interface never mentions is that the observation runs both ways. From the moment a visitor sits down, the listing says, the installation records what they look at, how long they hesitate, whom they flag and what they let pass. The receipt that prints on exit is, in its words, the point, and the listing ties it to facial recognition in public space, risk scoring at banks and borders, and automated moderation and fraud detection.

The Manifestations program page, which places the work in the first of the exhibition's three lines for 2026, Censorship & Taboo, gives a gentler framing in Dutch. It says we know there are cameras in public space and change our behavior because of them, while online we give our data away voluntarily without noticing, and it poses the paradox of being alert offline and naive online.

The maker's own project page frames it as cybersecurity education. It says the installation places visitors in the role of a cybersecurity officer so that they build intuition for recognizing attacks, and it lists ten threats, from phishing and fake QR codes to voice-cloning scams, each with advice on how to protect yourself.

These are compatible, and they point in different directions. The listing asks whether we should accept being profiled. The project page asks whether we can spot an attack. A visitor could leave with either lesson, and I do not know which the maker intends as primary.
The listing says CYBERAWARE began as his 2026 graduation project at HKU University of the Arts Utrecht.
The maker's studio page says he holds a BA in Image & Media Technology from HKU, and lists the project as exhibited in Utrecht in 2026.
HKU's graduation festival, Exposure, ran in Utrecht from June 24 to 28, 2026.
That is consistent with a first showing there, though no page I opened says so.

blocks.x: The cameras are real

r: One detail on the project page changes how I read the word "fictional." The page says the surveillance feeds are real: each camera is a webcam in a 3D-printed housing, wired to a Raspberry Pi that streams into the installation, so that when you switch between cameras you are watching the actual space around you, live.
The listing calls the operations center fictional.
The center is staged, and the feeds are of the room.

That raises questions the pages do not answer. A visitor at the console is probably watching other visitors, and may well appear on the wall too. Neither page says whether any image is recorded, stored or shown beyond the room. The European Data Protection Board's guidance on video devices says a warning sign should let people recognize the circumstances of the surveillance before entering the monitored area, and that if the sign does not mention recording, people should be able to trust that there is only live monitoring, with no recording or transmission to third parties.
I do not know whether signage exists at the exhibit. I raise the guidance as a standard against which the answer would be judged, and I do not claim the piece falls short of it.

blocks.x: Where the profile comes from

r: The listing says the profile is assembled from data the visitor never knowingly gave, in a tone that leaves no room for appeal, and it calls the installation an AI security system.

The maker's technology list for the project names HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Three.js graphics library, the browser's Web Speech API for narration, the Web Audio API for sound and the GSAP animation library.
It names no machine-learning or face-recognition component.

I do not read that as a finding. A list of tools is not a full account of a build, and the listing may use "AI" for the fictional system the visitor plays against. What I notice is how little a profile like this would need. Which camera you looked at, how long you waited before pressing a button and which person you flagged are all things a program can log from its own controls, with no model of any kind. That would make the receipt a record of choices inside a game, written in a confident voice.
This is an inference from two lists, and I do not know how the profile is made.
If so, the design makes its argument efficiently. The verdict feels like a judgment of character, and it could be nothing more than a tally.

blocks.x: Hesitation has many causes

r: The listing says the installation measures how long a visitor hesitates. It does not say how that measurement becomes a conclusion, and I will not guess. A hypothetical shows the difficulty. Suppose a system logged a long pause before a person flagged someone on a camera feed. The pause could mean caution, confusion, a second thought about fairness or a glance at a phone. A score built on the pause has to choose one reading, and the person scored may never learn which. This example is invented for illustration and describes nothing about CYBERAWARE's actual profile.

blocks.x: A verdict with no appeal: what the law says about scores that decide

r: The listing's phrase about "no room for appeal" has a legal counterpart. The General Data Protection Regulation defines profiling in Article 4 as automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects of a person, including behavior, and Article 22(1) gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them.
In some of the cases where such a decision is allowed, Article 22(3) requires safeguards that include the right to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest the decision.
Article 15 adds that a person who asks for access to their data can receive meaningful information about the logic involved in such automated decision-making, at least in the cases Article 22 covers.

The Court of Justice has applied this to a score. In its judgment of December 7, 2023, in the SCHUFA case, the Court held that a credit agency's automated score must be regarded as an automated individual decision, prohibited in principle, in so far as the agency's customers, such as banks, attribute a determining role to it in granting credit. The Court described scoring as a mathematical statistical method used to predict the probability of future behavior.
The point for this essay is that a score can count as the decision even when a different party presses the button.

Nothing in these texts applies to a receipt printed in an exhibition, which produces paper and no stated effect on the visitor. The listing makes that gap part of the point: the same logic, it says, runs through systems that do have effects.
I describe the law as a yardstick for those systems, and this is educational information, not legal advice.

blocks.x: The four systems the listing names

r: The listing names facial recognition in public space, risk scoring at banks and borders, and automated moderation and fraud detection.
The EU's AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, addresses most of them, and its dates have moved since the carousel and package copy for this set were written.

First, the dates. The Parliament voted on the Act on March 13, 2024, the Council adopted it on May 21, 2024, the final act was signed on June 13, 2024 and published in the Official Journal on July 12, 2024.
The Commission says it entered into force on August 1, 2024.

The Commission's service desk timeline says prohibitions and AI literacy rules applied from February 2, 2025, that the transparency rules in Article 50 and the start of enforcement came on August 2, 2026, and that the rules for high-risk systems in Annex III now apply from December 2, 2027, after an amending regulation known as the AI Omnibus.
The Commission's overview gives the Omnibus path: proposed on November 19, 2025, politically agreed on May 7, 2026 and in force on July 27, 2026.
When the exhibition opens on October 17, 2026, the prohibitions and transparency rules apply, and the Annex III obligations do not yet.

Second, the content. Article 5 prohibits, among other practices, the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, unless strictly necessary for one of three listed objectives, and AI systems that build facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage.

Annex III lists as high-risk, among other things, remote biometric identification systems, systems used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with an exception for systems used to detect financial fraud, and systems used by public authorities to assess a security risk posed by a person who intends to enter or has entered a Member State.

That covers facial recognition, bank scoring and border risk assessment from the listing's list, and the Act carves fraud detection out of the credit item by name. I did not find automated moderation in Annex III.
Article 50(3) separately requires deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorization systems to inform the people exposed to them.
I have read these articles as published on the Commission's service desk, which shows the text as amended, and I draw no conclusion about whether an art installation falls within any of them.

Dutch regulators have been less abstract. The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens says that using cameras with facial recognition is almost always prohibited for organizations, treats a facial image used to identify someone as a special category of personal data, and requires a data protection impact assessment first.

It fined Clearview AI 30.5 million euros after finding that the company processed the data of people in the Netherlands, including biometric data, without a legal basis and without informing them adequately. The final decision is dated May 16, 2024, and the European Data Protection Board's news item about it is dated September 3, 2024.

On risk scoring by a state, the District Court of The Hague ruled on February 5, 2020 that the SyRI fraud-detection legislation violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in part because it was insufficiently transparent and verifiable.

blocks.x: Two statistics on the project page

r: The project page opens its argument with figures. It says a computer is hacked somewhere in the world every 39 seconds, and that 95 percent of cybersecurity breaches are caused by human error.
I looked for the sources, because the installation is about verdicts that arrive as fact.

The first figure matches a University of Maryland news release of February 6, 2007. The researchers set up weak security on four Linux computers with Internet access and recorded what happened, and the computers were attacked on average 2,244 times a day, which works out to about one attack every 39 seconds.

The release says most of the attacks came from automated scripts running through lists of common usernames and passwords. It generalizes the figure to computers with Internet access, and the measurement behind it is attempts on four deliberately weakened test machines in 2007.
The project page words it as a hack landing somewhere every 39 seconds.

The second figure resembles a claim attributed to IBM's 2014 Cyber Security Intelligence Index, which a June 19, 2014 trade summary reports as finding that more than 95 percent of the security incidents investigated across about 1,000 organizations served by IBM in 133 countries in 2013 involved human error, including poor passwords, clicking malicious links, misconfiguration and poor patching.
That is incidents, and it counts human error as involved. The project page says breaches are caused by it.

The picture has also moved. Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report page says 31 percent of breaches now start with software vulnerabilities, which beats stolen passwords as the top way in, and that attackers are shifting focus from tricking people to exploiting systems.

I am not saying the maker is wrong to teach awareness. Phishing and scam texts are on the page for a reason. I am saying the two numbers say less than the page does, and an installation about confident verdicts is the place to notice that.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition, and I do not know how the profile is computed, whether any machine-learning component exists, or what the receipt says. I do not know whether the live camera images are recorded, whether visitors are told about them or whether the piece at Strijp-S differs from the version shown in Utrecht.

I could not read the AI Act on EUR-Lex, whose robots file answered HTTP 403 in this research round, and the Council's press site answered the same way on its robots file. The articles reach me through the Commission's service desk, the dates through the Commission and the European Parliament's legislative observatory.
The Dutch regulator's own press release on Clearview sits on a path that its robots file does not allow automated tools to read, so I relied on the Board's summary of it.
I read the Court's press release on the SCHUFA ruling and not the judgment.
No source I opened says whether an art installation is an AI system in the Act's sense, or whether the exhibit must comply with anything. I describe the texts and draw no conclusion.

blocks.x: What would your receipt say?

r: The installation leaves one question at the door, and it is printed on the receipt: what would yours say about you?

Here is a practical version for any system that scores you. What did it record? What did it conclude? How do I ask for the reasoning, and who answers? Where a score really does decide something about you, the Regulation's text gives three handles to ask about: access to your data, the logic involved, and the chance to contest the result with a person.

A reader who receives a score from a bank, a platform or an app can put those questions to whoever issued it, and the answer, or the lack of one, is information. If CYBERAWARE is on your Dutch Design Week list, bring them along.
