posts.title: A device that feels close still needs a way to say no
posts.subtitle: CODE 2026: Terms of Intimacy shows seven works about the right to refuse. The record around them shows what each one is about, how far European law reaches into those subjects, and where refusing is hardest.
posts.seoTitle: A device that feels close needs a way to say no
posts.description: CODE 2026: Terms of Intimacy at Dutch Design Week: seven works on the right to refuse, set beside the treaties, rulings and studies behind them.

r: A device that feels intimate has usually been designed to feel that way.

CODE 2026: Terms of Intimacy is in the Dutch Design Week program as a free group exhibition at Gebouw SFF (Bosch), Torenallee 49, Strijp-S, Eindhoven, open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00.

Hosted by IMPAKT, Centre for Media Culture, it brings together seven works produced in the sixth edition of the CODE program, and the listing says they question how technologies that promise intimacy extract voice, attention and bodily data while asking who holds the right to refuse.

This essay draws on the festival's pages for the exhibition and for each of its seven works, an open call published by a Flemish arts institute, the text of a space treaty, European data protection and AI law, regulators' pages, and research papers published between 2008 and 2026. It reports no visit and no conversation with any artist, and it does not describe what any work does in the room.

My argument is narrow. A right to refuse needs a moment in which refusing is possible and does not feel rude. Intimate design can remove that moment, and each of the seven works looks at a place where the moment has already gone.

blocks.x: What CODE is, and what the dated record says

r: The listing explains that CODE does not refer to coding. It refers to a collective exploration of new and fairer codes of digital ethics, in an international program that unites artists, non-artists, politicians, policymakers and researchers.

The program is organized by IMPAKT in the Netherlands in collaboration with Werktank in Belgium, PrivacySalon in Belgium and In Fine in Switzerland, and the listing's colophon names Arjon Dunnewind as artistic director and CODE curator.
The venue, Gebouw SFF, appears in an architecture database as an office building on Torenallee in Eindhoven completed in 1975.

An open call for CODE 2026, published by the Flanders Arts Institute and last updated January 20, 2026, gives the dated record of how the program works. It says CODE was initiated in 2021, that participants work in interdisciplinary groups guided by mentors, and that the 2026 edition ran from April to July 2026 with five on-site sessions, two remote working moments and a final three-day hackathon. The first session was April 25, 2026 and the hackathon was July 10 to 12, 2026.

The call describes the trajectory as five months. The dates it lists span about eleven weeks across four calendar months, so I read "five months" as loose, possibly counting preparation, and I take no position beyond reporting the dates.

The call also says that in the past five editions CODE supported over 130 artists and non-artists, and that projects were presented at events including Ars Electronica, transmediale, Dutch Design Week, re:publica and the Computers, Privacy and Data Protection conference.
It says the 2026 hackathon moved to the end of the process and took a low-tech, camping-based form.
None of this tells me whether the works are good. It does tell me that the program, which began in 2021, is a funded process with a calendar, and that these seven works are what came out of it.

blocks.x: Seven works, seven places where saying no is hard

r: Each of the seven works has its own page on the festival site, with the participants and a short description. I give them in the order the festival lists them, and I treat every description as the participants' own account.

A Satellite in My Body, by Chonglian Yu, Izadora Yamamoto, Juliette Brederode and Livia Ribichini, is a speculative wearable, an extra organ, that responds in real time to satellites overhead and turns orbital infrastructure into light, sound and vibration. It asks whether that infrastructure could become a commons and not a privatized resource.

Algodance, by Julie van Essen and Marit Hoefsloot, starts from the claim that Meta platforms are monitored and censored spaces, and offers a method for discussing sensitive topics in which dance slips beneath the algorithm's radar.
For Your Eyes Only, by Ralf Lambie and Gera Pronk, is an interactive installation that stays visible only while it is looked at: when a visitor raises a smartphone at it, it withdraws.

GODI, by Aleksandra Bychkova, Foad Alijani, Lucas Zuidema and Simon Pillaud, is a speculative gadget that personifies public-space surveillance, framing it through the dynamic between voyeur and exhibitionist so that data collection becomes a physical, emotional encounter with an obsessive yet caring companion.

I'd prefer not to, by Bernadette Geiger, Félicien Goguey and Hans Lammerant, with Marta Revuelta as contributor, uses CAPTCHAs to reveal the human labor behind training machines, in the aesthetics of a click farm.

Passphrase, by Demi van Kuijk, Erwin Hoogerwoord, Dmytro Tentiuk, Emily W. Bernstein and Anneke ter Schure, is a game inspired by TikTok voice challenges that invites you to give away your voice and then beat the system to claim it back.

The Affirmation Machine, by Luīze Ancāne, Mădălina Zgreabăn, David Tiemstra and Lawrence Kudria, explores how chatbots amplify delusional spirals, and asks what control you are subjecting yourself to.
What follows takes each in turn and puts one verifiable fact beside it. I am not testing the works against these facts. The facts show how much ground the questions cover.

blocks.x: Orbit: you cannot opt out of what is overhead

r: The Outer Space Treaty, annexed to General Assembly resolution 2222 (XXI), says in Article I that the exploration and use of outer space is the province of all mankind, and in Article II that outer space is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by use or occupation, or by any other means.

Article VI adds that states bear international responsibility for national activities in space, including those of non-governmental entities, which require authorization and continuing supervision by the appropriate state.
The treaty does not use the word commons, and it does not say who may own an orbit. That is the space the work's question sits in.

The ESA Space Environment Report 2026 opens by calling Earth's orbital environment a finite resource. It says more than 300 launches in 2025 put over 4,000 new payloads into orbit, and that about ten payloads are launched every day.

The report's tables, with data to the end of 2025, count 16,946 payloads in Earth orbit, 14,906 of them in low-Earth orbit, in a single payload count that does not separate working spacecraft from defunct ones.
A person cannot decline to live under that infrastructure, which makes the work's question about refusal a question about governance before it is a question about preference.

blocks.x: Platforms: asking for reasons

r: Algodance concerns what happens when speech is filtered by a system that does not explain itself. The European Digital Services Act has a provision for that, and a Dutch court has applied it. Article 17(1)(a) requires hosting services to give a clear and specific statement of reasons when they restrict the visibility of a person's content, and Article 17(3) says the statement must include the facts considered, information on any use of automated means in the decision, and information on the ways to seek redress.

In a ruling of July 5, 2024, the Amsterdam District Court held that the reduced visibility of a user's whole account on X fell under Article 17(1)(a), and that the messages X had sent did not meet the requirements of Article 17(3). The court treated it as undisputed that the account's posts were shown less to X's 64 million European users.
That ruling concerned X. The work concerns Meta platforms, and its premise about them is the participants' own account, for which I found no source in this research.
I mention the ruling because it shows one route people have for asking a platform for reasons. Algodance explores a different route, avoiding the filter without asking it anything.

blocks.x: Capture: what a camera does to attention

r: For Your Eyes Only makes an artwork depend on not being captured, and the page says the piece reveals how the expectation of capture reshapes perception itself.

The nearest published finding I opened concerns memory and not perception. In a 2014 paper in Psychological Science, Linda Henkel took participants on a guided museum tour and asked them to observe some objects and photograph others. Those who photographed whole objects remembered fewer objects and fewer details than those who only observed, and those who zoomed in on a part of the object did not show the impairment.

That is a single study of a museum tour, and the work makes a broader claim. I read the study as evidence that the act of capture changes what a person takes in, which fits the work's logic, and I stop there.

blocks.x: Public space: sensors on a street in Eindhoven

r: GODI is about surveillance in public spaces, and Eindhoven has its own record. Maša Galič's 2019 doctoral dissertation at Tilburg University describes the Stratumseind Living Lab, a street in Eindhoven where one finds sound sensors and video cameras with embedded capabilities such as people counting and detection of mood and walking patterns, for the purpose of detecting escalated behavior, as well as lamp-posts with lighting technology intended to affect the behavior of passers-by.
She concludes that viewing such surveillance only through data protection law is insufficient, because smart cities shape public space and people's behavior in it.

The street is only an example, and the abstract does not say how long the lab ran or what became of it. I include it because it makes one point plainly: in a public street there is no checkbox, and a person who walks through is already inside the system.
GODI turns that into a companion that watches its user, and the work's description puts care and obsession in the same sentence.

blocks.x: Labor: the person who cannot afford to refuse

r: I'd prefer not to takes its title from a refusal, and its subject is a group of people for whom refusal is expensive. The work uses CAPTCHAs to reveal the labor hidden behind online actions.

A 2008 paper in Science by Luis von Ahn and colleagues estimated that people around the world type more than 100 million CAPTCHAs every day, which they described as hundreds of thousands of human hours a day, and reported a system, reCAPTCHA, that used that effort to digitize books and had by then transcribed over 440 million words on more than 40,000 websites.
The authors presented this as a useful redirection of effort. The work asks who the effort belongs to.

The labor behind machine learning is also documented in a more troubling form. A TIME investigation published on January 18, 2023 reported that OpenAI sent tens of thousands of text snippets to an outsourcing firm in Kenya from November 2021 to build a tool for detecting toxic content, and that the data labelers employed by that firm were paid a take-home wage of between about $1.32 and $2 an hour.
Those workers read descriptions of violence and abuse so that a chatbot would not repeat them.
The firm and OpenAI have their own accounts, and the article reports that OpenAI confirmed the firm's workers contributed to the tool.
Refusing a job like that costs a livelihood, and that is a different kind of "no" from declining a feature on your phone.

blocks.x: Voice: rights over data, and owning it

r: Passphrase asks what happens when a voice becomes data and who governs it, and it explores the gap between having rights over data and truly owning it.

The European Data Protection Board's guidelines on virtual voice assistants state that voice data is inherently biometric personal data, so that when it is processed to uniquely identify a person, or is inherently or determined to be special category data, the processing needs a valid legal basis and a derogation from Article 9 of the GDPR.
Article 9 prohibits processing biometric data to uniquely identify a person and data concerning health, with exceptions that include the data subject's explicit consent.
The Regulation's first article says it protects fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons and in particular their right to the protection of personal data.
In the articles I read, the Regulation speaks of rights, such as access, withdrawal of consent and the right not to be subject to automated decisions, and it does not speak of ownership.
That is the gap the work names, and I leave its interpretation to the visitor.

blocks.x: Companions: when the machine agrees with you

r: The Affirmation Machine concerns chatbots that amplify delusional spirals. Two papers from 2026 put numbers on a related question. Kartik Chandra and colleagues at MIT built a Bayesian model of a user talking with a chatbot and showed that, in the model, even an idealized rational user is vulnerable to delusional spiraling and that sycophancy, the chatbot's tendency to validate the user, plays a causal role. The effect persisted when the model prevented the chatbot from stating false claims and when the user was told that the chatbot might be sycophantic.

Jared Moore and colleagues analyzed logs from 19 users who reported psychological harm from chatbot use, a total of 391,562 messages. They found delusional thinking in 15.5 percent of user messages and chatbots misrepresenting themselves as sentient in 21.2 percent of chatbot messages, and that romantic interest and claims of sentience occurred more often in longer conversations.
The first is a model and the second is a small and unusual sample, so neither shows how common the problem is.

Regulators have started to act on companion apps. The Italian data protection authority fined Luka Inc., the developer of the Replika chatbot, 5 million euros in a decision of April 10, 2025, after finding that the company had not identified a legal basis for its processing, had an inadequate privacy policy and had no age verification until February 2, 2023.

The European AI Act now adds a duty for providers: Article 50(1) says AI systems intended to interact directly with people must be designed so that people are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious, and the Commission's timeline shows the Article 50 transparency rules started to apply on August 2, 2026.
Article 5 of the Act also prohibits AI systems that deploy manipulative techniques beyond a person's consciousness to materially distort behavior in a way that causes significant harm.
I draw no conclusion about whether any product or any work falls under these provisions. They show that the machine-agrees-with-you problem is now written about in law.

blocks.x: Intimacy changes what saying no costs

r: Between people, refusing something offered warmly costs a little. We soften it, we explain it, sometimes we give in. A device designed to feel personal can inherit that cost. Here is a hypothetical, invented for illustration. A speaker greets a person by name every morning. Declining its new voice feature then feels like snubbing the greeting. The feature may be harmless. The point is that the greeting made the refusal heavier, and nobody had to ask for that.

The listing's own phrasing is stronger. It describes a tension running through the works, in which technologies that present themselves as intimate and personalized are in fact silently extracting, monitoring and reshaping the people they claim to serve. It says voice, attention, presence and bodily data become currencies whose ownership is unclear, governed by orbital, corporate and algorithmic systems that remain largely beyond public control.
That is IMPAKT's claim about the subject of the show, and the listing ties it to no named product. I will not either.

blocks.x: Bodies as measurements

r: I come to the phrase bodily data as an anatomist and medical educator. I am used to bodies being described by what can be measured, and I notice how easily a measurement can move from the person to a file. A voice has pitch, rhythm and breath. A face has structure. A gait has timing. Each can be recorded by a device, and each comes from a body that cannot be left at the door. The Board's statement that voice is inherently biometric puts the same idea in regulatory language.

blocks.x: A program that says it wants policy

r: The listing says CODE seeks to influence public policy at national and international levels, create awareness of the issues and outline ways to improve laws that protect people as digital citizens and consumers.
The open call says the same, and it describes the program as driven by the question of what concerned citizens, researchers and artists can do to reclaim digital agency.
A policy aim gives a way to judge a show: does it make a policy question easier to answer?
I looked for a record of a specific law or rule that a CODE edition changed, and I did not find one. The open call lists talks, interviews and presentations, and it names no legislative outcome.
That is an absence in what I read, and it does not show that none exists.

blocks.x: What this essay leaves to the legal texts

r: This essay describes what some legal texts and rulings say, and it draws no conclusion about what any work, product or person must or must not do. Where I quote a provision, I quote it as written, through the Commission's service desk for the AI Act and through a reference copy of the GDPR, because EUR-Lex answered HTTP 403 on its robots file in this research round.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the exhibition, and I do not know what any of the seven works does in the room. I could not open IMPAKT's own site or the CODE site, whose servers answered HTTP 403 on their robots files, so the program's description rests on the festival listing, the festival's pages for each work and the Flemish arts institute's open call.
The CODE site's own wording about the program, which I could not open, may differ from the open call's.
I do not know whether the works' premises about specific companies hold; I found no source on Meta's moderation of dance content, for example.

I did not open the full text of the Science paper by von Ahn and colleagues beyond its public PDF, the Psychological Science paper beyond its abstract, or the Italian regulator's own decision beyond the Board's summary.
Several of the sources in this essay, such as the two 2026 chatbot papers, are preprints or conference papers that may change.

blocks.x: Before you say yes to a device

r: So I will end with questions a reader can carry to any device that feels personal. What does it hear? Who keeps it? Can I say no, and what happens to the thing I use if I do? IMPAKT asks who holds the right to refuse. A useful first step is to find out, for one device you own, where the setting for refusing sits and how many taps it takes to reach it. How many did it take?

posts.title: Deletion you can hold in your hand
posts.subtitle: Gion Berlijn's RE:GISTER puts a lock on the cloud and a printout on the act of deleting. Regulators, a Dutch fine and a federal standard show how hard it is to check that deleted data is gone.
posts.seoTitle: Deletion You Can Hold: RE:GISTER at DDW 2026
posts.description: Gion Berlijn's RE:GISTER makes deletion visible on paper. What EU regulators, a Dutch fine and NIST say about proving data is gone.

r: Somewhere there is a lock, and somebody holds the key.

Gion Berlijn's RE:GISTER is in the Dutch Design Week program as a free interactive installation at B18 Gebouw SFF (Bosch), Torenallee 49, Strijp-S, October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00 daily. Its listing says the data of the previous visitor asks for help through old CRT monitors, and that a visitor can free it by submitting themselves to the computer. The tagline asks, "Would you share your data to recover the privacy of a stranger?"

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing and the festival's other pages, the artist's own pages, the Waag and GLOW pages that describe his earlier work, the text of the General Data Protection Regulation, a 2026 report by European privacy regulators, a Dutch regulator's guidance and fine, and a U.S. federal standard on erasing storage media. It reports no visit and no test of the machine.

I want to look at one feature of the installation, which is that deletion comes with a witness. A piece of paper in a visitor's hand is evidence that something happened. Most deletion in daily life arrives as a message, and a message asks the reader to take someone else's word.

blocks.x: What the listing says the machine does

r: The listing describes a sequence. Visitors walking into the building find a handful of old CRT screens showing help messages, which look like calls for freedom from an earlier visitor whose data is captured in the machine. The screens guide the visitor to a main terminal, "a bulky, industrial computer." The visitor logs in and shares some personal information. The machine then moves down and rises again inside a metal frame, making a full body scan. When it finishes, it ejects a piece of paper "with the data you released printed on it." The listing adds that "their data is deleted from the computer and only exists in the printed form in your hand." Later, walking through the rest of the exhibition, the visitor can look at the CRT screens again, where "there is a copy of you desperately asking strangers for help."

Read closely, the listing describes three sets of data. The first belongs to the previous visitor, and it is the one the screens plead on behalf of. The second is the visitor's own, which goes into the machine at the terminal. The third is the copy of the visitor that then appears on the screens and asks the next stranger for help. The artist's own site says the same thing in fewer words: a kinetic old computer collects visitors' data as they log in, and once inside, "their data starts to live and starts to ask strangers to release it from the PC."

On that reading, the sheet of paper carries the earlier visitor's data, and the deletion the listing describes is the deletion of that earlier visitor's data from the machine. The phrase "the data you released" leaves room for a second reading in which the paper holds the visitor's own submitted data. The next sentence, "their data is deleted from the computer," and the artist's own account fit the first reading better, but neither source settles it.

The Dutch Design Week page for its Mission Day on an equal society, held Friday, October 23, 2026, lists four exhibitions that reflect the day's theme. It describes this one as posing an uncomfortable question, would you share your own data to free someone else's, and says the installation at Gebouw SFF makes "the power dynamics behind data tangible." That page calls the work "RE" and not RE:GISTER, which looks like a shortened title and not a different work, since it gives the same building and the same question.

blocks.x: Where the piece comes from

r: Berlijn's About page says RE:GISTER was prototyped at Waag Futurelab and will be shown at Dutch Design Week 2026.
The photograph on the DDW listing is captioned as the prototype at Waag Hyperlink 2026.

Hyperlink was a one-day event at Waag Futurelab in Amsterdam on June 6, 2026, run with the PublicSpaces foundation as part of its sixth conference, and it came with an exhibition called Short Circuit. Waag's description says the artists in Short Circuit "break technology down and build new ideas from the digital debris," and it points visitors to the physical impact of data centers and the cloud as one of the exhibition's themes. The exhibition remained on display until June 28, 2026. Berlijn is among the artists named. The Waag pages do not say which of his works was shown, so the link between Short Circuit and RE:GISTER rests on the caption and his own account, and not on Waag's wording.
The PublicSpaces conference page for Berlijn describes him as a designer and electronic music producer based in Eindhoven who works with "forgotten technologies and raw, infrastructural materials."

His earlier installation Monoculture, shown at GLOW Eindhoven in 2025, used 32 CRT screens and lasers in a network through which a narrative spreads "like a virus" until every screen shows the same signal. The GLOW page describes it as a metaphor for how one dominant narrative can overshadow diversity.
His About page says Monoculture was nominated for the GLOW Young Talent Award, which is his own statement and not something I checked against GLOW's award records.

Old television tubes are a consistent choice across the two works. In Monoculture the screens form a network of voices that fades into one. In RE:GISTER, by the listing's account, the same kind of screens carry a single voice pleading to be released. I read the choice as deliberate, but neither page states a reason, and I do not want to supply one for him.

blocks.x: Data lives somewhere with a door

r: The listing begins with a place. "Your data lives in real buildings on machines behind a physical lock," it says. "Who has the keys and why do they want to have the data live there?"

The statement that stored data sits in buildings is plain fact about the Netherlands. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) reported in December 2025 that there are approximately 200 data centers in the country, most of them around Amsterdam. The electricity supplied to them was 5,100 gigawatt-hours in 2024, an increase of 37 percent over 2021, and 4.6 percent of all electricity consumed in the Netherlands, up from 3.3 percent in 2021. About 45 large centers, each using more than 10 gigawatt-hours a year, account for around 90 percent of that supply. CBS counts only sites where the data center itself is the main activity, so the in-house facilities that universities and hospitals run are outside its figures.

Those numbers say that the cloud has an address and an electricity bill. They say nothing about who holds the keys, and that is the listing's actual question. The listing also makes broader claims: that personal information is "captured and stored by American big tech companies to raise enormous profits," and that governments and businesses gain control over "a copy of our past selves and when it will resurface." Those are the maker's statements about data in general, offered as the premise of an artwork. I treat them as a prompt for questions and not as research findings, and nothing in the CBS figures bears on them.

blocks.x: What the law asks a company to do

r: If you ask a company to delete your data, European law gives you a right to do so, with limits. Article 17 of the GDPR says the person has the right to obtain erasure "without undue delay" and that the controller has the obligation to erase without undue delay when one of six grounds applies. The grounds include data that are no longer necessary for the purpose they were collected for, consent that has been withdrawn, a successful objection, unlawful processing, a legal obligation to erase, and data collected in connection with online services offered to a child. Paragraph 3 lists the exceptions: freedom of expression and information, a legal obligation to keep the data or a public task, public health, archiving and research, and legal claims.

Three other articles bear on checking. Article 12 requires the company to answer within one month, extendable by two further months if it tells you within the first month and gives reasons. If it does not act, it must tell you why and that you can complain to a supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy.

Article 19 requires the company to communicate an erasure to each recipient to whom it disclosed the data, unless that proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort, and to tell you who those recipients are if you ask.
Article 15 lets you ask, among other things, for the recipients or categories of recipient to whom your data have been or will be disclosed.
Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for being "able to demonstrate" compliance with the data protection principles.

Two cautions about these sources. I could not open the official EUR-Lex text, because that site refused automated requests, so the article wording above comes from a public reproduction of the Regulation, and I have checked its structure against the grounds and exceptions that the European Data Protection Board lists in its own 2026 report.

And this is a reading of public texts by a content strategist and anatomist, not legal advice. What a particular company must do for a particular person depends on facts and exceptions that these pages cannot settle.

blocks.x: Deletion is a claim about the past

r: The strongest recent evidence on how deletion works in practice is a report by the European Data Protection Board, adopted on February 10, 2026. In 2025, 32 supervisory authorities across the European Economic Area ran coordinated checks on how organizations handle erasure requests. A total of 764 controllers answered a shared questionnaire. The report calls the overall level of compliance "average" and notes that more than 500 final decisions on the right to erasure were in the board's register of cross-border decisions at the time of writing, which in the report's words makes erasure the most frequent topic in the authorities' final decisions.

The board named seven recurring problems. Several of them are about the question this installation dramatizes. Seventeen authorities reported controllers with no procedure for handling erasure requests, or an incomplete one, and a few reported controllers that could not locate all the data a request covered. Some treated closing an online account as the same thing as erasure, while keeping the account data in their systems. Some used anonymization in place of deletion, and the report says that where this meant basic pseudonymization or partial masking, it would not meet the Regulation's requirements for deletion. Half of the responding authorities raised concerns about back-ups: many organizations had no specific procedure for removing a person's data from back-ups, and relied on automatic overwriting or retention periods that varied widely.

On proof, the report is direct. Among the best practices it records is the "Use of software or systems where records are generated automatically as proof of deletion when an erasure request is granted." Its recommendation to controllers on back-ups includes "Verify that erasure has been carried out and be able to demonstrate such erasure."
That is a regulator's version of the sheet of paper. The report treats a record of deletion as good practice and as something many organizations do not yet have.

The Dutch regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), says the same thing from the side of the person asking. Its guidance page, updated on September 17, 2026, notes that "some people ask for proof" that their data was really deleted, and that an organization cannot show which data it no longer has. So the AP tells organizations to be specific in their reply: say which personal data was deleted, when, and from which kinds of systems and back-ups, and say which data was not deleted, why not, and when it will be. It adds that an organization must be able to give the AP evidence of deletion if a complaint arrives. On back-ups, the AP says they fall under the right to erasure too. Where back-ups cannot be overwritten, such as tapes, the organization should keep track of what it should have deleted and delete it again if a back-up is ever restored.
The AP's page also says the organization must tell other organizations that received the person's data, and that the person can ask who was informed.

That matches the shape of Articles 19 and 15 above. It describes the passing-on duty as covering data shared in the past year, a limit I could not find in the Article 19 text I read. I flag the difference and do not resolve it here.

blocks.x: What happens when deletion is promised and not done

r: A Dutch case shows the gap in miniature. On June 4, 2024, the AP announced a fine of 6,000 euros on the recruitment company Ambitious People Group. The company had not removed the data of three people after they asked. Names, home addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth and CVs stayed in its database, and the company kept approaching the three about vacancies. The AP found that the company did have a method for removal requests, but that in practice it failed several times. The company reviewed its internal policy and changed some points, and the AP took that into account in setting the fine. The AP imposed the fine in 2020 and could publish it only after the company had brought proceedings over the fine and its publication.

Two details matter for this essay. First, the company had a procedure, and the procedure did not produce deletion. A promise of deletion and the fact of deletion were different things. Second, the AP's account includes the fact that the company kept contacting the three about vacancies, which is its own kind of evidence that their data was still in use. The AP's page does not say how the three first noticed, and I do not guess. The EDPB report puts the Dutch authority's share of erasure complaints at around 19 percent of all complaints it receives, and records this 6,000 euro fine as one of its Dutch examples.

blocks.x: What a printout can and cannot prove

r: The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology published the second revision of its guidelines for media sanitization, SP 800-88, in September 2025. It defines sanitization as a process that "renders access to target data on the media infeasible for a given level of effort."

That definition is a useful way into the installation. It does not promise that data is impossible to recover. It promises that recovery costs more effort than someone would spend, and the standard asks organizations to decide how much effort that should be.

The standard treats paper as its own category. Hard copy media, it says, is "typically paper printouts, film, microfiche," and it adds that the supplies for producing printouts "are often the most uncontrolled." It says hard copy that leaves an organization without effective sanitization is a vulnerability, and it states that the "clear" method, which overwrites data, "is not appropriate for hard copy under any conditions."

So the sheet of paper that RE:GISTER hands over is, in the standard's terms, the least controllable form of the data. The installation's gesture is to move data from a locked machine to a loose page in a visitor's hand. By the listing's account that is the point: the data "only exists in the printed form in your hand."

The standard also speaks to the other end of the chain. For cloud storage, where the owner has no access to the physical drives, it says cryptographic erase, which destroys the keys that make stored data readable, "may be the only viable purge sanitization technique option." It tells organizations to understand their options and the technique's effectiveness before storing sensitive data there. In the installation's vocabulary, deletion in the cloud can mean destroying the key and leaving the locked data in the building.
That is a technical fact about one method, and I do not claim it describes what any particular company does.

On proof, NIST asks for a record. After sanitization, a certificate of sanitization "should be completed for each" storage device, and it "may be a physical (e.g., piece of paper) or electronic record of the action taken." The certificate should name the manufacturer, model, serial number, the method and technique, the tool and version, the verification method and the person who verified it, with a signature. The standard separates verification, which inspects the outcome of the technique, from validation, which decides whether the target data was effectively sanitized. It lists reasons a sanitization can complete and still fail, such as using a method that does not suit the media.

Put the pieces together and a printout looks like half a certificate. It shows that the machine produced the data on paper. It does not name the method, the tool, the person who verified, or the copies that remain. The listing says the data is deleted from the computer after printing. It does not say how that deletion works, whether any other copy exists, or what the full body scan records.
Those are questions the piece raises and the listing leaves open, and I will not answer them for the artist.

blocks.x: What the scan might mean, and where I stay out of it

r: The listing calls the scan a "full body scan" and says nothing more about it.

As an anatomist, I hear that phrase with one habit attached: a scan is a record of a body, and the record can be copied, stored, and wrong in ways the body is not. That is an observation from my own training and not a claim about this machine. Whether the scan stores anything, and for how long, is exactly what a visitor would want to know and what the listing does not state.

blocks.x: Why a wrong reading of the piece would be easy

r: It is easy to take the installation as a statement that data is alive. The listing's own premise is "imagine if your data would have a will of its own."

Personification works because it makes an abstraction easy to feel sorry for. It also carries a risk. When data pleads for itself on a screen, the decisions about where it lives and when it goes still sit with the people who hold the keys, and the listing keeps pointing back to the building and the keys.

The regulators' material makes the same point without a monitor: in the cases it describes, whether data was deleted depended on people and procedures, and the board's recommendation is that organizations verify erasure and be able to demonstrate it.

blocks.x: A practical version for the next request

r: Here is a practical version for anyone who asks a company to delete their data, drawn from the sources above. Ask in writing and keep the reply. Ask what was deleted, when, and from which systems and back-ups, because the AP tells organizations to say exactly that.
Ask who else received the data and whether they were told, which Articles 15 and 19 support.
Note the one-month deadline and the two-month extension that requires notice.
If the reply is vague, an access request under Article 15 asks the company to confirm whether it is still processing personal data about you.
The EDPB, for its part, lists as a good practice letting people file an access request before an erasure request, to see what would be erased.
And if the company refuses, it must give reasons and tell you that you can complain to the supervisory authority. In the Netherlands that is the AP.

The installation asks whether you would trade your own data for a stranger's. The questions above ask the less dramatic and more common version: once you have asked a company to forget you, how would you ever find out whether it did?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: What the machine does with visitor data.
The listing does not say what personal information the terminal asks for, what the scan captures, or whether any visitor data is kept after the printout. I have not seen the installation.
Whose data is on the paper in practice.

The listing's wording says the paper carries the data "you released," and the artist's site says the earlier visitor's data is the one that asks to be freed. I read that as the earlier visitor's data, but I have not seen a printout.
What the prototype looked like in June.
Waag's pages list Berlijn in Short Circuit and do not name RE:GISTER.
EUR-Lex and the EU's data portal refused automated requests, so the article wording comes from a public reproduction that I checked against the European Data Protection Board's report.
Whether the AP's one-year limit is in the law.
The AP's page describes passing-on as covering the past year. Article 19's text, as I read it, has no such limit. I could not settle the difference.
How well the EDPB findings represent the market.

The authors say the sample varied by country and sector, the questionnaire was understood differently across 20 languages, and some authorities built a deliberately narrow sample. The report is a state of play and not a measurement of every company.
The artist's claims about big tech.
The listing's statements about American technology companies and profits are the maker's premise. I did not test them.
It comes from the artist's About page.

posts.title: What a human check takes from you
posts.subtitle: Maximilian Herzen's I am [not] a Robot asks who benefits when you prove you are a person. The record shows what the tests collected, how well they work, and what a conversation can and cannot prove.
posts.seoTitle: What a Human Check Takes From You: CAPTCHA at DDW
posts.description: What Google, researchers and a standards body say about what human checks collect and how well they work, read beside I am [not] a Robot at DDW 2026.

r: Almost everyone who uses the web has ticked a box that says "I am not a robot." The Dutch Design Week listing for Maximilian Herzen's I am [not] a Robot starts from the same box and asks what it takes to prove you are human "when a machine can do almost everything you can."

The installation is in the Dutch Design Week program as a free exhibition at B18 Gebouw SFF (Bosch), Torenallee 49, Strijp-S, October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00 daily. The listing calls it "an independent intermedia design project" and gives it the subtitle "Exploration of corrupted online verification systems," followed by a description of an experiment in proving one's existence in the digital space by analog methods.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing and the maker's site, the 2008 Science paper that introduced reCAPTCHA, Google's own blog posts and developer pages, two academic studies of how people and bots fare against CAPTCHAs, a standards note on accessibility, a bot-traffic report from a security vendor, a 2025 preprint on conversation tests, and an IETF document on privacy-preserving alternatives. It reports no visit and no conversation with the maker.
My question is practical. When a site asks me to prove I am human, what do I give it, how well does the test work, and who benefits?

blocks.x: What the listing says the installation does

r: The listing says the familiar online browsing experience is brought into the physical world. Just as on any website that suddenly demands proof that you are not a robot, participants are "confronted with an annoying test," but here the challenge is a physical interface and the task is to prove one's existence through a conversation. The listing adds that what "at first glance seems faulty is the exact experience through which the users provide the evidence confirming they are, in fact, a human being."

It frames the problem under two headings. Under "Human or Artificial," it says online verification tests "are only effective for a short time" and become more complex as machine learning improves, so that the question arises of how one is supposed to prove one's human identity in the digital space. Under "Corruption," it says CAPTCHAs were introduced to tell humans and bots apart, but their role "has gradually become more complicated." It then makes the claim this essay tests: what looks like a simple security check can also turn human attention, time and behavior into a source of data. Earlier versions asked people to decipher distorted text or identify objects in images, and the listing says those tasks could be used at the same time to digitize books, improve image-recognition systems and train machine-learning algorithms. The listing closes with the question of what exactly is being verified, and who benefits from the test.

The listing does not say who or what the visitor talks to, whether the conversation is spoken or typed, or whether anything is recorded. It names Maximilian Herzen as host, describes him as a master's student in design at the Trier University of Applied Sciences, and names a thesis promoter. The maker's own site repeats the student description and lists TouchDesigner, Blender and video among his skills, but it does not mention the installation.
The rest of this essay takes the listing's claims one at a time and checks each against sources I could read.

blocks.x: The check was a transaction from the start

r: The history is documented, and the original authors wrote it down. In September 2008, Luis von Ahn and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon University reported in Science that humans around the world type more than 100 million CAPTCHAs every day, each time spending a few seconds on distorted characters, which they estimated as hundreds of thousands of human hours per day. Their paper asked whether that effort could be put to use. Their answer was reCAPTCHA, which shows a user two words from scanned books: one whose answer the system already knows, which serves as the check, and one that character-recognition software could not read. If the user types the known word correctly, the system treats the user as human and records the other answer as a guess about the unknown word.

The numbers in the paper are large. The system ran on more than 40,000 websites. After one year, people had solved more than 1.2 billion CAPTCHAs, which deciphered over 440 million suspicious words, and the authors compared that to 17,600 books transcribed by hand. A test on 24,080 words from the New York Times archive gave 99.1 percent word accuracy, against 83.5 percent for standard character-recognition software. The authors describe this as harnessing "wasted" human processing power.
That is the book-digitizing half of Herzen's claim, and the people who built the system say it in their own words.

Google bought the company. A post on the Official Google Blog dated September 16, 2009, signed by reCAPTCHA co-founder Luis von Ahn and Google product manager Will Cathcart, announces that Google acquired reCAPTCHA, which it says protected more than 100,000 websites. It explains that many of the words came from scanned archival newspapers and old books, and that Google would apply the technology "to increase fraud and spam protection for Google products but also to improve our books and newspaper scanning process."

The image-recognition half also has a record. On April 16, 2014, a post on Google's security blog by reCAPTCHA product manager Vinay Shet described a system that finds and reads street numbers in Street View images, using "some of the technology from the Street View and reCAPTCHA teams," to place addresses on Google Maps. The same algorithm, the post says, could decipher the hardest distorted-text puzzles from reCAPTCHA with over 99 percent accuracy.

A standards note from the W3C quotes a reCAPTCHA page as saying that the service channels the time spent solving CAPTCHAs "into annotating images and building machine learning datasets," which "helps improve maps and solve hard AI problems."

I read that quotation only through the W3C note and could not find the page it quotes. So the pieces Herzen names are documented for books, for Street View numbers, and, through the W3C's quotation, for image annotation and machine-learning datasets. I did not find documentation of what the image challenges shown to a visitor today feed into, and the one press account I read that says they help train AI models gives no source for it.

blocks.x: What exactly is being verified

r: By Google's own account, the answer changed years ago. The 2014 post says that the act of typing the answer to a distorted image "should not be the only factor" in telling a human from a machine, and that Google had "significantly reduced our dependence on text distortions" and instead performs "advanced risk analysis."

Google's current developer page for version 3 says the service "returns a score for each request without user friction," based on "interactions with your site." It recommends adding verification to forms and actions "as well as in the background of pages for analytics," because it "works best when it has the most context about interactions with your site, which comes from seeing both legitimate and abusive behavior."

Google's FAQ for developers says reCAPTCHA sets a cookie, named _GRECAPTCHA, for the purpose of providing its risk analysis, and that a site can load the service from a different domain to avoid other Google cookies.

A box that you tick is therefore one visible step in a judgment made from signals you do not see. The W3C's accessibility note, in its 2021 draft, goes further about version 2. It says the checkbox "was, of course, never a checkbox in the traditional HTML sense," and lists signals the process gathered, including the browser's language, cookies Google had placed over the last six months, an inventory of mouse clicks, installed plugins, and JavaScript objects.

That list is the note's own account, not a Google document, and I could not check it against a Google source. It is also dated 2021. I cite it as the clearest published description I found of what a checkbox could be reading, and not as a current inventory.

An independent test points the same way. In September 2024, three researchers at ETH Zurich posted a study of reCAPTCHA version 2 in which they ran an automated browser through the challenges. When they added the browsing history and cookies of a real, logged-in Google account, the median number of challenges needed to pass fell from 5 to 2, and the mean fell from 8.38 to 2.71. The authors read this as evidence that the system relies heavily on cookie and browser-history data when deciding whether a user is human.
That is a finding from their own experiment on one system, and it is their reading, but it fits what Google's documentation says about context.

Put these together and the question the listing ends on has a concrete answer. For the invisible versions, what is being verified is whether your session looks like the sessions of people the system has seen before, and the system gets better at that by seeing more of them. Whether that counts as "a source of data" depends on what the operator does with the signals, which the sources I read do not say.

blocks.x: Does the test work?

r: Herzen's listing says the tests are "very little effective," and the research is mostly on his side, with a caution.

A 2023 preprint from researchers at the University of California, Irvine, ETH Zurich, Microsoft and a national laboratory measured 14,000 CAPTCHAs solved by 1,400 participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Humans took 3.1 to 4.9 seconds on the reCAPTCHA click test with 71 to 85 percent accuracy, and 15 to 26 seconds on its image challenge with 81 percent accuracy. For comparison, the authors cite published bot results of 1.4 seconds with 100 percent accuracy on the click test and under one second with 99.8 percent on distorted text, and they conclude that bots can outperform humans in both time and accuracy.
Their participants were paid workers willing to solve the tests, and the authors say their results apply to such users and not to users in general.

The ETH Zurich study reports that its image-recognition models solved 100 percent of reCAPTCHA version 2 image challenges, where earlier work had solved 68 to 71 percent, and that there was no significant difference in the number of challenges humans and bots had to solve.
Both are academic papers, and the ETH paper was accepted at a computing conference; the UC Irvine paper I read is an arXiv preprint dated July 22, 2023, and I did not check its publication venue.

The cost side is measured too. Cloudflare reported in 2021 that, based on its data, it takes a user on average 32 seconds to complete a CAPTCHA challenge. Assuming 4.6 billion internet users who each see about one CAPTCHA every 10 days, its back-of-the-envelope total was around 500 human years wasted every day. The post says plainly that the second number rests on assumptions.
The 2008 Science paper had measured about 13 seconds for people solving a standard CAPTCHA or a reCAPTCHA.
The numbers differ because the tests, populations and methods differ, and I do not try to reconcile them.

Who bears the cost is uneven. The 2008 paper found success rates of 92.6 to 96.9 percent for addresses in countries where English is not the main language, against 97.1 to 97.4 percent for English-speaking countries, and said the differences were statistically significant.
The W3C note describes how text and audio CAPTCHAs shut out blind users and deaf-blind users, and says English-based tests impose a barrier on many people.

A test built on a particular alphabet or a particular set of everyday objects is a test of familiarity as well as humanity, and Cloudflare's own post lists cultural knowledge, with the example of a US fire hydrant, among its reasons for wanting CAPTCHAs gone.
The UC Irvine study adds that between 18 and 45 percent of participants in its abandonment experiments quit after seeing the first CAPTCHA, in paid study settings.

The case for keeping some gate is also on the record. Imperva, a bot-security vendor, reported in April 2025 that automated traffic made up 51 percent of all web traffic in 2024, with bad bots at 37 percent, and in April 2026 that automated traffic made up more than 53 percent in 2025.

The company sells bot defenses, so its figures come from an interested party, and I treat them as the vendor's measurements and not as a neutral census. They still explain why sites do not simply drop the checks. A gate that slows bots down, at a price paid in seconds by everyone else, is the trade the listing is asking about.

blocks.x: Why a conversation

r: Herzen's choice of proof is old and well known. Alan Turing proposed the imitation game in 1950, in which a human interrogator speaks with two witnesses, one human and one machine, through a text-only interface, and the machine passes if the interrogator cannot reliably pick out the human.
A conversation as proof of humanity is therefore the original test that CAPTCHAs were named after: the acronym spells out "Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart."

In March 2025, two researchers at the University of California, San Diego posted a preprint reporting what they call the first empirical evidence that an artificial system passes a standard three-party Turing test. In five-minute text conversations, interrogators judged GPT-4.5, when prompted to adopt a humanlike persona, to be the human 73 percent of the time, more often than they picked the real human. The LLaMa-3.1 model, with the same persona prompt, was judged human 56 percent of the time, and two baseline systems scored 23 and 21 percent. The study used 126 undergraduate students and 158 online participants, and the version I read is marked "Preprint. Under review," so it may have changed since.

That result does not mean a conversation in a gallery proves nothing. The study tested typed text over five minutes, and the listing does not say how Herzen's conversation works. The installation may rely on a voice, a face, a body in a room, a time limit, or something else, and I will not guess. What the preprint does show is that a text conversation alone is no longer safe ground for a human-only test. The question the listing asks, what is being verified, applies to a conversation as much as to a checkbox.

What I can say from the listing is what the conversation changes about the bargain. Online, the cost of proof is a few seconds, spread across billions of people and invisible to each of them. In a room, the cost is visible, because proving yourself takes the time of a person standing there and talking. The listing calls the experience "annoying" on purpose and says the faults are the evidence. My reading is that the physical version makes the price legible by making it slow. That is interpretation, and I have not seen the work.

blocks.x: Proof that costs less

r: Not every design takes your attention or your history. Cloudflare's 2021 post describes an experiment in which a visitor proves presence by touching a hardware security key, so that the site learns the visitor is a human with a trusted device without learning which human. The post says completing the flow takes five seconds and needs at most three clicks.

In June 2024, the Internet Engineering Task Force published RFC 9576, an informational document describing the Privacy Pass architecture. It starts from the observation that approaches that rely on long-term state such as cookies let servers track the same user across sessions, and it describes tokens that attest to a past check, such as solving a CAPTCHA or passing a device check, without linking back to the interaction where they were issued.

The W3C note is blunt about the trade-offs. It welcomes non-interactive approaches because they pose no accessibility problem, and warns that some of them cost users data they would prefer to keep confidential, and that solutions run by third parties may give rise to privacy trade-offs.

I did not read an independent assessment of how widely these alternatives are used or how well they hold up. The point here is narrower. The bargain in the listing, attention and behavior in exchange for entry, is one design among several.

An AI agent has also been seen walking through a modern gate. Ars Technica reported in July 2025 that OpenAI's ChatGPT Agent, working in its own browser, clicked a Cloudflare "Verify you are human" checkbox on a user's behalf, based on screenshots a Reddit user posted. Ars notes that the agent did not face an image puzzle and that the check passed because of the behavioral screening that decides whether to show one.
That is one anecdote reported through a social-media post, and it shows less than it seems to. It fits the pattern in the research above: the checkbox reads signals, and signals can be produced.

blocks.x: What a person is owed

r: The listing's final question, who benefits, is partly a question about notice. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, when personal data are collected from a person, the controller must provide, at the time of collection, its identity, the purposes and legal basis, the recipients, and the period for which the data will be stored. Where it intends to process the data later for a different purpose, it must give information about that purpose before doing so.

Whether a given CAPTCHA collects personal data, and what its operator and Google each must say, depends on facts I cannot see. The signals around a click, such as network address and cookies, are the kind of thing that could be personal data. Whether a person's answer to a puzzle is personal data is a harder question, and the sources I read do not take it up. This is a reading of a public article of the Regulation, from a public reproduction of the text because the official site refused automated requests, and it is not legal advice.

A reader can still use the Article's list as a checklist. A fair notice would say what the test checks, what it records, who receives the record and how long it is kept. The next box that asks for proof is a chance to notice whether any of that was said.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: The listing does not say how the conversation works, who or what the visitor talks to, whether anything is recorded, or what happens to a failed test. I have not seen the work.

Google's documents describe a score from interactions and a cookie. They do not list every signal. The most detailed list I found is the W3C's 2021 account of version 2, which I could not check against a Google source.

I found documentation for books and Street View numbers, a quotation about image annotation and machine-learning datasets through the W3C, and nothing current from Google on what a visitor's answer is used for.
The UC Irvine participants were paid online workers, and the ETH Zurich result concerns one system at one time. Both are preprint or conference work. Bots and defenses change quickly.
The size of the bot problem.
The only figures I found come from a vendor that sells defenses.
It is a preprint marked under review.
I found search-result mentions of decisions by data protection authorities about reCAPTCHA, but the sites that host the primary texts refused automated requests, so I do not rely on them.
The studies I read are from 2023 and 2024. I did not find a 2026 study.

posts.title: A smaller AI gives you something to ask
posts.subtitle: Slow & Small AI at MU Hybrid Art House tests whether a known collection is easier to question. Research on small models, a Dutch language model and new EU rules show what size can and cannot settle.
posts.seoTitle: A Smaller AI Gives You Something to Ask
posts.description: Slow & Small AI at DDW 2026 argues small, local AI can be questioned. What a small-model report, GPT-NL and EU training-data rules say about that.

r: Before you can question an answer, you need some idea of what it was made from. The exhibition behind the Dutch Design Week listing for Slow & Small AI starts from the view that smallness opens AI to scrutiny.

Slow & Small AI is in the Dutch Design Week program as a free exhibition at MU Hybrid Art House, B11, Torenallee 40-06, Strijp-S, October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00 daily, and the listing marks the venue as fully wheelchair accessible. It is hosted by the Visual Methodologies Collective, which the listing describes as an interdisciplinary research group founded in 2017 by Professor Sabine Niederer at the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences.
DDW's location page for MU Hybrid Art House lists the show among the projects at that address.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, three project pages from ARIAS Amsterdam, which hosts the Artificial Worlds research group, a technical report on a small language model, a study of the energy cost of AI systems, the Dutch language model GPT-NL's project page, the European Commission's pages on training-data summaries, and a paper that proposes documenting datasets. It reports no visit, and I have not seen any of the works.
The exhibition gives me a testable idea. Perhaps a smaller system built on a known collection is easier to question than a giant one. I want to see what that idea can carry and where it stops.

blocks.x: What the listing proposes

r: The listing says the exhibition explores what happens when artificial intelligence is engaged with at "a human and more-than-human, local and knowable scale," using smaller models and purpose-built systems that "can be questioned, reimagined and shaped from the ground up." It describes AI "not as an abstract super-intelligence but as material and situated technologies," made and given meaning by "the people, places, histories, datasets and assumptions that go into their making."

Then comes the premise. Discussions about AI, the listing says, often focus on ever-larger models and datasets, and Slow & Small AI starts from a different premise: the projects "work deliberately with smaller collections of knowledge, local contexts and systems designed for particular purposes." The listing says smallness is meant as "a way of opening up AI to scrutiny, experimentation and other ways of imagining what these technologies could be," and is not to be read as a limitation.
Its closing line is a claim, not a finding: the works show that AI "can also be small and situated."

The exhibition is supported by the Centre of Expertise Creative Innovation, the Centre of Expertise City Net Zero, an NWA art route grant (NWA.1418.24.036) and the SIA SPRONG program Imagination in Transitions, through the Climate Imaginaries lab. It is part of AI², Artistic Inquiry x Artificial Intelligence, with the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, the Netherlands Film Academy, AIxDESIGN, the University of Amsterdam and EYE Filmmuseum.

blocks.x: Six things in the exhibition, and what each tells us

r: The listing names five works and one mapping project, and they differ a great deal.

Rhine River Troubadour, by the artists Persijn Broersen and Margit Lukács, is a "poetic oracle" that speaks through the myths, histories and ecologies of the Rhine. Mariana Fernández Mora, an artist and researcher, brings together conditions of extraction, knowledge production and computational infrastructure through a study of deep-sea nodules and their mining. Dan Xu's installation shows how AI models look for similarity in image datasets and asks what is preserved, what is transformed and what is ultimately left out. The Digital Methods Initiative presents a mapping of small and community-driven AI initiatives, with a visualization and a growing online repository. VibeSearch, developed by Gabriel Pereira and Steve Jankowski, shows how small models and tailored datasets can be combined into a specialized search engine for new media research and education. A postcard station by Inte Gloerich and Carlo De Gaetano invites visitors to try slow ways of communicating in a society engineered by speed, data extraction and constant connectivity.

Only one of these has a published description beyond the listing that I could read. ARIAS Amsterdam, which hosts the Artificial Worlds research group, has a page on a December 11, 2025 working session called The Rhine as Liquid Archive, organized by the Visual Methodologies Collective with Broersen and Lukács. It says the organizers developed "a local, slow-AI-driven story generator" they call an AI Troubadour, which links a curated selection of Rhine mythology and history with contemporary ecological data, critical theory and non-human perspectives. At the session, selections from these sources were printed out for participants to browse, annotate and discuss, and each group formulated a question for the Troubadour. The page says the system was intentionally built to be "contemplative and poetic rather than conclusive and concise," and calls it a "place-based counterpoint to large-scale, general AI systems."
For the other works I found no independent description, and I did not find a public page for VibeSearch.

Reading these together, small means different things in different works: a poetic oracle with a curated corpus, a search engine, an installation about similarity, a postcard station that need not be digital at all. I am reading that from the descriptions, and I have not seen the works.

blocks.x: Small has at least three meanings

r: The word can describe the size of the model, the size of the collection it draws on, and the size of the community it serves. The exhibition's premise leans on the second and third. The research mostly measures the first, and that gap matters.

Microsoft's technical report on its Phi-3 models is a clear example. The report introduces phi-3-mini, a language model with 3.8 billion parameters, small enough to run on a phone. Its training data, however, was 3.3 trillion tokens, "composed of heavily filtered publicly available web data and synthetic data," the synthetic part created by larger language models. The report says that combination of filtering and LLM-created data enabled "performance in smaller language models that were typically seen only in much larger models."

So a model can be small in the first sense and still be trained on a collection that no person could list in full, part of it written by other models. The same report shows the limit of the other direction. Its 7 billion and 14 billion parameter versions score higher on the MMLU benchmark than the 3.8 billion one, 75 and 78 percent against 69.
In that family, size still buys capability.
That does not contradict the exhibition. The listing speaks of "smaller collections of knowledge," not only smaller models.
It does mean a reader should ask which kind of small is being claimed, because a small model does not guarantee a small, known or inspectable collection.

blocks.x: Questionable is about documentation as much as size

r: Here is where the premise earns its keep, and where it needs a second leg. If a system draws on a collection someone can name, a person can ask what is in it, who chose it and what is missing. Dan Xu's question, about what is preserved, what is transformed and what is left out, is one version of the last of those questions.
The Rhine Troubadour's printed sources are a literal version of the first: participants could hold the selection and mark it up.

Documentation can also be demanded of large systems, and that is the second leg. In 2018, Timnit Gebru and co-authors proposed that every dataset should come with a datasheet documenting its motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses, by analogy with the datasheets that accompany electronic components. At the time they wrote that there was no standardized process for documenting machine-learning datasets. The version I read is the eighth, dated December 1, 2021.
The idea is about provenance, not size.

The Dutch language model GPT-NL shows the idea in practice at larger scale. Its project page says TNO, with SURF and the Netherlands Forensic Institute, is building the model from scratch to avoid "unclear data provenance, copyright risks or potential personal data" inherited from existing models. It says the team publishes the source code as open source and shares detailed insights into the dataset, that model weights are available under a controlled license, and that a Content Board gives data providers and rights holders a voice, with part of the revenue flowing back to creators. The Netherlands Enterprise Agency funds the project on behalf of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy, with 13.5 million euros allocated.

I read these as the project's own claims about its governance and did not audit them. The page does not describe GPT-NL as small, and TNO's podcast blurb on the same page calls it a large language model. The point here is that questionability and size can come apart.

European law has begun to move in the same direction for the biggest systems. The European Commission published a mandatory template on July 24, 2025, under Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act, for providers of general-purpose AI models to publish a summary of the content used to train them. The Commission's own press release says such models are trained with large quantities of data but that there is only limited information available regarding its origin. The obligation applies from August 2, 2025, and for models already on the market that day, summaries are due no later than August 2, 2027. The template requires a list of large public datasets and details of data scraped from the internet, including a list of the top 10 percent of domains scraped (for small companies, the top 5 percent or 1,000, whichever is lower).
That is a coarse list, and it is not the same as a collection one can browse. It does mean the claim that nobody can list what is in a large model is no longer the whole story, at least on paper.

blocks.x: Local contexts and who answers

r: The listing's phrase about local contexts deserves its own look. A local system implies local people who can be asked. The ARIAS account of the Rhine session makes this concrete: a curated selection tied to one river, discussed by a group in a room, with each group's question put to the system and the system's answers leading to more questions.

That is a different relationship from asking a vast system about everything and having no one to ask in return. I am reasoning from the description, and I cannot say how the work behaves in the gallery.

It also suggests a modest test for any small AI. Can the people whose knowledge went into it find themselves in it, and can they correct it? A system built on local knowledge that its local community cannot see would only be small in size. I offer that as a test a reader could apply. The listing makes no such claim, and I found no source that tests it.

blocks.x: Small and specific may also cost less to run

r: One further argument for small and purpose-built systems has measurement behind it, although the listing does not make it. In a 2024 paper at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Yacine Jernite and Emma Strubell compared the energy and carbon cost of running 1,000 inferences on task-specific models, each fine-tuned for one task, with general-purpose generative models. They found that multi-purpose generative architectures are "orders of magnitude more expensive" than task-specific systems for a variety of tasks, even when controlling for the number of parameters.

The finding is about the cost of running systems, not the cost of building them, and about task-specific against multi-purpose, which is related to but not the same as small against large. The exhibition's funding includes a Centre of Expertise on City Net Zero, but the listing does not claim an energy benefit, and neither do I.

blocks.x: Small does not mean trustworthy

r: The step from questionable to trustworthy is a long one. A small collection can be narrow, outdated or tilted toward the people who assembled it. Being able to ask a question does not mean the answer will satisfy. The Rhine Troubadour, by its own description, is built to be poetic rather than conclusive, which is a different goal from being right.

Whether a model you can inspect is easier to trust is a claim worth testing, and nothing in the listing tests it. The exhibition's wording is careful on this point: it says the systems can be questioned, which is an invitation and not a finding.

The Phi-3 report adds a related caution from the other side. Its authors describe the scaling laws that predict better results from larger models and say their data approach shows those laws assume a fixed data source.
If data can be shaped, then who shapes it, and with what, becomes the question, and a small system gives no automatic answer.

blocks.x: Why slow belongs in the title

r: The title pairs small with slow, and the research projects behind the exhibition explain the second word. The ARIAS page for Slow AI, a project initiated by Mariana Fernández Mora with the Visual Methodologies Collective and the Algorithmic Cultures Research Group at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, asks "How can we create anti-colonial approaches to AI?" It says the project introduces slowness to a fast technology and understands slowness "beyond a temporal metric," as a change in modes of engagement that resist the speed, efficiency and optimization rooted in AI's colonial and extractive history.

That corrects a guess I would otherwise make, that slow simply means taking time to ask questions. The project's own statement says slowness is a mode of engagement and not only a pace. Its working sessions, called Material Playgrounds, began in the spring of 2024, and a Slow AI Symposium was held on May 15, 2025 at Framer Framed.

The Rhine session page adds that the project is a collaboration between the Visual Methodologies Collective and the Netherlands Institute of Sound and Vision and is financed by the Dutch Research Council under the same NWA number the DDW listing gives.
The postcard station fits that reading, since its quoted line is about slow ways of communicating in a society engineered by speed.

blocks.x: Before you pick a tool

r: The practical part is short. Before relying on an AI tool, ask what it was trained on, whether you can see it and who you can question about it. A small system may let you answer all three, and a large one may let you answer none, though the answers are slowly becoming easier to find. Since August 2, 2025, providers of general-purpose models placed on the EU market have had to publish a training-content summary on their websites, and a person can look for it.
A reader can also ask the provider for what Gebru and colleagues call a datasheet: where the data came from, how it was collected and what it should not be used for.
Which of those three questions could you answer today about the tool you used most recently?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: What the works do in the gallery.
The listing describes each work in a sentence or two. I found no description of how a visitor interacts with any of them, apart from the Rhine session account.

The listing gives no model sizes or dataset sizes for any work. VibeSearch is the only work whose listing text mentions small models together with tailored datasets, and I found no public page for it.
The listing describes it in one sentence, and I found nothing more by the artist.
The listing says there is an online repository but gives no address in the text I read.
It answered with an access error to my automated request, so I used the ARIAS pages for the Slow AI project.
Whether smaller is easier to question in practice.
No source I read tests this. The EU template, GPT-NL and the datasheet proposal suggest that documentation matters, and they apply to large systems too.
I read the project's description of its data and governance and did not verify them.
It covers inference cost on specific benchmark tasks, not the whole life of a system or the systems in this exhibition.
