posts.title: A tool arrives with decisions already made
posts.subtitle: Het Nationaal Design Debat asks whose values and whose tools shape Europe's digital future. Dutch audit findings, cloud market data, a court ruling on defaults and the history of the Evoluon show what the question means in practice.
posts.seoTitle: A Tool Arrives With Decisions Already Made
posts.description: Het Nationaal Design Debat asks whose tools shape Europe's digital future. What a Dutch audit, cloud market data and a court ruling say.

r: A tool arrives with decisions already made. The National Design Debate, held in the Dutch Design Week program on Friday, October 23, 2026, asks Europe to look at those decisions.

The debate is a seminar in the Philips Hall of the Evoluon, Noord Brabantlaan 1A, Eindhoven. The Dutch Design Week listing gives the hosts as Next Nature Museum, with Waag Futurelab named in its credits, and marks access as paid with registration. Its tagline asks, "How can Europe redesign itself, from infrastructure to imagination?" The listing's text says the event starts at 15:00, while the listing's structured opening hours show 16:00 to 17:30.
Waag Futurelab's own page for the event gives the time as 15:00 to 17:30, lists a full program and names the speakers.
A Waag announcement of March 19, 2026 had given 16:00 to 18:00, with drinks after, so three versions of the time are public.

This essay draws on those pages, on Dutch and European public documents about digital dependence, on a court-of-justice press release, and on the Philips Company Archives' history of the building. It reports no attendance, and I cannot say what anyone will argue.
I will take the debate's central phrasing seriously and ask what it means for people who choose software, platforms and equipment every day. The question has a design answer as well as a policy one.

blocks.x: What the program settles

r: The first thing the Waag page settles is the time. The event runs from 15:00 to 17:30. A keynote by Kristel Baele, Chair of the Council for Culture, is listed at 15:30, short statements at 16:00, an artistic intermezzo by the theater collective Urland at 16:30, the debate itself, moderated by Marsha Simon, at 16:40, and a closing discussion at 17:00 between Marleen Stikker, director of Waag Futurelab, and Koert van Mensvoort, director of Next Nature.

The 16:00 in the DDW listing's opening-hours field matches the start of the short statements. The text of the DDW listing and the Waag page both give 15:00 as the start of the event, so I read 16:00 as the start of the first discussion part and not as the start of the event. That is my reading of how the pages fit together, and the March announcement was a save-the-date that the detailed event page appears to have replaced. Anyone planning to attend should confirm the time with the organizers.
Waag's program line spells the Next Nature director's first name "Koen" while its speaker biography and the Philips archive text spell it Koert, and I use Koert.

The short statements are listed as coming from five people: the artist Tinkebell, the cultural entrepreneur Moktar Nabil, the artist Constant Dullaart, Roosje Klap, director of Noorderlicht and a designer, and the journalist and digital innovator Erwin Blom. The page describes Dullaart's practice as exploring the influence of the internet and digital platforms on society, and Blom's as using AI to lower the barrier between imagination and creation.
Those are the organizers' descriptions of their speakers. Neither the listing nor the Waag page says which language the debate will run in, and I found no announcement of a recording or report.

DDW's highlights release of September 29, 2026 says that the AI art event Prompt takes place at the Next Nature Museum following the National Design Debate. The sentence in the release is missing a word and a date, so I cannot give Prompt's date or time.

blocks.x: Where the debate comes from

r: The debate has a short history. Dutch Design Week's archive lists a Design Debate on Saturday, October 25, 2025, in the Philips Hall of the Evoluon, as the "second edition," led by Tracy Metz and Wouter van Noort and organized by Next Nature, Dutch Design Week and BIS Publishers. It was built around six propositions, each argued by two speakers with opposing views, who opened with an argument of no more than three minutes and then debated each other and the audience.

On March 19, 2026, Waag Futurelab announced that it and Next Nature Museum were joining forces for the National Design Debate, which it calls an annual platform for critical reflection on the role of design, with a three-year partnership to embed the debate in Dutch Design Week on a permanent basis. The announcement names BIS Publishers, the Institute of Network Cultures and NRC among the partners contributing to the program.
The 2026 format, a keynote, short statements, a moderated debate and a closing discussion, differs from the 2025 proposition format.

The announcement states the 2026 premise in terms the listing leaves out. Europe has a rich design tradition, it says, from Bauhaus to Dutch Design, but "designers mainly work with tools and platforms developed outside Europe, often by big tech companies in the United States." It asks whether Europe should develop its own tools or whether its role lies in critical reflection and cultural imagination, and whether Europe is a place where the future of design is created or one that is merely thinking about it.
That is a claim by the organizers about designers' tools. The announcement gives no figures for it, and the figures I found elsewhere cover cloud services, as the section below explains.

blocks.x: The question has three parts

r: Waag's page puts the question more sharply than the listing does. It says we "design with American software, train on global AI models, and communicate through platforms developed outside Europe," and adds that while Europe leads the way in regulating technology, "an important question remains: are we also leading in shaping our own future?" It asks whether Europe can develop its own design culture, one that offers an alternative to both American big tech and China's state-driven model.
The listing calls design "a cultural and political force that helps shape our digital future" and says the question includes what we design "with which values, using whose tools, and for whom."

Those are three questions. Values ask what a design is for. Tools ask what it is built on. The last, for whom, asks who is served. I think the middle one is the easiest to skip, because tools feel like neutral background until they change. The hosts disagree with that feeling in their own words: Waag's about page opens with the line "Technology is not neutral."

The debate's own range is worth a second look. It runs from infrastructure to imagination. Infrastructure is what sits underneath, the servers, standards and platforms that few people choose individually. Imagination is what a society can picture doing. A debate that spans both has to say how the lower layer limits the upper one. That is my argument, and the pages leave it to the room.

blocks.x: How far the dependence goes, in numbers

r: The hosts' opening claim is about software, AI models and platforms. The public numbers I could read cover one layer of that, cloud infrastructure, and they are large.

Synergy Research Group, a market-research firm, reported on July 24, 2025 that European cloud providers' share of their home market fell from 29 percent in 2017 to 15 percent in 2022 and has stayed around 15 percent since. Amazon, Microsoft and Google together account for 70 percent of the European market, which was worth 61 billion euros in 2024. The firm's chief analyst says no European company has come close to the scale needed to challenge the leaders.
That is a commercial analyst's measurement and an opinion, and it concerns market revenue, not what any design studio uses.

The Dutch case has an audit behind it. On January 15, 2025, the Netherlands Court of Audit published a report finding that the central government started using cloud services without thoroughly considering the implications and risks. Across 1,588 cloud services reported by the ministries, the type of cloud was unknown for 26 percent. No mandatory risk assessment had been made for 84, or 67 percent, of the 126 most important public cloud services. More than half of those important services are procured from Amazon, Microsoft and Google. The Court's Vice-President, Ewout Irrgang, said there is a risk that foreign governments, particularly the US government, can access and even modify information on the Dutch government and citizens, and that "Whether they do or not is secondary but if they want to, they can." The Court's main recommendation was that the government present itself to the major providers as a single organization.

The Tweede Kamer debated these findings on March 13, 2025. The parliament's own summary records members from several parties warning that digital dependence on American companies could be used as a lever, and a D66 member calling for investment in European alternatives on the logic that if European governments create demand, European supply will follow. It also records a PVV member who found it unwise to stop using American tech companies altogether. On the government side, it records that the state secretary for digitalization planned a new central-government cloud policy for mid-2025, taking digital autonomy into account, and aimed for a government-wide sovereign cloud. For the registry of the .nl domain, the minister of Economic Affairs said there was no complete Dutch or European alternative yet, so part of the registry was moving to Amazon, with a switch planned once one exists.
I did not read the cloud policy that followed, so I do not know what it decided.

None of these documents measures the design tools that the hosts' first sentence names. A reader should keep that gap in view. The evidence supports the claim that European institutions depend heavily on American cloud infrastructure. It does not, by itself, show how much of European design practice runs on American software.

blocks.x: A tool carries decisions

r: The sources suggest what leaving looks like. The Court of Audit names the risks it fears: a foreign government requesting data from a provider, a provider collapsing, a provider being hacked.

The Dutch origin of one widely used design tool shows the middle case. Blender began as an in-house tool of Ton Roosendaal's 3D animation studio, NeoGeo, in 1994. A company set up to market it, Not a Number, was closed in early 2002 after its investors fell out with it, and development stopped. Roosendaal started a non-profit, the Blender Foundation, in May 2002 and launched what the Foundation's history calls the first-ever crowdfunding campaign, Free Blender. The community raised 110,000 euros in seven weeks, enough to buy the rights back, and on October 13, 2002 Blender was released under the GNU General Public License.

That is the Foundation's own account of its history, and Blender is one case. It shows a tool whose users could change its ownership because they had the means and the license to do so. Most tools do not give their users that option.

Values also enter a tool through its defaults, and here European law has already ruled on a case. In Planet49, decided on October 1, 2019, the Court of Justice of the European Union held that consent to storing cookies on a user's equipment is not validly given through a pre-ticked checkbox that the user must deselect to refuse. The press release adds that the ruling applies whether or not the stored information is personal data.
The GDPR's recital on consent says the same in general terms: "Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not therefore constitute consent."

The press release is not the judgment, and it carries a note saying it is not binding, so I read the ruling only as the Court's own summary. The point for a debate about Europe is narrow. Someone chose that pre-ticked box, the choice served one party's convenience, and it took a court case to say so. Policy talk about values has to reach this level of detail, down to who sets the default, or it stays a statement of good intentions.

blocks.x: Two hosts with stated positions

r: The hosts' descriptions are worth reading as claims. Waag says it contributes to a sustainable, just society by researching emerging technology and questioning underlying cultural assumptions, by designing alternatives on the basis of public values, and by developing an open, fair and inclusive future with civil society. It says it was founded in 1994 by Marleen Stikker and Caroline Nevejan, with De Digitale Stad, which it calls the first public access portal to the internet, as its precedent.

Next Nature Museum describes itself as a place where humans, nature and technology come together and challenge each other, and its site says Next Nature's international future lab for design and technology is located in the museum.
Both are self-descriptions. They explain why these two organizations would frame a debate around values and tools, and they do not tell us what the debate will conclude.

blocks.x: The building has its own history

r: The venue adds a layer, and the Philips Company Archives tell it. The Evoluon was designed by Louis Kalff, head of Philips Design from 1925 to 1960, and Leo de Bever. It was built to mark Philips' 75th anniversary and opened on September 24, 1966. The archive text says Philips' board decided on January 2, 1961 to build a museum with an ever-renewing exhibition of Philips products instead of taking part in world fairs.

The archive account also records an argument about whose tool the building would be. The scientific adviser Jan Schouten thought the early plans too technical and proposed that the exhibition focus on the relationship between humans and technology, and that it should not be a showroom for Philips products. His alternative plan was accepted. The Evoluon closed in 1989 because of its high operating costs. Next Nature Network, supported by cultural funds, reopened it with the exhibition RetroFuture on September 24, 2022, the anniversary of the 1966 opening.

I find it fitting, as my own reading and not as the organizers' claim, that a question about whose tools shape the future is asked in a building a technology company made partly to show its own tools, and whose own planners argued that it should be more than that. The listing makes no such link, and nothing in the pages says the venue was chosen for this reason.

blocks.x: A list worth making

r: A practical step needs no ticket. List the tools you depend on at work: the software, the platform, the hardware. For each, ask what the Court of Audit asked of the ministries: what kind of service is it, has anyone assessed the risk, and who can access or change what you put into it?

Then mark the ones where the answer is someone you cannot reach. That list is a small version of the debate's middle question. Which tool on it would you most want a say in? If you go to the debate, the same list gives you questions for any speaker: what is your answer built on, who can change it, and what happens if they do?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: The March 19, 2026 announcement gave 16:00 to 18:00, the DDW listing's text says 15:00 and its hours field says 16:00 to 17:30, and the Waag event page says 15:00 to 17:30. I follow the detailed event page.
The pages give a program and speaker biographies, not positions. Programs can change, and I have not attended.
The DDW release is missing the word that would say.
The cloud data cover market revenue and central government, not design software or studios.
What the government's new cloud policy decided.
The parliamentary summary says it was due in mid-2025; I did not read it.
The full text of the Planet49 judgment.
I read the Court's press release and a reproduction of the GDPR recital.
It is one tool with an unusual history, told in its Foundation's own words.

posts.title: Putting an industry at the core of a policy
posts.subtitle: ekip's final event asks what it would take for creative industries to sit at the center of European innovation policy. The project's own recommendations, EU and Dutch policy documents and employment statistics show how that claim can be tested.
posts.seoTitle: Creative Industries at the Core of Policy: ekip
posts.description: ekip's final event asks for creative industries at the core of innovation policy. What its recommendations, EU and Dutch documents say.

r: Putting an industry at the core of a policy is a statement about who decides what the policy is for.

ekip, the European Cultural and Creative Industries Innovation Policy Platform, holds its final event, From Policy to Action, on Friday, October 23, 2026, from 09:30 to 12:30 on the Main Stage at Natlab, Kastanjelaan 500, Strijp-S, with doors and registration from 09:00. The event is a seminar in the Dutch Design Week program, it is part of the Mission Days, registration is required, and the venue is marked fully wheelchair accessible.
The listing says that "if Europe is serious about future-ready innovation ecosystems, CCIs must move to the core," using the abbreviation for the cultural and creative industries.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, ekip's own site and published recommendations, the European Commission's project record, European statistics, policy documents from the European Commission and the Dutch government, and an announcement from the European Institute of Innovation and Technology. It reports no attendance, and the listing names no speakers, so I cannot say what anyone will propose.

I want to take the phrase seriously. It is a short way of asking whether creative work gets a real seat in innovation policy, and what would show that it did. The good news is that ekip has published enough to test the phrase against.

blocks.x: What ekip is

r: ekip describes itself as a platform that boosts the innovation capacity of ecosystems by including the cultural and creative industries. Its site says it is rooted in open innovation: it brings together broad groups of stakeholders to co-create evidence-based policy recommendations through a process it calls the ekip Engine, which runs through identification, prioritization, investigation and formulation phases. The formulation phase uses Policy Labs, collaborative sessions on one policy area each, and City Prototyping to test recommendations in real local settings.
The DDW listing adds that the consortium has 5 universities, 4 cultural and innovation consultancy firms, 4 cultural and creative organizations, 4 cities and over 50 network organizations.

The European Commission's project record gives the funding facts. ekip is a Horizon Europe coordination and support action under grant agreement 101112111, funded under the program area Culture, creativity and inclusive society, in response to a call topic titled "A culture and creativity driven European innovation ecosystem, a collaborative platform." It was signed on May 16, 2023, started on June 1, 2023 and ends on November 30, 2026. The EU contribution is 5,987,856 euros, and the project is coordinated by Lund University in Sweden, with 16 participants.
So the final event comes about five weeks before the project's formal end, and the listing's agenda closes with "ekip beyond."
I name the program and grant number here because the Commission's own record and ekip's published documents both give them.

blocks.x: What the project has produced

r: The old question of what ekip actually recommends has an answer, and it is public. The site's policy documents page lists thirteen policy recommendations and thirteen matching policy posters, on topics from AI and the cultural and creative industries, the New European Bauhaus, immersive media and crafts-led innovation to platformization of the music industry, inclusivity in the video game industry, performing arts, fashion and circularity, cultural heritage institutions, new funding models, spaces and infrastructures, deep tech and digital commons.
Three of them show what the recommendations look like.

The AI recommendations come from a Policy Lab held in Brussels on January 25 and 26, 2024 and are dated July 2025. They say small creative players often lack in-house capacity to develop AI, which makes them dependent on external specialists, and they point to an asymmetric power relation between small players and large companies and online platforms. Their recommendations include introducing AI literacy policies within creative start-ups, a skills agenda for the creative industries, an open-source innovation platform to share practices, and "a dedicated monitoring body for the CCIs at member state level."

The recommendations on spaces, infrastructures and ecosystems define such infrastructures as shared, hybrid environments, from makerspaces and fab labs to museums and cultural centers, and propose six actions. Among them are explicitly positioning these infrastructures in EU and regional innovation frameworks such as smart specialization strategies, "establishing permanent inter-ministerial coordination bodies" and securing stable long-term funding, developing impact methods that go beyond conventional indicators such as technology readiness levels, and redesigning grant programs with flexible conditions that reflect the diversity of the sector.

The recommendations on cultural heritage institutions argue for a broader meaning of innovation that values cultural, social and civic outcomes as well as technological progress, for recognizing such institutions as equal partners in innovation ecosystems, and for supporting the scaling of experiments, which the document says rarely continue once initial funding ends.

These are the project's recommendations, produced through its own process, and I have read three of the thirteen. I did not assess how many stakeholders took part in each lab or how the recommendations were weighed against each other.

blocks.x: What the panels ask

r: The draft agenda on the DDW listing runs from registration at 09:00 to a networking lunch at 12:30 to 13:30. A welcome and an introduction to ekip's results at 09:30 is followed at 09:40 by a keynote titled "How the Cultural and Creative Industries come into play contributing to the competitiveness of Europe?" Then come three panels. Panel 1, at 10:00, asks how to move beyond ambitious national CCI strategies and from strategies into action. Panel 2, at 10:45, asks whether universities as hubs for innovation in local ecosystems can be the drivers to implement innovation policies, and how to develop the ekip ecosystem building blocks to serve the CCIs. Panel 3, at 11:30, asks how to use insights into emerging new jobs to evolve CCI communities with new roles and competences. The agenda closes with reflections on the day and ekip beyond at 12:20.

The listing's opening questions are broader. It asks how the EU and its member states can make better use of the unique competences and skills of the CCIs to strengthen innovation, and how to better include them in innovation policies to meet objectives on sustainable and digital transitions, inclusion, competitiveness and technological sovereignty.
On the Mission Day page, DDW describes the event as exploring how policy for the cultural and creative sectors can be translated into concrete change.

As my own framing, the three panels map onto three questions about a seat at the table. National strategies ask who writes the plan. Universities ask where the work happens. Jobs ask who benefits when it does. The listing does not organize the panels that way, and I offer the framing so a reader can test it against the sessions.

blocks.x: What a seat would look like, using ekip's own tests

r: A seat in policy can be tested with plain evidence, and ekip's recommendations supply some of the tests. A seat could be a body: a dedicated monitoring body at member-state level for the AI recommendations, permanent inter-ministerial coordination bodies for the infrastructure recommendations.
It could be money: stable long-term funding and grant programs designed for the sector's diversity.
It could be a role: recognition as an equal partner, in the heritage recommendations' words.
These are my reading of what the documents propose and not ekip's criteria for "the core." They show that the phrase can be checked, which is what separates a policy claim from a slogan.

The listing's own sentence carries a hint of the difficulty. A core has limited room. ekip's site names designers, artists, researchers, museums, start-ups and public agencies as members of the cultural and creative industries, and its heritage recommendations cover archives, libraries and heritage sites.
When the definition is that wide, a policy that puts the sector at the core has to say which parts of it the budget lines reach.

blocks.x: How big is the sector, and by whose count?

r: Two numbers circulate, and they differ, at least in part, because they define the sector differently. The AI recommendations state that the cultural and creative industries represent 5.3 percent of the EU's gross value added and employ more than 12 million people, 7.5 percent of the European workforce.

Eurostat's cultural employment statistics, using Eurostat's own definition, put the EU's cultural sector at 8.9 million people, or 4.3 percent of total employment, in 2025 (release of July 10, 2026). Eurostat counts culture-related occupations in the cultural sector, non-cultural occupations in the cultural sector and culture-related jobs outside it, such as a designer in the motor vehicle industry.
The highest share of cultural employment among EU countries in 2025 was in the Netherlands, at 5.7 percent.
I could not trace the source of ekip's 12 million figure, and I do not try to reconcile the two. The comparison shows why a "core" claim needs the definition stated first.

blocks.x: What the host country decided

r: The Dutch case gives the question a live example. On October 17, 2025, the cabinet agreed to a new industrial policy that ends the current top sector policy on January 1, 2026 and focuses on six markets: semiconductors, biotechnology, defense-related applications, digital services (especially AI), machine building and innovative chemistry. The government's news release says the former top sectors keep generic innovation schemes such as the WBSO, tax schemes and other financing, but that there are no or fewer tailored programs for them.

The minister's letter to parliament of the same date says the cabinet keeps its attention on all sectors, including the creative industry, that the ministry has sector contacts for every sector, and that the design power of the creative industry is a precondition for the country's earning capacity and innovative strength (my translation of "randvoorwaardelijk").

Read side by side, those lines show the difference the ekip event is about. A precondition is acknowledged in the text. A focus market gets a dedicated program. The creative industry appears in the first category in this letter and not in the second. I do not claim the letter is wrong to choose that way, and I did not read the programs that followed. The point is that "at the core" and "a precondition for everything" are different positions with different budgets, and the first can be checked by looking for a program, an owner and a line in the budget.

blocks.x: The EU's side of the story

r: At EU level, the European Institute of Innovation and Technology opened a call to create a ninth Knowledge and Innovation Community, EIT Culture & Creativity, with about 300 million euros under Horizon Europe available for two new communities, applications due March 24, 2022, and a mandate to unite education, research and business in the cultural and creative sectors.

That is an earlier attempt to give the sector an innovation structure, and it resembles the university-and-ecosystem theme of the second panel. On November 12, 2025, the Commission put forward a Culture Compass for Europe, which says culture contributes to economic growth and competitiveness and lists among its key actions an AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors.

Whether those instruments put the sector at the core of innovation policy is the question the event poses. These two pages describe intentions and structures, and I did not look for evidence of results.

blocks.x: From recommendation to action

r: The event title promises a move from policy to action, and that move is where I would look for a gap. This is a general observation and not a judgment of ekip. For a recommendation to become an action, someone has to own it, someone has to fund it and someone has to say by when. A recommendation with no owner is a wish with good formatting. The ekip documents I read name the bodies they would like to see, such as a monitoring body or an inter-ministerial coordination body, but they are recommendations to others, and the project itself ends on November 30, 2026.
What the project hands over, and to whom, is a question for the panel on ekip beyond.

blocks.x: Where should creative work sit?

r: The question that matters most may be the one the listing leaves to the room: where should creative work sit in innovation policy, and who should decide? A reader who plans to attend, or who reads ekip's published recommendations, can bring one question per panel: who owns the plan, where does the work happen and who gets the jobs. A fourth, from the Dutch letter, is worth adding: is the sector a market the government builds a program for, or a condition it says everything else depends on? Which of those would you ask first?

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: The listing gives a draft agenda and no speakers. The agenda is marked draft.
I read three of the thirteen documents and not the underlying evidence, stakeholder lists or the consortium's internal process.
Where ekip's 12 million figure comes from.
The AI document states it without a source I could trace.
What the Dutch programs after October 2025 contain.
I read the cabinet's letter and news release and not the programs. I also did not confirm from a primary page that the creative industry's own top sector program is among those ending.
Whether EU instruments put the sector at the core.
The two pages I read describe intentions.
The list of speakers and the fee.
The listing shows a registration button and does not state a price.
The record gives the project's end date and the agenda item "ekip beyond" and nothing else.

posts.title: One camera, two feelings: what Blind Spots asks about safety
posts.subtitle: A Dutch Design Week installation puts cameras, nets and recorded voices around one question: who is safety designed for? Dutch municipal law, Eindhoven's own camera policy and decades of research say a good deal about it.
posts.seoTitle: Blind Spots: one camera, two feelings
posts.description: A Dutch Design Week installation of cameras, nets and recorded voices asks who safety is designed for. What the listing says, and what it leaves open.

r: A camera can make one person feel safe and another feel watched, and both reactions can be reasonable.

Blind Spots is in the Dutch Design Week program as an installation by Fairspace, Studio Shruthi Venkat and Sagitta Creatives, on Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S, Eindhoven. It is open October 17 to 25, 2026, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, with free access. Its published account describes poles, concrete ballast, steel cables, oversized CCTV cameras and brightly colored scaffolding nets, with recorded testimonies that visitors hear as they move through. Those are the makers' descriptions.

This essay draws on public documents only: the festival listing, the organizations' own pages, a Dutch ministerial letter about municipal camera law, Eindhoven's published camera policy, and research reports and statistics. It reports no visit, no conversation with the makers and no result from the installation. The three images on the listing are captioned as AI-generated concept visualizations, so I treat them as plans and describe none of them as the built work.

I want to take the question seriously, because "more cameras, safer street" is a sentence people say with confidence and rarely test against a particular person. The sources I could open let me test it in three ways: what the law lets a Dutch city do with a camera, what studies found about cameras and safety, and who the lens has been shown to follow.

blocks.x: The listing builds its argument out of materials

r: The listing's first section says public space is designed, and so are the systems meant to make it safe. Cameras, barriers, concrete, steel and protective netting, it says, all carry ideas about who is protected and who is watched. It states the central claim in plain sentences: a camera reassures one person and makes another feel exposed, and a barrier protects and excludes at once.

The makers then name what they mean by "one person" and "another." Under the heading "A city with many truths," the listing says there is no single experience of safety, and that gender, ethnicity, disability, sexuality, class and documentation status intersect and shape how each person moves through public space. The nets overlap and cut sightlines. Recorded testimonies emerge from different points in the structure, some close and clear, others distant, partial or overlapping. The places where sightlines disappear are the "literal blind spots" of the title.

I like seeing an argument built out of materials. A structure can make a claim about perception that a chart cannot carry. It cannot tell me how common each experience is, and the listing does not say it can. That question needs a different kind of evidence, and the rest of this essay is about where that evidence exists.

blocks.x: Who is behind it

r: The listing names three hosts and credits a creative team by role: a creative lead, execution and production, a textile designer, research and publications, a sound designer and a visual designer. I leave individual names out, since the argument does not need them.

Fairspace describes itself as an organization working toward safer spaces by ending harassment, with the tagline "Safer spaces for all." Its home page lists work in four settings: communities, workplaces, education and government. It names partners including Amsterdam and Rotterdam, and its projects page lists fifteen titles, one of them a project on training special enforcement officers on social safety. The page text I read gives no description of any of them.

An about page, which I read through a page-text fetch and could not reopen later, says Fairspace was founded in 2017 as the successor to Hollaback! Nederland, a volunteer group that began with students in Utrecht responding to street harassment. It says the founders' own experiences of harassment led to research in Amsterdam in 2015, and that the two co-founders received a Dutch human rights award in 2019. I could not find the award announcement, so I treat that as the organization's own claim.

Shruthi Venkat's site describes her as a designer, researcher and facilitator. It lists Woven Streets (2025) as a participatory project on women's safety and surveillance in Rotterdam, in which participants co-create speculative wearables that resist surveillance while building networks of care. The page says the project was presented at the Coalition of Safety Conference during Dutch Design Week 2025, where she hosted a workshop in which visitors described what safety means to them.

The listing's phrase "speculative care infrastructure" therefore comes from makers who have worked on harassment, safety and surveillance before. I found nothing public about Sagitta Creatives beyond its name on the listing.

blocks.x: What the law lets a Dutch city do with a camera

r: Because the installation stands in Eindhoven, I started with the rules for municipal cameras there. The Minister of Justice and Security described them to the Dutch parliament in a letter dated April 12, 2022. Municipalities can use cameras to maintain public order under Article 151c of the Gemeentewet (the Municipalities Act), a basis that took effect in 2006. The power is layered. The municipal council can authorize the mayor, by ordinance, to use cameras when that is necessary to maintain public order. The mayor then decides on a deployment and sets the period after consulting the public prosecutor in the regular meeting of mayor, prosecutor and police. The mayor uses the police, who work under his authority.

A 2016 amendment allowed flexible camera surveillance, so cameras can move within a designated area, and it requires the mayor to withdraw the decision once cameras are no longer necessary. The letter says the footage falls under the Police Data Act, and that the police chief is the party responsible for it. The letter presents an evaluation by researchers for the Ministry's research center, which I could not open directly. Everything I say about that evaluation comes from the Minister's account.

Eindhoven's camera policy applies this. According to its text, the council gave the mayor the power in 2008 by adding an article to the general local ordinance. The policy was adopted by the mayor after advice from the data protection officer on May 17, 2023 and a council view of June 6, 2023. When the policy was written, Eindhoven had 38 public order cameras: 35 fixed cameras in three areas (the city center from the station area to Stratumseind, Baekelandplein and the area around the PSV stadium) and three mobile units. Footage is kept for at most 28 days unless it is needed for a criminal investigation.

The policy's foreword is blunt about the cost. In my translation, it says every camera infringes the privacy of the people who come into view, and that nobody wants a city where you are watched always and everywhere. It sets two tests. Proportionality means heavy tools only for problems of matching size, which the policy illustrates with the Dutch saying about not shooting a cannon at a mosquito. Subsidiarity means lighter measures come first, such as street lighting or community policing.

The legal test matters for a work like Blind Spots. Under Article 151c, the question a mayor must answer is whether cameras are necessary to maintain public order. How safe different people feel is not the legal test. In Eindhoven's policy it appears as an evaluation indicator: whether residents, visitors and businesses say they feel safer because of the cameras. The policy adds that feelings of safety are exceptionally hard to measure, that there are no perfect information sources, and that the best available method is a street survey of random passers-by, before and after the cameras go up.

The same policy lists other cameras on the same streets. The police can place their own under Article 3 of the Police Act. Semi-public organizations such as rail and transit operators, schools and hospitals use cameras under data protection law. Private individuals and businesses film the street too, and the policy estimates there are at least five hundred times as many private cameras in the Netherlands as municipal ones. Eindhoven chose not to regulate cameras of third parties, and says anyone who suspects an unlawful private camera can complain to the national Data Protection Authority.

The Minister's letter adds two points that bear on the installation's themes. Very advanced technology such as automatic facial recognition or sound analysis is hardly used by municipalities, according to the evaluation as summarized there, because of disappointing pilots, privacy worries and a lack of political support. And the evaluation found that municipal evaluations of camera schemes are rare and of lower scientific quality than they were a decade earlier.

blocks.x: Cameras and crime: a modest, uneven record

r: What do cameras do? The largest review I could open is a 2019 systematic review with meta-analysis by Eric Piza, Brandon Welsh, David Farrington and Amanda Thomas, published in Criminology & Public Policy. The abstract on the US National Criminal Justice Reference Service says CCTV is associated with a significant and modest decrease in crime, with the strongest results in car parks and some reduction in residential settings. Actively monitored systems did better than passive ones, and schemes combined with other measures did better than stand-alone ones. The authors conclude that CCTV should not be used as an isolated intervention.
The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention, which commissioned the review, says it covers 80 studies, up from 44 in a 2007 review.
I could not open the full text, so I do not report effect sizes or per-crime breakdowns.

A British Home Office evaluation from 2005 by Martin Gill and Angela Spriggs looked at 13 projects (14 systems) in town centers, car parks, hospitals and residential areas. Six showed a relatively substantial fall in crime compared with control areas, but only two showed a statistically significant fall, and in one of those the change could be explained by other factors. Crime rose in seven areas, though the authors could not attribute that to CCTV. Impulsive crimes such as alcohol-related offenses were less likely to fall than premeditated ones such as vehicle theft.

The Dutch picture, in the Minister's summary of the national evaluation, is a policy that is popular with municipalities but thinly evidenced. Researchers concluded that municipalities are willing to bear the financial and privacy costs, which suggests the law meets a need, but that the empirical basis for conclusions about effectiveness is missing. In 95 percent of municipalities, lighter measures such as extra police patrols, better street lighting or youth work were tried first.

None of this says cameras are useless, and none of it says they are the answer. Where they help, the strongest evidence is about vehicle and property crime in parking facilities, not about how a person walking home feels.

blocks.x: Feeling safe is a different measurement

r: The Home Office study also asked people. In all surveyed areas worry about being a victim of crime fell after cameras went in, but in only four areas did it fall more than in the comparison area. In the two areas where the fall was significantly larger, people who knew about the cameras reported more worry than people who did not, by 19 percent in one and 10 percent in the other. The authors suggest the cameras may signal that the area has a problem. They conclude there is little to suggest that the fall in fear is attributable to CCTV, and that it more likely reflected the fall in reported victimization.

The report also cites an earlier study of Southwark town center in which almost two-thirds of respondents aware of the cameras said they felt safer because of them. Ninety percent said so for the daytime, and 45 percent for the night.
I find the daytime and night-time split the most useful number in this section, because it says the feeling changes with the hour even when the camera does not.

Dutch national statistics show who is doing the avoiding. In the 2023 Safety Monitor and Emancipation Monitor, reported by Statistics Netherlands on July 18, 2025, 45.0 percent of women aged 15 to 25 said they sometimes walk or drive around to avoid places they consider unsafe in their own neighborhood, against 21.5 percent of men the same age. Among women in highly urban areas the figure was 44.4 percent, and in non-urban areas 21.3 percent.
These figures measure behavior. They say nothing about cameras, and I will not suggest they do.

Put the two sets of findings side by side and the listing's claim becomes a testable one. If a camera reassures one person and exposes another, then a single survey answer averaged across passers-by can show a rise in safety while hiding who is missing from the average. That is my reasoning, not a finding from these sources. The Eindhoven policy's own evaluation plan, a street survey of random passers-by, is the kind of instrument that would have this limit.

blocks.x: Who the lens follows

r: The most direct evidence I found on the "feel watched" half of the sentence comes from a study of three British CCTV control rooms. Clive Norris and Gary Armstrong observed 592 hours of monitoring between May 1995 and April 1996 and recorded 888 instances in which operators followed a person or group for more than a minute or at someone else's request. Nine in ten of those were men (93 percent), four in ten were teenagers (39 percent), and three in ten were black people (31 percent). The authors calculated that black people were between one-and-a-half and two-and-a-half times more likely to be targeted than their presence in the population would suggest.

More than a third of the targeted surveillances (36 percent) had no obvious reason. That was so for 68 percent of those involving black people against 35 percent for whites, and for 65 percent of teenagers against 21 percent of people over 30. The authors say one in three people (31 percent) were followed on categorical suspicion alone, for belonging to a particular social group.

Women made up 52 percent of the population but 7 percent of the primary people surveilled. In nearly 600 hours the authors saw one woman followed for protective reasons. They also report that 10 percent of the targeted surveillances on women were for voyeuristic reasons, which outnumbered protective ones by five to one.

That finding is the reverse of the usual claim that cameras watch over women. It is also a study of human operators at three British sites in the mid-1990s; I found nothing that tells me how Dutch control rooms operate today, and I am not suggesting Eindhoven's do this.

The authors argue that being followed without cause carries a message even when no arrest follows. In their words, two youths followed by one camera after another are treated as "persons who do not belong."
That is close to the listing's idea that safety systems carry assumptions about who counts as the standard.

A Dutch example concerns sensors rather than street cameras. Amnesty International's 2020 report, "We Sense Trouble," studied the police Sensing project in Roermond. Amnesty says the police collected data on vehicles in and around the city through cameras and other sensors, then fed it into an algorithmic risk model, and that some of the indicators were designed to establish whether a person was of Eastern European origin. Amnesty concluded the project amounted to mass surveillance and ethnic profiling, and that the police could not show it prevented the pickpocketing and shoplifting it targeted.
That is an advocacy organization's analysis, based on media, public documents and an interview with two senior police officers, not a court ruling.
I did not check what became of the project afterward.

Eindhoven's policy acknowledges the same family of risk. It says "neutral" technology, or a combination of neutral datasets, can end up discriminating against certain groups, and it cites the Living Lab Stratumseind, an Eindhoven sensor project whose evaluation found that technology suppliers benefited more than the city.

blocks.x: Two newer rules for the street

r: The EU AI Act sets one limit on the most intrusive camera technology. Article 5(1)(h) prohibits law enforcement from using real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, unless strictly necessary for one of three objectives: targeted searches for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons, preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or a genuine terrorist threat, and locating or identifying a suspect of certain serious offenses. Each use needs prior authorization from a judicial or independent administrative authority, with narrow exceptions for urgency. Article 5(1)(g) separately prohibits biometric categorization systems that infer race, political opinions, religious beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation.
Chapters I and II of the Act, which include Article 5, have applied since February 2, 2025.
Those rules cover facial identification and categorization. They do not cover an ordinary fixed camera, which stays under Article 151c and the Police Data Act as described above.

A second change concerns what people do to each other on the street. Since July 1, 2024, the Wet seksuele misdrijven (Sexual Offenses Act) has made sexual intimidation in public a crime under Article 429ter of the Criminal Code. Victim Support Netherlands describes it as approaching someone sexually in an intrusive way in public, online or offline, through remarks, gestures, sounds or touches that are humiliating, hurtful or insulting or that cause fear. The same sheet warns that the new law lowers the threshold for reporting but leaves the rules of evidence unchanged, so a report does not mean a conviction.
I found no source on whether camera footage is used in such cases, so I draw no line between the two.

blocks.x: The fabric strips ask about needs

r: Visitors respond to two prompts on fabric strips: "What would you need to feel held here?" and "When did a stranger make you feel safe?" They tie the strips onto the nets, and over the nine days the contributions accumulate, according to the listing.

Neither prompt mentions a camera. The first asks for conditions, the second asks for a memory. I can imagine answers such as light, company, a clear way out or being believed. Those are my hypothetical examples, and the listing does not say what visitors write.

I find that shift useful as a design habit. A debate about whether a camera is good or bad tends to end in two camps. A question about needs produces a list that a designer, a city official or a neighbor can act on, whatever they think of cameras.

It also differs from the instrument Eindhoven's policy prefers. The city's evaluation plan surveys random passers-by about whether they feel safer because of cameras. Blind Spots invites self-selected visitors to say what they need. The first gives a count and the second gives a range, and the listing does not claim the strips are a sample.

blocks.x: After the week, the answers are meant to travel

r: According to the listing, after Dutch Design Week the responses feed into the People's Blueprint for Care Infrastructure, a policy advisory document the makers describe as co-authored by those who contributed, carrying their experiences into conversations with municipalities, ministries and other decision-makers.

That plan is the part I would most like to see documented. A pile of fabric strips becomes a document only through choices: who reads the strips, who groups them, which sentences survive into a summary, and how a contributor who wrote something personal is protected. The listing describes none of those steps and does not say which municipalities or ministries will receive the document. That may simply reflect where the project is, since by the listing's own account the Blueprint comes after the week.

If the Blueprint reached a Dutch city, the legal structure above suggests where it would land. A camera decision in Eindhoven runs from council to mayor to the meeting with the prosecutor and the police, on the test of public order. A document about care would arrive in a system whose camera power is framed around order. That is my reading of the sources, not something the makers say.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the installation, and the listing's images are concept visualizations, so I do not know how the finished structure will look or feel.

I do not know who receives the Blueprint, what visitors will write, or how many will take part. I found nothing public about Sagitta Creatives. The founding story and the 2019 award for Fairspace come from an about page I could read once and could not reopen when I tried to check it again, and I did not find the award body's own announcement.

I could not open the Dutch ministry's research center report on Article 151c cameras, and I could not reach the Data Protection Authority's website, so I rely on the Minister's letter and on Eindhoven's own policy for the municipal rules. I did not open the General Data Protection Regulation or the Court of Justice ruling on private cameras that film the street.
I could not open the full text of the 2019 review, only its abstract, so I give no effect sizes.
The British control-room study is from 1995 and 1996. The Home Office evaluation is from 2005. Both concern British systems of their time.

I found no comparable observational study of a Dutch control room. I also did not read Kimberlé Crenshaw's 1989 article, whose title names the intersection of race and sex; I could open only its catalog record, and its argument is not summarized here.
The statistics on avoidance by young women are national, and they say nothing about cameras or about Eindhoven's streets.

blocks.x: Before you call a street safe

r: The installation's question travels well beyond Eindhoven. The next time someone tells you a camera keeps everyone safe, try three questions. Safe for whom? Watched by whom? What would you need to feel held here? Which of the three changes your answer first?

posts.title: Who signs an object that a person and an AI made together?
posts.subtitle: Aalto University's art-ai-fact is in the Dutch Design Week program. Its six projects give the machine six different jobs, and U.S. and European sources show why each job matters for authorship.
posts.seoTitle: Who signs an object made with AI?
posts.description: Aalto University's art-ai-fact gives AI six different jobs. What U.S. and European sources say about authorship of AI-assisted objects.

r: Most talk about AI-made work is about screens, which makes it easy to forget that someone will eventually have to put a name on an object.

art-ai-fact is an Aalto University initiative in the Dutch Design Week program, at Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, Eindhoven, from October 17 to 25, 2026, with a Dutch Design Week ticket required. The listing describes it as "Explorations of designing the material world together with AI approaches" and names six projects.

This essay draws on the DDW listings, Aalto's project page and two Aalto news items, plus court records, a Copyright Office report, an EU Council document and a law firm's summary of a European ruling. It reports no visit, no interview and no assessment of any object.

My question is narrow. When a person and an AI shape a physical thing together, what would you need to know before you could say who made it? The six projects turn out to be six answers to a different version of that question: what did the machine actually do?

blocks.x: What the initiative says it is

r: Aalto's page calls art-ai-fact an initiative that curates, funds and exhibits creative design projects with an AI element. It describes a three-year program that produces creative outputs in design-related fields, "especially including a physical component," and plans a hybrid physical and digital exhibition of the outcomes in the second half of 2027. The page was published on December 19, 2024 and last updated on June 14, 2026. A steering group of three Aalto arts academics oversees it, and the page says the initiative is made possible by an endowment from Fiskars Group.

One passage on the page speaks to authorship without using the word. Under the heading "Original and appropriate," Aalto says creativity needs originality or novelty as well as appropriateness, and that physical-world constraints and the humans operating in it set different fitness criteria than those for immaterial outputs.
I think that sentence explains why an object is a good test case. A joint that fails, fails in front of everyone, so someone had to decide, test and decide again.

The page also shows where the idea came from. It cites a light installation called Evolumination, shown at Dutch Design Week in 2023 and credited to four people, as an example of work aligned with the initiative's objectives.

blocks.x: Six projects, six jobs for the machine

r: An Aalto news item published on October 7, 2026 describes the projects in the DDW show. The listing names six: CraftBot, LUCID, Shipwreck Dress, SketchFold, Textile Design Meets AI and When Tree Types Matter.
The two sources differ in one respect: Aalto's project page lists four active projects, and the show also includes LUCID and the Shipwreck Dress.
According to Aalto, here is what the AI does in each.

items: The AI writes Python code that builds the structure in the 3D modeling program Blender, working from photographs, drawings and construction manuals, and improving its design through repeated code tests and visual feedback. Aalto says the system still needs human guidance to resolve inconsistencies.
AI generates and develops shapes, patterns and textures, and the system turns them into instructions a digital knitting machine can use. Aalto says the designers remain involved throughout.

Designers draw simple pen sketches, with colors marking different folds, and the system translates the sketch into a digital 3D model that can be refined by simulation and then folded from paper, cardboard, aluminum or steel.

AI adjusts a simple stool's design to the wood that is locally available. It decides the number and placement of supporting braces while using as little material as possible, so weaker wood gets more braces and stronger wood fewer.

Designers and AI work together to turn visual ideas into 3D-printed objects. Aalto says the system makes the logic of the form visible so designers can understand and change it, and that it keeps track of how each design evolves.
AI-assisted tools explored and developed the knitted patterns of a dress made from wood salvaged from a 17th-century shipwreck.

r: These are the university's descriptions, not results I verified. They matter because the law, as far as I can read it, cares about exactly this question: whether the human contribution is a choice about expression, or an instruction to a system that makes the choice. I cannot say which of these six jobs lands on which side of that line.

blocks.x: One dress, four ways of giving credit

r: The Shipwreck Dress is the best-documented object, and it shows how many credit formats a single piece can have.

The wood comes from the Hahtiperä wreck, a cargo ship discovered in 2019 beneath a parking lot in Oulu, Finland, during the renovation of a hotel. Aalto researchers turned leftover wood from it into fiber, spun it into yarn and left it undyed. Aalto lecturer Anna-Mari Leppisaari designed and knitted two identical dresses from the yarn, one for the Oulu Art Museum and one for Aalto.

The surface pattern came from an experimental knitting design program that Aalto describes as developed by senior lecturer Severi Uusitalo and based on an evolutionary algorithm. Leppisaari says different pattern proposals were generated on her own computer, and she describes the work as co-creativity.
Now compare the credits. The DDW listing for the dress names Leppisaari as designer, with Aalto as host.
The Aalto news item for DDW 2026 credits her as designer, credits the "AI-assisted design process" to Uusitalo and Leppisaari, and lists eighteen collaborators.
Aalto's May 2026 release names twenty people who "continued the wreck's unique story," and it separately describes Uusitalo's program as the tool Leppisaari used.
Meanwhile the main art-ai-fact listing pairs the dress with Leppisaari and Uusitalo together.

None of these credits is wrong. Each answers a different question: who designed it, who built the process, who made the material, who made the show. The algorithm appears in all of them as a process, never as a named party. That matches the law I describe below, which looks for a human author. It also shows why a name on a label tells you less than the surrounding paperwork.

The same pattern appears in smaller ways elsewhere. LUCID is credited on the DDW listing to two people, and in Aalto's news item to a company, "arbitrary aesthetics Ltd," described as an AI startup by the same two people, with one name written in the opposite order in the two places.
The Textile Design project is credited on the listing to two named people "and others," while Aalto's item names four team members and two assistants.
One more note on terms. The release calls the dress's tool AI-assisted, and also describes it as based on an evolutionary algorithm.

An evolutionary algorithm is a different kind of system from the large generative models behind most copyright disputes. Whether that difference matters legally is a question I cannot answer from these sources, and I raise it only because the same word covers both.

blocks.x: What U.S. law says so far

r: In January 2025 the U.S. Copyright Office published the second part of its report on copyright and AI, on whether outputs can be protected. Its conclusions include that existing law is enough, that using AI to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect protection, that copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material or to material with insufficient human control over the expressive elements, and that each case must be analyzed individually.

The report adds that, given current generally available technology, prompts do not alone provide sufficient control. Human authors keep copyright in what they author that is perceptible in AI outputs, in their creative selection, coordination or arrangement of outputs, and in their creative modifications.

The Office also draws a line that fits these projects: assistive uses that enhance human expression do not limit protection, while uses where an AI system makes expressive choices require further analysis.

A court has now taken the next step on the narrow point. On March 18, 2025, the D.C. Circuit held in Thaler v. Perlmutter that the Copyright Act requires eligible work to be authored in the first instance by a human being, so a machine listed as sole author cannot be the recognized author.

The court was careful about the limit of its holding. It said the rule does not prohibit copyrighting work made with the assistance of AI, and that the author must be the person who created, operated or used the AI. It called disagreements over how much AI contributed to a human author's work "neither here nor there" in that case.
The Supreme Court denied review on March 2, 2026.

That leaves the middle ground open, which is where the six projects sit. A U.S. court has said a machine cannot be the author, and the Office has said a human's creative selection and modification can be. How much human control over expressive elements is enough for a made object is not settled by either.

blocks.x: What the European sources say

r: European law has no matching Copyright Office report, but there is a useful document. In December 2024, the Council of the EU published a summary of member states' answers to a questionnaire on generative AI and copyright. It says there was a clear understanding that only a natural person should be considered an author, so purely AI-generated works cannot be protected. It says numerous member states noted that AI-assisted works can obtain protection if they meet the general requirements, and that the general view was that works may be eligible only if the human input in the creative process was significant.

The same document reports that most member states had no relevant case law. Three reported court decisions. In one, a supreme court ruled that the mere use of AI does not automatically disqualify a logo from protection and that each case must be assessed for the extent of human input. In another, a court found an image not eligible because the plaintiff created it by using AI rather than by his own creative activity.

The most relevant European development for objects is a ruling on furniture. On December 4, 2025, the Court of Justice of the EU decided two joined cases about copyright in applied art, one about dining tables and one about a modular furniture system. I have not read the judgment. A Dutch law firm's summary says the Court held that works of applied art are assessed under the same originality criteria as any other work: the object must be its author's own intellectual creation, reflecting the author's personality through free and creative choices. According to the summary, factors such as the creator's intentions or sources of inspiration may be considered but are neither necessary nor decisive, and the focus must stay on the object itself.
The same summary notes that EU design rights, by contrast, require novelty and individual character rather than creativity.

Read together, those points suggest that for a physical object, the European question will be whether a human's free and creative choices can be identified in the thing itself. That is my reading of a secondary source, and it is not a statement about any art-ai-fact piece.

The Copyright Office's survey of other countries adds scattered data points. It reports that Japan's guidance looks at four factors: the amount and content of the user's instructions, the number of generation attempts, the user's selection from the outputs, and later human additions and corrections. It reports that a Beijing court in 2023 treated a person as the author of an image after more than 150 prompts and later adjustments, and that a Czech court in 2024 held that an AI tool cannot be an author. It also notes that a UK statute protects "computer-generated" works and names as author the person who made the arrangements for creation.

I did not open the Finnish or Dutch copyright statutes. Aalto is a Finnish university and the show is in the Netherlands, and I cannot tell from these sources which national law would govern a dispute over any one object.

blocks.x: Why a record of decisions matters

r: Put the sources side by side and a pattern shows. The Office looks at selection, arrangement and modification. Japan's guidance counts instructions, attempts, selection and later changes. The Council's summary and the Thaler court both keep returning to the extent of human input.
Every one of those is a fact about a process, and a process leaves traces only if somebody keeps them.
That is why one detail in Aalto's description of LUCID stands out to me: the system keeps track of how each design evolves.

A tool that records its own history gives a maker something most people working with AI do not have. I do not know what that record contains or whether it was built with authorship in mind, and the university does not say.

My opinion, offered as reasoning and not as a finding: any maker who works with AI on an object should keep a plain log. Which tool produced which proposal. Which proposal was chosen, by whom, and why. What was changed by hand afterward. A log like that cannot decide who the legal author is, and the sources above do not say that any particular log would satisfy any particular court. It can make a later conversation about credit shorter and less heated.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I have not seen the show. I do not know which objects will be on view beyond what Aalto's news item describes, or whether the shipwreck dress at Klokgebouw is the Oulu piece or its twin; the sources I read do not say.

I do not know how the makers credit or contract with the AI tools they use, who holds rights in any object, or whether any piece raised an authorship question during the three years. The pages say nothing on rights, and I did not interview anyone.
I could not open the Court of Justice judgment itself, so the European paragraph relies on one law firm's summary.
I did not read the Finnish or Dutch statutes. The Copyright Office's account of other countries is its own description, which I did not check against the original decisions.
The U.S. sources concern copyright in outputs. They do not address physical objects as such or any art-ai-fact project. This is educational information, not legal advice.

blocks.x: The credit line is a design decision too

r: If you see an object described as made with AI, look at the label before the object. Does it name a person, a team, a company, a tool or all of them? A credit line is a small summary of who decided what, and the Shipwreck Dress shows that one object can carry four of them.
If you were the maker, what would your record of decisions say?
