posts.title: Can a creative sector count the good it does elsewhere?
posts.subtitle: A Dutch Design Week workshop asks cultural organizations to look beyond their own footprint. The idea has a short history, three slightly different definitions in the Dutch program's own documents, and a measurement problem that the published material does not yet solve.
posts.seoTitle: Can a creative sector count its handprint?
posts.description: A Dutch Design Week workshop on the Climate Handprint. Where the idea came from, how the Dutch program defines it, and what is missing.

r: A footprint records what an organization took, and a handprint is meant to record what it left behind for someone else.

The Sustainable Cultural Sector Programme, known in Dutch as Programma Duurzame Cultuursector and coordinated by Kunsten '92, has a workshop on that second idea in the Dutch Design Week program. The listing places it at The Social Hub Eindhoven, Stationsweg 1, on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, from 16:00 to 17:00, with a drop-in session from 16:00 to 19:30. Access is free, with registration.

The subject is the Climate Handprint, which the listing describes as the positive impact that creators, venues and other cultural and creative organizations can have on promoting sustainability in other sectors. The listing says the program is coordinated by Kunsten '92 and made possible by the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science.
Kunsten '92 describes itself as the advocacy organization for the whole cultural and creative sector, with about 430 members.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, the program's website and roadmap, Dutch statistics and planning agency reports, research on handprints and on art and behavior, and commentary on green claims. It reports no visit to the workshop and no conversation with the organizers.

I like seeing an organization ask about its effect on other people's work. Most sustainability reporting I can picture starts and ends at the organization's own door. A handprint question points outward, and I think that is a useful direction for a sector whose main output is not a physical product. It is also a direction where a careless number can do real damage to trust.

blocks.x: The idea came from industry, and it came with rules

r: The version of the handprint that reached industry came through Gregory Norris of the Harvard Center for Health and the Global Environment and a consortium he co-directs called SHINE, according to a 2015 article in Trellis by Asheen Phansey of Dassault Systèmes, one of the consortium's founding members. The article describes a handprint as the credits side of an environmental ledger, set against the debits that a footprint records. It says a company-level handprint minus the footprint, if above zero, would make a company net-positive on that metric.

The same article lays down three rules that matter for culture. First, you must decide what would have happened without your action, which it calls business as usual, because a benefit only exists against that comparison. Second, you must pick the indicators, and it says to use the ones you use for your footprint. Third, when several actors are involved, a distinction applies between enabling a handprint, as a road enables both an electric car and a lumbering SUV, and inducing one, as when you persuade someone to change. Only in the second case, the article says, can you claim the handprint yourself.

Finnish researchers built a more formal version. In December 2018 VTT and LUT University announced a method and guide for the carbon handprint of products, defined by the effect a product has when customers use it to reduce their own footprint, and built on standardized life-cycle assessment.
A second edition of the guide, published by VTT, extends the framework beyond climate to other environmental impacts and discusses organization and project levels.

In 2025 the World Business Council for Sustainable Development issued version 2.0 of its guidance on avoided emissions, which compares a solution with an alternative scenario and adds guidance on defining the reference scenario and validating the contribution, plus optional steps for allocation.

These sources agree on the shape of a careful claim: a baseline, a stated indicator and an honest account of who caused what. They were written for products and companies. A play is not a product that replaces a baseline product, and a visitor who sees it is not a customer whose footprint can be measured against a counterfactual. That mismatch is the core of the problem for culture, and none of these documents solves it.

blocks.x: The program uses three definitions of the idea

r: The listing's definition is about impact on sustainability in other sectors.

The program's FAQ words it differently. Climate-conscious action, it says, is aimed not only at limiting the damage a sector causes, directly or indirectly, but also at using and activating the specific power of the cultural and creative sector to help tackle the climate crisis, and that is what it calls the Climate Handprint.

The roadmap on which the program builds uses a third phrasing: the ecological handprint is the positive influence that arises when visitors, participants and other sectors are prompted to contribute to a sustainable future.

The three versions overlap, and none contains a unit. The listing speaks of impact on other sectors, the FAQ of power and activation, the roadmap of influence on people. They point in the same direction without saying what would count. The roadmap's committed actions deal with buildings, operations, materials and mobility, including sector-wide monitoring of energy and CO2 from operations. The word handprint appears in its text only twice, both times as an aim to grow, and I found no handprint indicator or measurement action.

The program itself has a clear setting. The Routekaart Duurzame Cultuursector, which the program's site hosts as a PDF uploaded in November 2025, cites the Council for Culture's 2023 advice Cultuur Natuurlijk, which urged the sector to speed up and stressed the need for one central knowledge point. The roadmap sets the goal of a climate-neutral and circular sector by 2050 and ties its numbers to the national climate agreement, which it states as 55 percent less CO2 by 2030 and 95 percent less by 2050 compared with 1990.

The national enterprise agency RVO says the initiative for the roadmap came from the sector and the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, and that Kunsten '92 started the program to support implementation.
The program's pages list four work packages: buildings, operations, mobility and the Climate Handprint.
The FAQ adds that the sector is not legally obliged to produce a roadmap.

blocks.x: Why a small emitter would want a handprint

r: A Statistics Netherlands study from June 2025, commissioned by the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, estimates that the media and cultural sector was responsible for about 0.616 megatons of CO2 in 2022, roughly 0.4 percent of the national total of 169 megatons, while contributing about 3.3 percent of gross domestic product and 4.1 percent of labor volume. An alternative method based on employment also stayed under 0.5 percent.

The authors stress that the data needed to measure the sector's environmental impact are not directly available, so the figure is a rough estimate resting on assumptions, and that one broad category of industry adds the most uncertainty.

That is a useful number to hold beside the handprint idea, for two reasons. A sector with a footprint under half a percent would change the national total very little by cutting its own emissions, and I read that as the strongest argument for looking outward. It also shows how hard measurement already is: if the footprint of the sector can only be roughly estimated from other statistics, a handprint of influence on other people's behavior will be harder still.

The wider setting is a climate target that is slipping. The Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency's 2026 climate and energy outlook says it is very unlikely that the national 2030 target of 55 percent emission reduction will be reached, that emissions have not fallen for three years, and that there is a large gap between ambition and policy toward 2040 and 2050.

In a letter posted by the program on September 28, 2026, ahead of a parliamentary debate on climate policy progress, Kunsten '92 asked the government to use the cultural and creative sector as a partner in climate policy, to treat festivals and institutions as test sites for climate solutions, and to give the sector access to funds for circular and low-travel practice.
That is the argument for a handprint in the sector's own words: it can reach people and build support.

blocks.x: What the program's survey asks

r: The program has published some of its working method. On May 6, 2026, its Climate Handprint work package posted a survey for the sector, open until May 31, 2026, to inventory what knowledge exists and what is already being done. It sorts actions into three categories: what an organization communicates about its sustainability plans and measures, what climate-related content appears in its products, such as exhibitions, education or festival programs, theater productions and design, and which partners it works with on climate action and positive change.

That is a sensible first step for mapping a sector, because you cannot assess what you have not found. I also notice what the three categories collect. They collect communication, content and partnerships, which an organization can list. They do not, as published, ask what changed in another sector afterward. The post does not define the handprint or say how results will be used beyond identifying needs and offering practical tools.
The program's home page carries the line together, clear, measurable, which I take as a fair standard to hold a handprint to.

blocks.x: Does art change what people do?

r: A handprint of culture rests on the claim that cultural work moves people. A theater maker and podcast guest summarized on the program's knowledge base argues that the climate crisis is a cultural crisis and that storytellers should take over the relay baton from science.
That is a sector's own thesis, and it is a serious one. The research on whether it holds is thinner than I expected.

A scoping review published in Frontiers in Psychology on December 4, 2025 looked at empirical studies of visual art projects meant to influence pro-environmental behavior, published between 2001 and 2024, and found eight that qualified. Among the art forms covered, which included films, festivals, exhibitions, murals and immersive installations, none was able to directly and significantly affect behavior, although all could affect environmental attitudes or awareness to some degree. The authors report that art appears to act mainly on intentions, attitudes and emotions, and that this role remains minimal without wider social and cultural norms that support it. They recommend mixed methods, longitudinal studies and baseline profiles of participants as better research designs.

That does not say culture has no effect. A review of eight studies is a small base, and visual arts are only part of the sector. It does tell us that a claim that a program led to behavior change in another sector needs more evidence than a count of attendees or an attitude survey.

blocks.x: Three questions for any handprint

r: The three questions I would bring to any handprint claim follow from the sources above.

What changed? A festival can report that its program raised awareness, but attendance and attention are activities. A change is something different afterward, in a budget, a practice, a material or a rule. The business-as-usual rule in the handprint method says the same thing from the other side: without a baseline there is no benefit to count.

Who measured it? A figure from the organization claiming the credit is one kind of evidence. A figure from the party that changed, or from an outside reviewer, is another. The enabling and inducing distinction also belongs here, because the party that made the change can claim it, while the cultural organization can claim a share only when it actually induced the change.

Could someone else check it? A claim that can be repeated from published data is worth more than one that must be taken on faith. WBCSD's second edition asks for reference scenarios, contribution validation and templates for third-party review, which suggests how much documentation a careful claim carries.

A fourth worry belongs beside these. If two organizations each claim the same improvement, the sector's total is inflated. The Trellis article describes multi-actor claims as a problem for the same reason, and WBCSD's guidance lists allocation as one of its steps.
That is reasoning about how counts go wrong, and it applies to any shared credit, not only to this program.

blocks.x: Claims that go public now carry rules

r: From September 27, 2026, new European rules on misleading environmental claims apply under the directive known as Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition. The program's site reprints an article from the Dutch Museums Association explaining that claims must be clear, concrete and substantiated, that the rules are aimed at dealings with consumers and can reach a nonprofit when it carries out commercial activity such as selling tickets, and that stricter requirements apply to claims about climate neutrality and CO2 compensation.

A law firm's summary lists, among the practices that become high risk, claims about a whole product or business when the benefit concerns only one aspect, and generic claims such as green or eco-friendly unless backed by recognized performance or accompanied by the specific benefit.

I am not giving legal advice, and whether the rules reach a given cultural organization's handprint statement depends on facts I do not have. The point I take from it is narrower. A sector that wants to communicate its good in public will do so under a stricter standard than before, and a vague handprint claim is the kind of statement that standard targets.

blocks.x: Why the good still deserves a count

r: I would not respond to those risks by dropping the idea. A sector that reports only its harm has no way to say what it is for. A theater, a museum or a design studio exists to put something into the world, and an honest account of that contribution belongs in public. The roadmap makes a similar point when it says culture can do more than cut its own emissions, because makers and institutions can make change imaginable and move people.

I would want any handprint to sit beside the footprint and not replace it. The handprint method as Norris and his collaborators describe it contemplates subtracting the footprint to reach a net figure.

I am more cautious about that for culture, where the handprint is so much softer than the footprint. A good done in another sector does not reduce the emissions of the building where the work was made. Reporting the two side by side keeps the first from excusing the second, and it makes an organization answer for both. That is my opinion, and the sources I read do not settle it.

blocks.x: What to look for in the examples

r: The listing promises three take-aways: what the Climate Handprint means for your own work, concrete examples of how other creators and organizations put it into practice, and a first step toward contributing to the ecological transition through culture.
The concrete examples are the part I would read most closely. I do not know what they will be, and the listing does not say.

A reader who goes, or who reads the published material afterward, can run each example through the questions above. Note what changed, note who measured it, and note whether the method is open enough for someone else to repeat. Here is a hypothetical, labeled as such: a theater stages a play about household energy, and a year later a housing association in the same city insulates a street of homes. Did the play contribute? It may have. It may also have been one voice among many, or no voice at all, and the business-as-usual question is what the association would have done without the play. An example that answers all three questions is a model. An example that answers one is a story, which can still be worth hearing.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I did not find a published method for measuring a Climate Handprint in the program's documents: not in the listing, the roadmap, the FAQ, the survey post or the workshop's agenda page.

The program may have material that is not yet public, and the workshop may present it. I do not know what examples the workshop will use, how many people can attend, or who will present. I do not know whether results of the May 2026 survey have been published.
The three definitions are compatible without being identical, and I cannot tell from the sources which one the workshop will use.
I also cannot say whether the green-claims rules reach a given handprint statement.
Finally, the evidence I found on art and behavior covers visual arts and eight studies. It does not cover theater, music, design or festivals as a group.

blocks.x: The question to take with you

r: If your own work did some good inside someone else's sector, what is the first thing you would need to see before you believed it?

posts.title: What changes when the window is also the power source?
posts.subtitle: Teresa van Dongen's Between Lights puts energy harvesting where people look. The published numbers on see-through solar cells show what that costs, and what the listing leaves open.
posts.seoTitle: When the window is also the power source
posts.description: Between Lights at Dutch Design Week puts organic solar in a window. What the published see-through solar numbers say, and what the listing leaves open.

r: Solar panels usually sit on the roof, where nobody has to look at them.

Between Lights, by the designer Teresa van Dongen, puts the technology in the window instead. It is in the Dutch Design Week program at Klokgebouw, building B4 on Strijp-S in Eindhoven, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00, October 17 to 25, 2026, with a DDW ticket. The listing classes it as an exhibition.

Its published account says the project combines organic photovoltaics, known as OPV, with printed electronics, and that its translucent surface collects energy from sunlight and from indoor light. During the day the surfaces harvest light, and as daylight fades the collected energy powers embedded LEDs, which turn the panels into a soft, atmospheric light source. The listing's subtitle calls the project a quiet exploration of how light can live twice.

This essay draws on public documents only: the listing, the Dutch Design Awards record of the designer, and published research and reports on see-through solar cells. It reports no visit and no conversation with the designer. The listing's lead image is captioned as the work visualized in an everyday setting, so I treat it as an illustration and not as a photograph of the installation.

Dutch Design Week's 2026 theme is R.A.W., which its September 29, 2026 release describes as design that is unpolished, investigative and experimental, with a focus on experimentation and material research.
The release does not name this project, so I read the theme as context and not as a description of the work.
I want to take the idea seriously by asking what a window is for, because that question decides what the project can and cannot promise.

blocks.x: The designer's earlier work asks the same kind of question

r: Teresa van Dongen graduated with distinction from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2014. Her graduation lamp, Ambio, was described as a living lamp, and in 2015 she won the Dutch Design Awards Young Designer category. The jury wrote that she translates research into aesthetic products with a concrete purpose and often addresses topical issues such as energy consumption, and noted her collaborations with Delft University of Technology and the National Glass Museum.
That record fits what the Between Lights listing says about her practice, which combines design research, material experimentation and collaboration with scientists.

The idea of a window that collects light also has a Dutch Design Week history. In 2015 the designer Marjan van Aubel showed Current Window at Strijp-S, a contemporary adaptation of stained glass made from dye-sensitized solar cells, with a USB port in the window ledge. Its description says the glass uses the properties of color to create an electrical current, much like photosynthesis in plants.

That is a different cell technology from OPV. It is useful as context because it shows that the window as a power source has been argued in design before, and that its makers also reach for photosynthesis as an image.

blocks.x: A window already has a job, and the physics charges for it

r: A window lets light in so people can see, and it lets people look out. A harvesting window adds a third job, and the jobs compete. The research is direct about this. A UNSW article from 2018 explains that for a window there is a trade-off between absorbing light to turn into electricity and transmitting light so we can see through it, that an average visible transmittance of 25 percent is generally considered a benchmark for solar windows, and that passing a quarter of the light makes it hard to generate much current.

A 2020 paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences from the University of Michigan group puts numbers on the trade. Their color-neutral semitransparent OPV reached a power conversion efficiency of 8.1 percent with an average photopic transmission of 43.3 percent, which multiplies out to a light utilization efficiency of 3.5 percent. A slightly green-tinted version reached 10.8 percent efficiency at 45.7 percent transmission, for 5.0 percent.

The authors note that efficiencies of semitransparent OPV had hovered around 7 percent for several years, which they call too low for substantial market penetration, and that the most efficient devices tend to show an unwanted tint.

Three things follow for a design project. First, a see-through cell is a compromise by construction, and the look of the thing is part of the performance. The Between Lights listing says as much when it says the project explores what solar technology can look and feel like through color, form and transparency.
Second, tint is an unavoidable design question, which the UNSW authors also describe in terms of how accurately colors are rendered through the glass.
Third, the best published numbers come from small laboratory devices, and the UNSW authors say transparent electrodes can be brittle and contain rare elements such as indium.
The Between Lights listing gives none of these figures for its own panels.

blocks.x: What organic photovoltaics buy, and what they cost

r: The U.S. Department of Energy describes OPV as promising for building-integrated solar because various absorbers can create colored or transparent devices, with low-cost, roll-to-roll manufacturing and flexible substrates among the benefits. The same page lists efficiency limits and long-term reliability as significant barriers and says the operating lifetime of OPV modules remains significantly lower than for inorganic devices.

The page also says OPV had reached efficiencies near 11 percent. It is undated, and I could not confirm how current that figure is, so I cite the page for the qualitative picture and not for the number.

On lifetime, the Michigan paper adds a figure that matters for a window, which people expect to last for decades. The authors write that the most stable of the nonfullerene devices they cite degrade to 80 percent of their initial efficiency within only a few years, by extrapolation, which they identify as a barrier to commercialization.
I read that as the strongest reason to hold any OPV window to a modest claim. The listing gives no lifetime figure.

The first commercial OPV product shows both the promise and where the window fits. Heliatek, a German company, describes its HeliaSol film as the only commercially available, IEC-certified organic solar product. The film is less than 2 millimeters thick, weighs under 2 kilograms per sheet, carries an adhesive back so it can be stuck onto roofs, facades and other surfaces, and is certified under IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 and under UL 61730. The company advertises a 20-year certified performance guarantee.
Those are the maker's claims, and I have not seen independent test data. The product pages I read describe a film for roofs and facades and do not describe a see-through window product.

That sits beside the Michigan authors' lifetime warning without contradicting it, because the devices differ: the warning concerns semitransparent nonfullerene cells, and the guarantee concerns the company's own film. I found no independent lifetime data for either one in a window.

OPV also has a local connection that is easy to miss. A 2011 announcement describes Solliance, a thin-film solar research cluster at facilities in Eindhoven, as working on organic photovoltaics, transparent conductive layers and roll-to-roll processing.
I cannot tell from the listing whether Between Lights has any link to that research environment, and I do not suggest one.

blocks.x: Sunlight, indoor light and the night glow

r: One detail in the listing that I did not expect: the surface collects energy from indoor light as well as sunlight.

Indoor light is a real research field for OPV. A 2021 review in Nano Energy reports that indoor OPV has reached power conversion efficiencies above 30 percent, with an output power of 150 microwatts per square centimeter under artificial light, and says that is enough to drive many low-power indoor applications such as sensors, remote controls and watches.
The review does not say at what illuminance that figure was measured, so I treat it as a best case.

Here is a worked example, labeled as hypothetical arithmetic. 150 microwatts per square centimeter is 1.5 watts per square meter. A square meter delivering exactly that for eight hours would collect 12 watt-hours. A lamp that draws 3 watts, an arbitrary number I chose, would use up 12 watt-hours in four hours. So indoor light alone could in principle carry a modest glow, and a plain window in a dim room would carry far less. The point is that the answer depends on window area, light level and LED draw, and the listing gives none of them.
The listing does say how the two states connect: the collected energy powers the embedded LEDs.

That settles a question I would otherwise have asked, whether the night light is borrowed from the grid. What it does not say is how much energy is stored, in what, or for how long the LEDs run. The introduction to the project says it imagines a future in which collecting and storing energy becomes part of our surroundings, so storage is part of the idea, but the hardware is not described.
Those remain the numbers I would ask for.

blocks.x: A window does not face the sun the way a roof does

r: Orientation matters before transparency does. A 2019 report from Hanze University of Applied Sciences in Groningen found that a vertical south-facing panel produces about 70 percent of the electricity per year that a panel tilted at 35 degrees produces in the Netherlands, though its output is spread more evenly through the year, which suits electricity use better and loads the grid less.

That figure is for a south-facing panel. A window faces whatever way the building faces, and other orientations would presumably do worse. So even in the best case a harvesting window starts with about 30 percent less yield than a tilted roof panel of the same efficiency, and then gives up more to transparency.

That does not make the project pointless. It tells me what kind of project it is. A window is a poor place to maximize energy and a good place to be seen. The listing says as much when it describes making a normally invisible process of energy generation perceptible through transparency, printed electronics and color, and exploring how energy generation can move closer to people, not as hidden infrastructure but as an autonomous system that becomes part of a spatial experience.
I read Between Lights as an argument made with an object, and I judge it by the questions it raises more than by kilowatt-hours. That is my reading, not a claim by the designer.

blocks.x: Making power visible

r: Most energy infrastructure is hidden by design. The wires, panels and meters sit where they do not trouble anyone, which is convenient, and it also means few people have a feel for where their power comes from.

Imagine, as a hypothetical, a household whose living-room window is also its collector. Would the occupants notice the weather differently? Would a gray week feel like a shortfall instead of just gray? I do not know, and the published account does not say. It is a question the object raises, and a design exhibit is a reasonable place to raise it. The listing describes the object as changing with its surroundings, from a transparent surface in daylight to a glowing presence at night.

There is a cost to that visibility as well. A window is a feature people choose for the view, and a tinted or patterned surface changes the view. The research says tint and color rendering are real constraints for see-through cells.
What I would like to learn is how a person who does not care about energy feels about it on an ordinary morning.

blocks.x: What a leaf can and cannot teach a window

r: The listing's inspiration is photosynthesis, where, as it puts it, energy is part of a living cycle.

The comparison with efficiency is humbling. A 2011 review in Science, reported in a release from the U.S. National Renewable Energy Laboratory, put the annually averaged efficiency of photovoltaic electrolysis based on silicon at about 10 percent, against about 1 or 2 percent for a plant using photosynthesis to form biomass. The release says plants are less efficient mostly because they have to power a living thing, and photosynthesis must stay conservative because mistakes make toxic byproducts that kill the organism.

I take two things from that. A leaf is not optimizing for kilowatts, and a window that takes a leaf as its model is not obliged to either. The other is that a leaf repairs and renews itself while a window does not, which is why the lifetime numbers matter more for a window than for a plant.

The second point is my reasoning, not the release's. Van Aubel's earlier window used the same image, and I treat the comparison as an inspiration the designer names, not as a claim that the window works like a leaf.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: The listing does not tell us how much energy the panels produce, how much is stored and in what, how long the LEDs run, what window area the figures would refer to, how transparent the panels are or how long they are expected to last.
It does not say who built the cells or the electronics, and the text I read under its partners heading names no one.
Its mention of indoor light is a single sentence.
I also cannot tell whether the exhibit is a working prototype or a visualization. The listing's image is captioned as visualized, and the text uses the word application and the phrase explores.
The designer's own website was not available to me because its robots.txt disallows automated reading, so I did not use it.

The research I cite concerns laboratory devices. The 2020 paper reports small cells under simulated sunlight, and the indoor review covers small cells under artificial light. None of the sources I opened tests a window like this one.

blocks.x: The questions to take with you

r: If you plan to see it, take five questions: how much it captures, how much it stores, where the night light comes from, how long it lasts, and what the view looks like through it. And if you live with a window you love, would you trade some of that clarity for a share of your own power?
